achad-egyptian-revival-1923:
Achad turned his new key on Egypt and the tarot in his second major book of 1923. The Egyptian Revival reads the ever-coming son, a figure of the new age, in the light of the cards. Charles Stansfeld Jones writes here as Frater Achad, Crowley's breakaway student.

Egyptian gods and signs are matched to the tarot trumps by his revised scheme of the Tree. The son who ever comes stands for the god of each new age, crowned and conquering. The book carries the project of Q B L into myth and image. It is the middle panel of his Kabbalah trilogy.
aeneas-tacticus-asclepiodotus-onasander-:
A 1923 Loeb volume binds three Greek works on military science together. The Illinois Greek Club translated Aeneas Tacticus, Asclepiodotus, and Onasander into English. Greek text faces the translation in the Loeb manner throughout.

Aeneas, writing around 350 BCE, teaches how to hold a city under siege. Passwords, gates, signals, and spies fill his practical chapters. Asclepiodotus offers a drill book of formations and commands for infantry. Onasander advises generals on character, strategy, and choosing the moment of battle. Together the three founded the literature of ancient military technology. Officers and historians still read them for Greek warfare's working details.
akeley-in-brightest-africa-1923:
Carl Akeley went to Africa to kill gorillas for museums and stayed to save them. In Brightest Africa, printed in 1923, is his classic of the hunt and the wild. Akeley was the great taxidermist of his age and a sculptor of animal groups.

He tells of elephants, lions, and the mountain gorillas of the high volcanoes. His gorilla work showed the beast as shy and grand, not the fiend of old tales. The book helped turn hunters into guards of the great ape in time. Akeley's prose is as clean and bright as his museum glass.
anderson-constitutions-1723:
James Anderson wrote The Constitutions of the Free-Masons in 1723. The Grand Lodge of England had been formed six years past. Anderson gave the new body its laws and its tale of the past. The book is the root text of the craft as a world guild.

A long tale traces Masonry from Adam through kings and saints to London. The Charges then lay down the faith, morals, and peace each Mason owes. Rules for lodges, ranks, and meets fill the last part. The book fixed the shape of the craft for the age to come.
anderson-horses-men-1923:
Horses and Men, published in 1923, gathers Anderson's later stories of the American Midwest. Horses run through the book as measures of human worth: creatures of grace beside men cramped by money, shame, or longing.

'The Man Who Became a Woman' tells of a young horse-hand's frightening, tender awakening at a county fair. Other stories follow grooms, trainers, and small-town dreamers in Anderson's halting, musical prose. The racing world gave him some of his finest material. The collection confirms his gift for lives that official America overlooked, told from inside their own confusion and hope.
anderson-many-marriages-1923:
Sherwood Anderson published Many Marriages in 1923, the most outspoken of his novels. Anderson had been through divorces of his own and wrote obsessively about the gap between respectable marriage and inner desire. The book shocked some readers and was banned in places for its frankness.

John Webster, a washing-machine manufacturer in a Wisconsin town, walks through his house at midnight and confesses everything to his daughter. He tells her of his dead wife, his erotic discontent, and his plan to begin life again with his secretary. The confession takes the whole novel, part sermon and part breakdown. Anderson's plain, groping style tries to say what his characters cannot. Many Marriages remains his most daring treatment of marriage.
arxiv-2510-00023:
Le and colleagues introduce ToolBrain, a new lightweight framework for training language model agents to use tools well through flexible reinforcement learning. Instead of relying on prompting or one-off fine-tuning. Its Coach-Athlete design lets users define custom reward functions directly on an agent's execution traces, or fall back on a ranking-based LLM-as-judge. And it supports GRPO, DPO, and supervised training within one simple codebase for researchers.

Practical features include knowledge distillation from large to small models, automatic task generation from tool descriptions alone, tool retrieval for large tool libraries, and efficient QLoRA fine-tuning with quantized inference. In the central case study, a CodeAct agent trained to run email search tasks improved its tool-use performance by up to 30.0 percent over its starting baseline, showing fast, targeted gains while the framework stays publicly available and extensible for developers.
arxiv-2510-00123:
Niko Jokela and four colleagues wrote this 2025 theory paper on defects inside a strongly coupled quantum field theory. Their setting is the famous N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, pictured through branes in string theory. A flat defect splits the theory, and the authors track entanglement across a ball around it. They use holography, which turns hard field theory sums into gravity calculations.

Adding a mass on the defect starts a renormalization group flow, a slide toward simpler low-energy physics. Along that flow, the authors compute an entanglement-based C-function in closed form. The function decreases steadily, as a count of active degrees of freedom should. A second setup, an interface between two gauge groups, also shows steady decrease. There the reading as a degree count is murkier, so the authors weigh other candidate measures.
arxiv-2510-00423:
Thomas Zdyrski, Scott Pauls, and Feng Fu published this 2025 paper on why brain-like networks settle into half-synchronized states. In a chimera state, some neurons fire in lockstep while others drift incoherently. Classic oscillator models show such states exist but not why neurons would choose them. The authors let phases and communication strategies evolve together under game-like payoffs.

Their network is directed and weighted, and one-way communication can make payoffs asymmetric. Both connection weights and direction shape which strategies stay stable over time. Applied to the roundworm C. elegans connectome, the framework reproduces chimera formation in the real wiring. The payoff structure that emerges resembles the snowdrift game from evolutionary game theory. In that game, partial cooperation is the stable outcome, matching the partial synchrony observed. The work offers a neurogame-theoretic lens on coordination in neural populations.
arxiv-2510-00523:
Wei-Yao Wang and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on embedding models that accept pictures as instructions, not just words. Embedding models map text and images into shared vectors for search and matching. Users often care about one object in a scene, which plain text cannot pinpoint. Their model, VIRTUE, lets users point with a dot, box, or mask instead.

A segmentation model reads the visual prompt and steers the embedder toward that region. Global scene context and entity-level detail then blend into one representation. To test the skill, the team built a million-sample benchmark of segmentation paired with scene captions. VIRTUE set state-of-the-art scores across thirty-six standard embedding tasks. On the new visual-interaction benchmark, gains ran from about fifteen to twenty percent. The authors see pointing as a natural next channel for human-AI retrieval.
arxiv-2510-00823:
Gruntkowska and Richtárik extend the Broximal Point Method to non-Euclidean geometry in this 2025 arXiv note on optimization theory. The original method repeatedly minimizes the objective exactly over a norm ball around the current point, and it enjoys striking finite-step and linear convergence guarantees for convex problems. Its analysis, though, assumed ordinary Euclidean distance. New deep learning optimizers such as Muon and Scion suggest other geometries fit real loss landscapes better.

The authors ask which guarantees survive when the balls use an arbitrary norm, and they answer mostly yes. Most of the elegant convergence results carry over, while a few provably break down outside the Euclidean setting. They frame the generalized method as a blueprint that explains why geometry-aware optimizers work in practice. Stochastic gradients, momentum, and non-convexity are left for future work.
arxiv-2510-00923:
Kamieneski and twenty-three co-authors forecast how often gravitationally lensed supernovae will be found in dusty starburst galaxies, in this 2025 arXiv paper on time-delay cosmography. Lensed supernovae can measure the universe's expansion rate, yet fewer than ten are known after six decades. The authors target the PASSAGES sample, about thirty hyperluminous infrared galaxies with extreme star formation rates. Such starbursts are supernova factories, and lensing magnifies their explosions into view.

From lens-corrected star formation rates they estimate intrinsic core-collapse rates of roughly two to sixty-five per galaxy per year, plus up to several Type Ia events. Einstein radius correlates strongly with time delay, and cluster lenses give delays of months, ideal for precise expansion measurements. Dust is the catch: a sensitive infrared monitoring campaign, ideally with JWST, is needed to see through it. The sample already delivered the multiply imaged supernova H0pe.
arxiv-2510-01023:
Satsevich and six co-authors present Prometheus in this 2025 arXiv paper, an open-source teleoperation system with force feedback for collecting robot learning data. Imitation learning needs many demonstrations, and motion-capture teleoperation supplies them, but operators cannot feel how hard the robot grips. Excess force deforms or damages objects and poisons training data. Prometheus pairs HTC Vive trackers with a custom haptic controller, a UR3 arm, and a Robotiq gripper fitted with fingers.

Force sensors in the gripper stream compression readings to the controller in real time, so operators feel the squeeze they apply. Experiments showed the feedback cutting gripping force by thirty-six percent. Success rates when training vision-language-action models rose as high as ninety percent on fragile objects. Every part of the stack is open source: hardware designs, circuit boards, firmware, and guides. The authors target labs that need demonstration datasets without budgets.
arxiv-2510-01123:
Madaan and eight co-authors rethink how language models spend their thinking tokens in this 2025 arXiv paper. Long chains of thought raise accuracy on hard problems, but they inflate context length, cost, and answer latency. The authors view a model as an improvement operator acting on its own drafts, with a range of strategies between one long pass and many short refinements. Their Parallel-Distill-Refine method generates diverse drafts in parallel and distills them into a bounded textual workspace, and refines from there.

That loop beat long chain-of-thought accuracy at lower latency in their tests, because context length is controlled by the degree of parallelism. Training an eight-billion-parameter model with reinforcement learning to suit the method pushed gains further. On AIME 2024 and 2025 maths contests, iterative pipelines improved over single-pass baselines by about eleven and nine points at matched sequential budgets.
arxiv-2510-01423:
Idoko and a large collaboration extend the known energy levels of gallium-69 to high spin and watch collective behavior switch on. Nuclei near mass seventy balance single-particle motion against whole-nucleus rotation, especially near a subshell closure. How deformed this odd gallium isotope becomes at high spin was unsettled.

Extended level schemes and new gamma-ray observations supply the evidence base. A possible signature partner band appears among the new structures. Angular momentum alignment traces two neutrons settling into a shape-driving orbital. Quasicollective structures emerge exactly where the intruder orbitals take hold. Gamma-ray spectroscopy is the instrument that reads spinning nuclei. The N equals forty subshell closure frames the whole investigation. Single-particle excitations evolve measurably as spin climbs. Proton intruders share credit with the neutron pair for deformation. Odd-mass systems expose structure that even-even nuclei hide. Spin is the dial the experiment turns.
arxiv-2510-01923:
Han, Park, and Choi speed up adiabatic quantum state preparation without knowing the spectrum in advance in this 2025 paper. Adiabatic methods steer a quantum system slowly along a path of eigenstates. The runtime is governed by the smallest energy gap along that path. Generic schedules scale with the inverse gap squared, although theory allows one power less.

Their constant speed schedule moves the system along the eigenstate path at a uniform rate. That uniformity alone cuts the runtime bound by one order in the inverse gap. A segmented version computes each stretch from eigenstate overlaps measured on the fly. No prior knowledge of the spectrum is needed at any point. Numerical tests covered adiabatic search, the nitrogen molecule, and an iron-sulfur cluster. In small-gap regions the method hit the optimal scaling, a quadratic gain over linear schedules.
arxiv-2510-02123:
Wang and six co-authors tackle interaction effects in conjoint survey experiments in this 2025 methods paper. Conjoint designs let political scientists vary many attributes at once and read off preferences. Researchers increasingly want subgroup and context effects, not just averages. Low statistical power makes those interactions treacherous to estimate.

The authors systematically benchmark the leading toolkits across many simulation regimes. Post-hoc corrections, sparse regression methods, and Bayesian models each faced varied sparsity, noise, and sample sizes. Alongside the audit, they propose a black-box inference framework built on machine learning. It recovers both main and interaction effects from conjoint data. The framework balances computational efficiency with estimation accuracy. Their guidance tells researchers when each classical approach can be trusted. The new tool gives a practical route for heterogeneous-effect studies that surveys can actually power. Subgroup claims in published conjoint work stand on firmer ground as a result.
arxiv-2510-02323:
Hwang and co-authors split storage traffic live between a fast cache and remote disks. Their 2025 systems paper presents a framework called NetCAS. Classic caching serves reads from the cache only on hits. Modern devices, though, have narrowed the speed gap. Using both devices at once can beat cache alone. Remote backends suffer network congestion that shifts by the minute. NetCAS watches real network feedback as it runs. A precomputed performance profile guides each split choice. A batched round-robin scheduler enforces the split cheaply.

Tests showed gains up to about one hundred seventy four percent over classic caching. NetCAS also beat a converging rival scheme by up to three and a half fold. The lead held while network conditions fluctuated. Disaggregated storage is now common in data centers. Steering requests toward the momentary best device is the lesson.
arxiv-2510-02423:
Wu and co-authors rebuild a benchmark that tests whether models understand film craft. Their 2025 paper refines ShotBench into a new suite called RefineShot. Cinematography covers camera choices that shape story meaning. A model may name objects yet miss those choices entirely. The leading benchmark had ambiguous answer options. Its top model, ShotVL, also reasoned inconsistently and ignored instructions. The team restructured options for consistent size and clean separation. They added a protocol that scores core skills beside task accuracy. Reasoning, prompt adherence, and output consistency now count openly.

Deep analysis of ShotVL exposed overfitting to dataset quirks. High scores had hidden weak general reasoning. RefineShot makes such gaps visible by design. Fair comparison between models becomes possible again. Film and media tools need models that grasp intent, not just content. A stricter benchmark pushes builders toward that goal.
arxiv-2510-02823:
Chahine and co-authors study state space models, a fast family of sequence models. These models keep a hidden state that updates as data flows in. A bigger state can express more, but it costs more to run. The team asks whether a model can start big and shrink while it trains. Their method is called CompreSSM. It borrows a classic tool from control theory called balanced truncation.

The tool ranks each state dimension by its influence. The ranking uses values drawn from a Hankel matrix. Dimensions with low influence are cut during training. The rest keep learning without a restart. Tests used linear recurrent units on tasks of varied difficulty. Shrunken models beat models trained small from the start. They also trained faster per unit of progress. The authors sketch how the idea may extend to selective models like Mamba.
arxiv-2510-03023:
The H.E.S.S. Collaboration hunts dark matter around mid-size black holes. Such black holes weigh from a hundred to a million suns. Theory says dense dark matter spikes should hug them tightly. Particles in a spike could annihilate and flash gamma rays. The team searched survey data for that kind of glow. Sources included the galactic plane, deep sky fields, and dwarf galaxies. The archive held about sixty-two hundred hours of viewing.

No point-like signal with the right spectral shape appeared. The team therefore set upper limits on the annihilation rate. Limits cover particle masses from under one to one hundred tera-electronvolts. For the heaviest band, the limits dip below the classic thermal relic value. That band runs from ten to one hundred tera-electronvolts. The null result still narrows where dark matter can hide.
arxiv-2510-03223:
Zhang, Tian, and Zhang keep a reasoning model's attention anchored to its own key steps. Long reasoning chains bury the original question and early steps. Attention drifts, and errors creep into later steps. Prompting tricks avoid retraining but suffer that drift. Self-Anchor breaks the chain into a structured plan first. It then aligns attention to the most relevant steps automatically. Focus returns to the steps that matter at each moment.

Six benchmarks tested the pipeline against rival prompts. Self-Anchor beat the state-of-the-art prompting methods overall. The gains held across varied reasoning task types. Ordinary models closed much of their gap to specialist reasoners. No weights changed and no training data was needed. Any capable model can adopt the scheme at inference time. That makes the method cheap to bolt onto existing systems. Complex problem solving gets more reliable without new models.
arxiv-2510-04023:
Rahman and colleagues present this 2025 survey paper on AI agents that automate data science work. These agents plan, call tools, and reason across text, code, tables, and charts to carry out whole analyses. The field has grown fast and fragmented, with dozens of systems claiming overlapping abilities. The authors map forty-five of them onto the six stages of the data science lifecycle.

Each system is also scored on five design dimensions, from planning style to safety mechanisms. Most agents cluster on the middle stages: exploring data, visualizing it, and building models. The opening stage of understanding the business problem and the closing stages of deployment and monitoring get far less attention. Most strikingly, over ninety percent of systems lack explicit trust and safety mechanisms. The survey closes with directions for building agents that are more transparent, governable, and broadly accessible.
arxiv-2510-04123:
Chen and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on numerical schemes that keep simulations of Temple-class flow systems physically valid. These systems model two-phase flow, elasticity, traffic, and sedimentation through related conservation equations. Their solutions must stay inside an invariant region, which here is non-convex, and careless schemes produce non-physical values. A moving mesh adds further difficulty to preserving those bounds.

The authors design bound-preserving finite difference WENO schemes tailored to non-convex admissible sets. A parameterized flux limiter restrains high-order fluxes near trouble spots, applied to non-convex sets for the first time. Numerical experiments confirm the schemes stay robust and respect the bounds. The framework covers general Temple-class systems rather than one equation. It can be specialized to Aw-Rascle-Zhang traffic flow networks. Keeping simulated quantities physical is what separates a plausible traffic or sedimentation forecast from numerical garbage.
arxiv-2510-04823:
Hadzic, Joham, and Urschler wrote this 2025 paper on creating CT scans from other scans with flow matching. Therapy planning needs CT data for dose calculation. But CT adds dose, and many treatment rooms have MRI or cone beam scanners instead. A synthetic CT built from those scans would enable adaptive treatment. The authors use a three dimensional flow matching model for the conversion.

The model starts from a volume of noise. It follows a velocity field that sculpts the noise into a CT image. Features from the input scan, extracted by an encoder, guide the sculpting. Models handled MRI inputs and cone beam inputs across three body regions. Judgment came through a challenge with more than two thousand cases. The method rebuilt anatomy in their results. Fine detail lagged, because memory limits forced training resolution. The authors plan patch training and latent space flows to sharpen detail.
arxiv-2510-04923:
Alec K. Peltekian and colleagues at Northwestern University present REN, a system for diagnosing interstitial lung disease from chest scans, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Interstitial lung diseases scar the lung tissue and can be hard to tell apart. REN is built to respect lung anatomy instead of treating a scan as one flat picture.

The system splits the lungs into regions and assigns expert models to each one. Some experts use deep learning, while others use radiomics, which measures texture and shape. A learned gate weighs the experts region by region. In tests, the radiomics-guided ensemble reached an average AUC near 0.90 in the lower lobes, beating clinical benchmarks. Its gating weights also show which regions drove each call, which aids review.
arxiv-2510-05223:
James W. Johnson tests whether gas flowing inward can explain the Milky Way's strange chemical history in this 2025 arXiv paper. Stars of very different ages show almost the same metallicity across the disk. That flat pattern surprises modelers, who expect steady enrichment over time. Johnson runs chemical evolution models with five different radial flow prescriptions.

Every flow model steepens metallicity gradients and lowers overall metallicity compared with static models. Flows also tilt the age pattern in opposite directions in the inner and outer disk. That tilt clashes with the observed flatness at most radii. A constant inflow near one kilometer per second can match the data beyond six kiloparsecs. Johnson instead favors an early chemical equilibrium, set by mixing, star formation, and fresh accretion rates.
arxiv-2510-05723:
Gracey squeezes critical exponents for two classic problems from six-loop field theory. Lee-Yang theory and percolation both reduce to a scalar theory with cubic interaction. Schnetz recently computed its renormalization group functions to six loops. Gracey's 2025 paper turns those functions into exponent estimates.

The epsilon expansion expresses each exponent as a series around six dimensions. Two-sided Padé approximants then resum the series at lower dimensions. Gracey extracts values for three, four, and five dimensions. The new estimates sit close to the lower-loop ones, suggesting convergence. Weighted approximants even improve uncertainties in a few cases. Lee-Yang exponents also feed QCD studies of the equation of state and baryon number. Percolation exponents govern how connected clusters grow near their threshold. All values agree with Monte Carlo, bootstrap, and other independent approaches. Six-loop precision narrows the error bars for both physics problems.
arxiv-2510-05823:
Moriya defines mutual entropy for infinitely extended quantum lattice systems. Finite systems enjoy a thermal area law bounding correlations across surfaces. Extending that law to infinite spin and fermion lattices needs algebraic machinery. His 2025 paper builds the definition inside the C-star algebraic framework.

The proof rests on local thermodynamical stability, a variational principle. Conditional free energy on local subsystems drives the argument. The resulting area law covers general interactions with well-defined surface energies. The definition avoids Tomita-Takesaki theory and also covers ground states. Deriving the law from stability rather than equilibrium conditions broadens its reach. In one dimension, left and right half-chains share finite mutual entropy at any temperature. That holds for all translation-invariant finite-range interactions. Even a small positive temperature suppresses the critical entanglement drastically. Heat thus destroys the huge entanglement of critical ground states.
arxiv-2510-05923:
Singh and colleagues co-design a one-legged jumping robot for height and efficiency together. A monoped's jump depends jointly on mechanical design and control strategy. Prior frameworks optimize one objective and oversimplify actuator mass. Their 2025 three-stage framework optimizes design and control in one loop.

Realistic actuator mass models replace the usual crude approximations. Gearbox parameters, gear ratios, and link lengths are optimized alongside control. Planetary gearbox internals, long omitted, finally enter the optimization. The optimized design jumps to zero point eight meters. Mechanical energy consumption falls by half versus the baseline design. Height and energy trade off, and the framework respects both explicitly. Outputs feed an automatically generated parameterized CAD model for fabrication. That automation cuts manual design iterations between concept and hardware. Multi-legged systems are the planned extension of the approach.
arxiv-2510-06123:
Ma, Stathaki, and Lazarou present a way to stretch scarce medical image labels in a 2025 paper. Deep learning for medical imaging stalls when annotated scans are few and disease classes are badly imbalanced. Privacy rules, annotation cost, and rare conditions all keep datasets small.

Their framework, SSGNet, wraps around existing baseline models instead of replacing them. Class-specific StyleGAN3 generators synthesize extra training images, especially for underrepresented conditions. An iterative pseudo-labeling loop then assigns labels to unlabeled images and refines them over rounds. Across several medical imaging benchmarks, the augmented training improved both classification and segmentation accuracy. A Fréchet Inception Distance analysis confirmed that the generated samples were high quality. The authors release the code publicly. For clinics and research groups that cannot buy more annotations, SSGNet offers a practical route to stronger, less biased models.
arxiv-2510-06423:
Hennessey, Kermorgant, and Zhu compute mod-5 Galois images for abelian surfaces in a 2025 number theory paper. Each abelian surface carries Galois representations on its torsion points. The mod-ell representation is typically surjective onto its full symplectic group. A smaller image signals extra arithmetic structure.

Probabilistic tests already decide surjectivity, and earlier work computed images for primes two and three. Prime five resisted systematic treatment until now. The authors probabilistically compute mod-5 images for Jacobians of genus-two curves in the LMFDB. Their computation covers ninety-five percent of curves with previously unknown images. For the remainder, they determine the image's order exactly. They supply a short candidate list for each holdout. The results extend the arithmetic record for thousands of curves. Number theorists gain mod-5 data feeding conjectures on Sato-Tate distributions and rational points.
arxiv-2510-06523:
Kevin Smith works in analytic number theory, the branch of mathematics that uses calculus to study whole numbers. His 2025 paper studies Dirichlet series, which are sums built from number sequences. He treats these series as linear maps on a space of meromorphic functions, a class of functions with isolated poles. The main question is how a series behaves at the edge of the region where it converges.

Smith links the jumps of a series on that boundary line to the poles and zeros of the functions behind it. He then applies a theorem of Delange to a classic counting problem. The result shows that the expected growth formula for the additive divisor problem holds, provided certain functions never vanish on the imaginary axis. That turns a hard counting claim into a clear condition that other researchers can test.
arxiv-2510-06723:
Alexander Falk, Andreas Habring, Christoph Griesbacher, and Thomas Pock speed up a workhorse sampling method. Their 2025 paper improves the Langevin algorithm, which draws samples from probability distributions. Sampling underlies Bayesian inference, image cleaning, and training energy-based models. The basic algorithm moves slowly when the target distribution is awkward.

Their method adds inertia, borrowing Polyak's heavy ball idea from optimization. A matching rescaling of the noise keeps the target distribution correct. The scheme matches a continuous process called kinetic Langevin dynamics. The authors prove it settles to the right distribution in both continuous and discrete time. They also bound its bias in a standard distance measure. Their proofs allow smaller friction settings than earlier work allowed. Numerical tests span toy examples, image denoising with total variation, and learning a model of molecular structures. Faster mixing in the proofs matched the gains seen in practice.
arxiv-2510-06923:
Giulio Malavolta, a single author, extends a famous cryptography result into the quantum world. The 2025 paper concerns zero-knowledge proofs, which convince a verifier without leaking the secret behind a claim. Classically, everything provable can be proven in zero knowledge. The twist here is that the problem instance itself is a quantum state.

Such problems arise when the statement concerns physical quantum data. Malavolta shows that any quantum problem with an interactive proof also has a zero-knowledge one. The protocol keeps unconditional soundness and computational secrecy under standard cryptographic assumptions. The same techniques handle the Uhlmann transformation problem, a core task about converting between quantum states. That protocol stays meaningful even against a cheating verifier. A boundary appears for mixed states, where a similar class seems unlikely to admit such protocols. The result settles what zero knowledge can mean when evidence is quantum.
arxiv-2510-07023:
Adam Gammon-Smith, Michael Knap, and Frank Pollmann review efforts to create exotic quantum states on today's quantum processors. Their 2025 perspective covers topological order, a phase of matter defined by nonlocal entanglement. Such states host fractionalized excitations called anyons. They also promise a platform for quantum error correction, which draws intense interest.

Unlike ordinary phases, topological order has no local marker to measure. Long string-like operators serve as the fingerprints instead. The review surveys recent experiments realizing these states on digital processors. It weighs what the demonstrations prove and what they leave open. Scaling to more qubits while preserving fidelity remains the key challenge. Noise threatens the very invariants that define the phase. Better error mitigation and smarter circuit designs are both needed, the authors argue. Protected gate implementations will matter for any fault-tolerant ambitions. The piece maps a route from laboratory curiosities toward useful topological hardware.
arxiv-2510-07223:
Gosset, Kothari, and Zhang show that a key quantum gate can be built with far fewer costly parts than exact designs demand. Their 2025 paper targets the multi-qubit Toffoli gate, a workhorse of quantum circuits. The authors relax exactness by a hair. They allow a vanishingly small error that practice can ignore. That small freedom changes the cost completely.

A randomly chosen circuit design uses only a number of T gates that grows with the log of the precision. That is exponentially fewer than the exact requirement. The team proves no design can do better on this measure. They also show that purely unitary builds with even constant error still need many T gates. The sampling trick extends to other Boolean functions too. Cheaper Toffoli gates could shrink the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computing.
arxiv-2510-07323:
Robertz and Seiss attack the direct problem in differential Galois theory for the classical matrix groups. Their 2025 paper asks which symmetry groups can arise from linear differential equations, and how to build equations for a group given in advance. Building on their earlier joint work, they use a general construction with several differential unknowns. That construction yields an extension whose Galois group is exactly the chosen classical group. The present paper dissects the structure of that extension in detail.

Standard parabolic subgroups act on the extension, inducing a rich internal anatomy the authors analyze. They then specialize the general equation to concrete rational settings. The specialization analysis covers the main classical families, labeled A, B, C, and beyond in Lie theory. The results serve algebraists studying solvability and symmetries of differential systems.
arxiv-2510-07423:
Nguyen, Luong, and Nguyen present ProSEA, a multi-agent framework that solves problems by exploring and revising its own plans. Their 2025 paper notes that most agent systems plan once and then act rigidly. When the world pushes back, brittle plans fail outright. ProSEA organizes a manager agent above domain-specialized expert agents. The manager splits tasks, assigns pieces, and replans as results arrive. The key design choice is feedback with substance: experts report not just failure, but why they failed and which new constraints they discovered along the way.

Those exploratory traces drive dynamic plan refinement without any human in the loop. On FinanceBench, a hard financial reasoning benchmark, ProSEA beat leading retrieval and reasoning baselines. It matched a rival system that leans heavily on human intervention, while running fully autonomously. Human collaborators can still join seamlessly when wanted.
arxiv-2510-07523:
Pinzi and Savare map the geometry of the space of random measures, a space of distributions over distributions. Their 2025 paper endows that nested space with the Wasserstein-on-Wasserstein distance, the cost of transporting one random measure to another. The centerpiece is a metric superposition principle in the spirit of classical work by Lisini. It represents motion in this huge space as an average of motions of underlying particle systems.

Continuity equations for random measures, written abstractly with derivations on cylinder functions, are recast through concrete nonlocal vector fields. Solutions of the nonlocal continuity equation then decompose into interacting particle systems, making them simulable in principle. A counterexample in the paper marks where the borderline exponent case breaks the pattern, a useful honesty about the theory's edge.
arxiv-2510-07623:
Lawrence and four coauthors wrote this 2025 position paper on generative AI in mental health care. Most public debate in this field centers on therapist chatbots. The authors argue that the debate misses a safer and more useful target. They say AI should instead help train the people who provide mental health services, from clinicians to peer supporters.

Inside, the authors explain how training tools can draw on playbooks, ethical guidelines, and strong examples. They present a real case study with veterans. In that program, generative AI helped veterans learn to support fellow veterans with mental health needs. The authors also argue that speeding up current clinicians would not close the global provider shortage. Training more helpers well, they conclude, could expand care without handing treatment itself to a chatbot. The authors write for researchers, funders, and program designers.
arxiv-2510-07923:
Lee, Jeon, Jang, and Yu wrote this 2025 paper on teaching small models to reason through multi-step retrieval. Hard questions need facts gathered in stages, with different skills at each stage. A doctor first lists possible causes, then tests them, then concludes. Standard distillation trains a student on whole teacher rationales and ignores those stage differences. The authors propose StepER, which supervises each reasoning step on its own terms.

StepER splits reasoning into initialization, expansion, and aggregation stages. Training is difficulty-aware, shifting focus toward the steps a student finds hardest at each moment. The method plugs into many multi-step retrieval frameworks, whether they reason through queries or sub-questions. On multi-hop question benchmarks, StepER beat earlier distillation methods. A small eight-billion-parameter student matched a seventy-billion teacher's performance in their tests. Stage-aware teaching could make capable research assistants far cheaper to run.
arxiv-2510-08123:
Rezaei, Kovacevic, Locatello, and Mondelli wrote this 2025 paper asking which properties of synthetic data actually help classifiers trained on it. Generative models can mint unlimited training data, yet results are mixed. Working through high-dimensional regression, the authors prove a sharper answer for linear models. A shift in covariance between synthetic and target data harms generalization. A shift in the mean, surprisingly, does not.

In some settings, matching the target covariance exactly is provably optimal. The team turned that into a selection procedure matching synthetic covariance to the target's. The findings carried over to deep networks in experiments. Covariance matching beat several recent selection methods across paradigms, architectures, datasets, and generators. The result replaces a vague resemblance heuristic with one measurable property. Generators can look realistic while quietly distorting the covariance learning depends on.
arxiv-2510-08623:
Anubhav Shrimal, Aryan Jain, Soumyajit Chowdhury, and Promod Yenigalla let language models rewrite their own extraction schemas in a 2025 arXiv paper. Software agents increasingly pull structured data from unstructured text using JSON schemas. Teams treat those schemas as static contracts written for human developers. Ambiguous or incomplete schemas then cause extraction errors, hallucinations, and unreliable agent behavior.

Their system, PARSE, treats schemas as contracts the model can systematically improve. One component, ARCHITECT, optimizes schemas for model consumption while a code generator, RELAY, preserves backward compatibility. A second component, SCOPE, performs extraction with reflection and both static and model-based guardrails. Evaluation covered dialogue, web extraction, and internal retail conversation data sets. PARSE improved extraction quality by up to 64.7 percent in their tests, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-08823:
Hang and Kuznetsov compute a family of transforms for a special class of wavy functions, in this 2025 arXiv paper in pure mathematics. The functions pair Jacobi elliptic functions, which generalize the familiar sine wave, with smooth bell-shaped weights. A Fourier transform restates such a function as a blend of waves at different frequencies. In many of their cases, the transform lands back inside the same family, a tidy closure property.

Feeding those results through a second transform, the Mellin transform, produced sixteen new number series of Eisenstein type. For these series the pair prove three things. The series can be extended smoothly beyond their first domain, a mirror-like equation links each series to its partner, and exact formulas give their values at whole-number points. Such series sit at a crossing of analysis and number theory, where they help probe deep patterns in numbers.
arxiv-2510-08923:
Fu and co-authors model how the heaviest quarks travel and settle into particles inside a droplet of primordial matter, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Heavy-ion collisions at the LHC melt protons and neutrons into a quark-gluon plasma, a fluid last common in the infant universe. Heavy quarks are born in the first instant and then wander the plasma, so their final patterns report on its traits. Tracking them faithfully demands both motion and transformation physics.

Their model follows the quarks with a random-walk equation that includes energy lost to radiation, coupled to a simulation of the expanding plasma itself. Interaction strengths come from calculations that capture temporary bound states near the melting point. At the end, quarks become ordinary particles through two competing routes, merging with nearby light quarks or spraying into fragments. Predictions for suppression and sideways flow patterns are compared with lead-lead collision data.
arxiv-2510-09023:
Nasr and a large team of security researchers show that most published defenses against AI jailbreaks collapse under serious attack, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Jailbreaks and prompt injections trick models into revealing harmful knowledge or taking malicious actions. Defenses are usually tested against frozen attack strings or weak optimizers that never adapted to the defense itself. The authors argue the attacker moves second, and evaluation should honor that order.

They attacked twelve recent defenses with adaptive methods that retune themselves against each defense: random search, human-guided exploration, gradient descent, and reinforcement learning. Nearly every defense fell, with attack success above ninety percent for most, despite original papers reporting near-zero success. Human red-teamers succeeded in every scenario tried. The authors conclude that robustness claims mean little until defenses survive attackers who know the defense and optimize hard against it. The team spans several institutions and OpenAI.
arxiv-2510-09123:
Auricchio and Toscani measure how fast a spreading population settles into balance, using distances borrowed from modern machine learning, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The equations are of Fokker-Planck type, which describe diffusion pulled by a steady drift, and they model everything from gas particles to income distributions. The classic yardstick for settling speed tracks relative entropy, a cousin of information loss. The authors instead use the Cramér and energy distances, which compare probability distributions directly.

Wherever these distances can be applied to such equations, the solutions prove to approach equilibrium faster than earlier entropy-based results promised, with decay better than exponential in their cases. The energy distance also has a simple form built from averages, which could make simulating the approach to equilibrium much cheaper numerically. The paper develops the one-dimensional theory alongside the general case, including equations used for socio-economic dynamics.
arxiv-2510-09223:
Nadeem and Fathi compare ways of fusing scattered medical knowledge into one graph that rescue teams can actually use, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In an emergency, the right treatment knowledge exists somewhere: in guidelines, databases, and expert systems. The challenge is gathering those sources into a single structure that supports fast, patient-specific decisions when lives are at stake. Knowledge fusion promises exactly that, but the integration method matters.

The authors present several conceptual models for fusion organized around a knowledge graph, the web of linked medical facts. They evaluate how each model enables fusion and show how varied sources, from treatment protocols to operational knowledge, can be integrated into the graph for rescue operations. Their comparison is meant to help health professionals pick context-aligned sources for critical decisions. The paper positions knowledge graphs as the meeting point where medical expertise and a patient's own information combine.
arxiv-2510-09323:
Gopal Chandra Dutta, Amit Kumar Paul, and Subhankar Sau study motion planning for teams of robots in a 2025 arXiv paper. Several autonomous robots must move through a space with obstacles whose positions are not known in advance. Each robot has to visit its own list of target states in order, and the lists can differ in length from robot to robot.

The authors frame the problem with a fibration, a mathematical structure that organises all possible motions, and compute its topological complexity. That number measures the least instability any collision-free planning algorithm must have under changing parameters. Their analysis covers odd and even dimensional spaces separately. It includes the cohomology computations behind the invariant and explicit constructions of planning algorithms that match it, extending earlier work on sequential planning by Farber and Paul.
arxiv-2510-09423:
Yankun Han, the sole author, studies how the starting weights of a neural network shape its training, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Weight initialisation sets the random values a network begins with, and poor choices make signals vanish or explode as they pass through layers. Han compares classic rules with modern practice across small networks and a transformer in the style of GPT-2.

A sweep over starting scales maps where training stays stable, finding a broad safe band. In feed-forward networks with the common ReLU activation, Kaiming initialisation converged faster and more steadily than Xavier initialisation, matching variance-preserving theory. In the twelve-layer transformer, the spread of weights settled into narrow bands during pretraining, shallow layers expanding quickly while deeper ones changed slowly. The paper closes with simple recipes meant to make training more robust.
arxiv-2510-09523:
Ian Gill, Ryan Hamilton, and Helen Caines probe how quarks and gluons lose energy in extreme matter in a 2025 arXiv paper. When heavy nuclei collide at near light speed, they create quark gluon plasma, a hot dense medium. Fast partons crossing it lose energy, which suppresses the high-momentum particles seen in the detectors compared with proton collisions.

Measuring how that loss changes with collision energy is hard, because the underlying particle spectra also shift steeply with energy. The authors use a spectrum shift model to estimate the average momentum loss directly. They find a striking correlation between that loss and the initial energy density estimated from Glauber models, holding over a hundredfold range of collision energy and several nuclear species. Coupling the model to event shape estimates also yields predictions for elliptic flow, the directional pattern of the loss, that agree reasonably with data.
arxiv-2510-09623:
Álvaro Otero Sanchez, the sole author, sorts derivations on twisted group algebras in a 2025 arXiv paper. A derivation is a map that obeys the product rule familiar from calculus, and twisted group algebras deform ordinary group algebras by a phase factor in the multiplication. Knowing all derivations of an algebra reveals much about its structure.

Otero Sanchez writes the derivations through the group's generators and defining relations. He gives exact tests for when a map defined only on the generators extends to a full derivation of the twisted group ring. The results generalise known theorems for ordinary group algebras to the twisted case. He applies them to abelian groups, whose elements commute, and to dihedral groups, the symmetry groups of polygons. The machinery also computes, for twisted group algebras, the first Hochschild cohomology group, a standard measure of how an algebra can change.
arxiv-2510-09823:
Kevin Flaherty and seven co-authors weigh the planet-forming discs around tight binary stars in a 2025 arXiv paper. Binaries are common sites of planet formation despite the companion's disruptive pull. Surveys had found diminished disc masses around medium-separation binaries, but tight pairs, closer than ten astronomical units, might keep a shared circumbinary disc safe from the worst disruption.

The team surveyed over one hundred spectroscopic binaries in the Orion A star-forming region with the ALMA radio array. They detected significant continuum emission from twenty-one of them, with disc masses from one to one hundred Earth masses. Compared with single-star surveys, the binary discs are systematically lighter, suggesting reduced planet-forming potential. The fraction showing infrared excess matches single stars, though the binaries without strong ALMA emission show hints of weaker warm excess. The authors note that clearing alone struggles to explain the missing cold dust.
arxiv-2510-10023:
He, Abhishek Panigrahi, Yong Lin, and Sanjeev Arora introduce STAT in this 2025 arXiv paper on fine-tuning language models. Models often saturate under plain supervised fine-tuning: training on data much like their original training set brings little or no gain. More of the same data does not teach new skills.

STAT, short for skill-targeted adaptive training, uses a stronger teacher model to diagnose which skills the student lacks. The teacher's metacognition, its judgment about what the student gets wrong, guides the choice of training data. Training then targets the weak skills instead of repeating mastered material. The authors aim to break the saturation plateau that wastes compute in standard fine-tuning pipelines.
arxiv-2510-10123:
Joydeep Chandra, Satyam Kumar Navneet, and Yong Zhang present the Hybrid Multimodal Graph Index in this 2025 arXiv paper on database systems. Modern datasets mix content types, and search must handle both meaning and relationships. Vector databases excel at semantic similarity but cannot run deep relational queries.

Graph databases invert that strength: they traverse relationships well but handle high-dimensional vector search poorly. HMGI is a framework that integrates relational and vector search in one index. The aim is queries that filter by graph structure and rank by vector similarity in a single pass. Such hybrid search serves recommendation, retrieval, and knowledge systems that today must stitch two separate engines together.
arxiv-2510-10423:
Ehsan Heidari and three co-authors improve a fairness guarantee for dividing indivisible goods, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The maximin share is a leading fairness notion: it is the best value an agent could guarantee by splitting the goods into bundles and taking the worst one. For additive valuations, where each item adds a fixed value, earlier work capped any possible guarantee and gave an algorithm reaching about three quarters of the share.

The team narrows the gap between those bounds. Their new algorithm guarantees each agent at least ten thirteenths of their maximin share value, improving on the best previously known guarantee. The known ceiling shows no method can promise a factor better than one minus a tiny term that shrinks with the number of agents. Such results matter for allocating courses, estates, or shared equipment, where items cannot be split.
arxiv-2510-10523:
Ricardo Alonso and Milana Čolić study how smooth solutions of the polyatomic Boltzmann equation become over time, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The equation models gases whose molecules carry internal energy, such as rotation, on top of motion. The team works with the space homogeneous version and with physically relevant collision kernels of hard potential type whose angular part is integrable. They prove three main results about regularity, meaning smoothness, of solutions.

First, the gain part of the collision operator has a smoothing effect. Second, first order derivatives in velocity and internal energy propagate from the initial data. Third, singularities in the initial data decay exponentially fast. Together these lead to a decomposition theorem: any solution splits into a smooth part plus a rough component that decays rapidly. Such results matter because they justify numerical schemes and clarify how molecular chaos smooths out irregular starting states in realistic gases.
arxiv-2510-10623:
Ahmed J Abdelmaksoud and three co-authors design a chip architecture that speeds up the matrix multiplication at the heart of transformers, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Transformers dominate modern AI but demand heavy memory and computation. Lower precision arithmetic, called quantization, cuts memory use. Their design, ADiP, is a systolic array of reconfigurable processing elements that adjusts its precision dynamically, with shared shifters and accumulators.

ADiP supports multiplying one matrix pair, or several matrices that share an input, improving data reuse. Adapting precision yields up to four times the throughput and four times the memory efficiency of fixed precision designs in their analysis. They modeled latency and throughput, explored the design space in commercial 22 nanometer technology, and tested transformer workloads from GPT-2, BERT, and BitNet models. For attention in the BitNet model, total latency improved by up to 53.6 percent and energy by up to 24.4 percent across the reported runs.
arxiv-2510-11023:
Josefa Caballero, Łukasz Płociniczak, and Kishin Sadarangani speed up models of slow diffusion with memory, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The model is a time fractional diffusion equation. Its special derivative gives the process a memory of its past. Such models describe subdiffusion, where spread is slower than normal. Their solver combines three parts. The parareal algorithm splits time stepping across processors. An L1 scheme handles the fractional derivative. A spectral method handles space and is exponentially accurate.

The headline result is a proof. It is the first rigorous convergence proof for this parareal L1 pairing in the nonlinear setting. The parallel iterations reach the serial solution exactly, in finitely many steps. Their rates do not depend on the fractional exponent. Tests on subdiffusive and classical problems confirm the theory. Run time fell by up to tenfold against the serial solver.
arxiv-2510-11423:
Community Notes on X lets users attach corrections to misleading posts, but for health misinformation the crowd is slow: notes wait hours before readers see them. Jiaying Wu and co-authors analyze that delay and propose an AI-augmented version in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their analysis of 30,800 health-related notes found a median delay of 17.6 hours before a note receives a helpfulness status, a gap during which false claims spread freely.

Their framework CrowdNotes+ adds two language-model modes, evidence-grounded note augmentation and utility-guided note automation, plus a three-step evaluation that checks relevance, then correctness, then helpfulness. They instantiate it as HealthNotes, a benchmark of 1,200 health notes with a fine-tuned helpfulness judge. Experiments on fifteen language models exposed a loophole in helpfulness scoring, where fluent style is mistaken for factual accuracy. Their hierarchical evaluation and augmented generation improved factual precision and evidence utility.
arxiv-2510-11623:
When a smooth curve degenerates into two components meeting at a point, the linear series on it, degenerate too, and moduli spaces must hold the limits. Eduardo Esteves, Antonio Nigro, and Pedro Rizzo construct such a space in this 2025 arXiv algebraic geometry paper. Their curve is the union of two smooth components crossing transversally at a single point. Their new object is the continuous linear series, a maximal family of generalized linear series on that singular curve.

The authors parameterize all these degenerations by a fine moduli space, a projective scheme, a Hilbert quotient in Kapranov's sense. The space compactifies Osserman's moduli space of exact limit linear series and, consequently, the Eisenbud-Harris moduli space of refined limit linear series, the classical Brill-Noether tools. They are parameterized by an Artin stack from a chain of rational curves modulo a torus action.
arxiv-2510-11723:
Mélodie Andrieu, Shalom Eliahou, and Léo Vivion study number systems built on fractions instead of whole numbers. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns rational bases, introduced in 2008 as a generalization of ordinary counting bases like ten. Within this system two families of endless digit strings appear, called minimal and maximal words. A word is normal when every block of digits shows up equally often, as chance would predict.

The authors conjecture that all minimal and maximal words are normal over a suitable part of the alphabet. To support the claim, they run extensive numerical experiments. They measure the richness threshold, which tracks pattern variety, and the discrepancy, which tracks how evenly digits spread. The paper also maps what the conjecture would unlock if true. It touches several old open problems, including Mahler's Z-numbers from 1968 and a Collatz-inspired puzzle known as the four-thirds problem.
arxiv-2510-11823:
Caelin Kaplan, Alexander Warnecke, and Neil Archibald introduce BlackIce, a ready-made toolkit for red teaming artificial intelligence systems. Red teaming means attacking a model on purpose to find its weaknesses before real adversaries do. Many testing tools exist, but picking among them is hard and their software requirements often clash. In their 2025 paper, presented at the CAMLIS Red conference, the authors model their answer on Kali Linux, the standard bundle for traditional penetration testing.

BlackIce packages fourteen carefully chosen open-source testing tools into one Docker container. Versions are pinned, so every user runs the same reproducible setup. Everything is reachable through a single command-line interface, and an assessment starts by simply launching the container locally or in the cloud. The toolkit covers both large language models and classical machine learning models. Its modular design lets the community bolt on new tools as fresh threats appear.
arxiv-2510-12123:
David Parra, Felipe Gutierrez-Barragan, Trevor Seets, and Andreas Velten design camera codes that respect the camera's limits. Single-photon 3D cameras time-tag individual photons with exquisite resolution, but bandwidth, laser power, and on-sensor memory throttle them. Compressive histograms squeeze the data on-chip, yet standard designs underperform under real illumination constraints. Their 2025 arXiv paper optimizes the coding functions directly.

A constrained optimization, solved by gradient descent, jointly designs the illumination pattern and the coding matrix to obey hardware limits. Extensive simulations show the learned designs consistently beat traditional ones under both bandwidth and peak power constraints. The advantage is largest exactly where systems hurt most, when peak power binds. The method also adapts to imperfect hardware: evaluated on a real system with a non-ideal impulse response, it reshaped its codes accordingly.
arxiv-2510-12523:
Ben Yahia, El Ferchichi, Abeille, and Perchet study bandit problems where every option must earn a guaranteed minimum total reward, in a 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. A multi armed bandit is a repeated choice problem balancing exploration against exploitation. Here each arm's reward must reach a floor when aggregated across contexts, capturing settings like fair revenue allocation among products or regions.

Aggregating the constraints across contexts makes feasibility easier and performance better, but it destroys the closed form optimal allocations available in standard bandit settings. The authors design algorithms with two temperaments: optimistic ones that prioritize performance, and pessimistic ones that enforce constraint satisfaction. For each they derive problem dependent bounds on both regret and constraint violations. A lower bound shows their dependence on the time horizon is optimal in general. The analysis also exposes fundamental limits of the free exploration principle that earlier work relied on.
arxiv-2510-12623:
Doyle and Schwartz prove that a family of paper tori, flat donut surfaces built from eight pieces, is far more flexible than expected, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. A paper torus is a piecewise linear length preserving embedding of a flat torus into three dimensional space, bending without stretching. Eight vertex examples were recently discovered, raising the question of which flat tori they can realize.

The authors prove universality and collapsibility results for these objects. One corollary says any flat torus without mirror symmetry is realized as an eight vertex paper torus. Another says that for any tolerance, some eight vertex paper torus lies within that distance of a unit equilateral triangle, the two shapes nearly coinciding as sets. In other words, the same eight piece construction can approximate a flat triangle arbitrarily well while remaining a genuine torus. The results complete the picture of its reach.
arxiv-2510-12923:
Chernin and Konyaev classify coordinate changes for a special class of operator fields in this 2025 arXiv paper. The fields take upper triangular Toeplitz form, meaning each downward diagonal of the matrix repeats the same entry. They appear in Frobenius manifold theory, reductions of hydrodynamic chains, soliton gas studies, and Nijenhuis geometry. The authors ask which coordinate transformations preserve this form.

Under a regularity condition ensuring the operator resembles one maximal Jordan block at each point, they solve the problem in full. In short, every preserving transformation is described by one function of a single variable. It also involves a family of functions of two variables, one fewer than the dimension. Given those functions, the transformation can be built through a recursion that solves triangular linear systems and integrates step by step.
arxiv-2510-13423:
Sottile, Tekriwal, and Sarracino call for richer challenge problems to test correctness methods in scientific computing. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues that verification tools struggle with realistic scientific applications. Part of the gap is mutual: two research communities lack a shared picture of correctness. Challenge problems would give tool builders shared, machine-checkable targets. The paper is a position piece rather than an experimental study.

The authors propose several dimensions of correctness that matter for scientific codes. They also set out guidelines and criteria for designing such challenge problems. The new problems should augment, not replace, the general problems formal methods researchers already study. Performance benchmarks have long steered computing research, the authors recall. Correctness needs the same steering effect, they argue, as codes and machines grow more complex. Well-chosen challenges would show whether new verification techniques meet real scientific needs.
arxiv-2510-13523:
Ma and Yu prove that two large families of unipotent ideals are weakly unipotent. Their 2025 arXiv paper sits in the representation theory of reductive groups, where such ideals shape unitary representations. Weak unipotence is a key property of certain primitive ideals in enveloping algebras. The authors introduce a stronger, more checkable condition they call mild unipotence.

They show that mild unipotence always guarantees weak unipotence. With it, they settle the property for q-unipotent ideals defined by McGovern. They also settle it for ideals attached to covers of nilpotent orbits by a recent construction. The proof leans on a bijection between special orbits in two Lie algebra types. That link, between type D and metaplectic type C orbits, is used in an essential way. The argument is conceptual rather than case-based, the authors stress.
arxiv-2510-14023:
Maksym Luz and Mykhailo Moklyachuk tackle optimal filtering for random processes whose increments are stationary, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Filtering means estimating hidden features of a process from observations corrupted by noise; here the observations mix the process of interest with an unrelated stationary noise, and only past observations are available.

The targets are linear functionals, weighted averages of the process's unknown past values. When the spectral densities of both processes, the fingerprints of their frequency content, are known, the authors give formulas for the mean-square error and the spectral characteristic of the best linear estimate. When the densities are known only to lie in an allowed set, they switch to a robust minimax stance. They derive the least favorable densities, the worst cases, and the matching minimax spectral characteristics. That way the filter performs well even under the least friendly spectrum in the set.
arxiv-2510-14123:
José Carrillo and co-authors determine how flocking systems settle down over time, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their model is the pressureless Euler system with nonlocal forces. It is a continuum of agents whose velocities align with neighbors'. The agents attract or repel through an interaction potential. The framework is used for animal flocks, swarms, and opinion dynamics.

They prove convergence in three settings, depending on the interaction potential and the communication weight, which sets how strongly distant agents influence each other. When the weight is bounded, density and velocity converge exponentially fast. When it is weakly singular, meaning it blows up at short distances, convergence is algebraic, a slower power-law rate. The rates are sharp. A Coulomb-quadratic potential gets an analysis. The density converges, up to a shift, to the minimizer of the interaction energy. The velocity aligns to a constant.
arxiv-2510-14423:
Antonio Quim Cervantes, Ajinkya Desai, and Tirtha Banerjee simulate how canopy structure shapes the rising hot plume above a wildland fire, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Understanding plume dynamics matters for predicting fire spread and smoke transport, yet the trees, their gaps and edges, redirect the flow in ways models miss.

Using large eddy simulation with the PALM model, the team ran six canopy configurations. They ranged from no canopy and uniform canopy to canopies edged inside or outside the plume. Others had hundred- or two-hundred-meter gaps. Each ran with and without a heat patch, under three crosswind speeds. Canopy structure modified plume behavior, mean flow, and turbulence budgets: updraft speed and plume tilt varied with configuration and wind, and pressure gradients changed how much the crosswind slowed near it. Absorption above the canopy was strongest for the crosswind cases, with the greatest enhancement in the gap canopies.
arxiv-2510-14523:
Silva, Klami, Mesquita, and Urteaga ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, when the hidden sizes inside a tensor model can be pinned down from data. Tensor factorization splits a multiway array into simpler parts. The ranks are the sizes of those parts. In practice, researchers often pick ranks by trial and error.

The authors match moments that a model predicts before seeing data. They turn the matching conditions into equations that are linear in the logarithms. Whether ranks can be identified then reduces to whether that system can be solved. The test succeeds for the PARAFAC, Tensor Train, and Tensor Ring models, whose layouts give solvable systems. It fails for the Tucker model, whose symmetric layout leaves the system underdetermined. For the solvable cases, they derive direct formulas that estimate ranks from observed data alone, and they check the estimators in experiments.
arxiv-2510-14623:
Cao and co-authors introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a method for explaining image classifiers with counterfactual examples. A counterfactual shows the smallest change to an input that would flip the model's decision, which helps users see why it decided as it did. Existing generators have real weaknesses. They can suffer vanishing gradients, work in broken latent spaces, or fail when the model's learned boundary differs from the true one.

Their method, LeapFactual, is built on conditional flow matching, a technique that learns how to morph one distribution into another. It produces counterfactuals that stay realistic and informative even when the learned and true boundaries diverge. The method is model-agnostic, meaning it does not need a differentiable model underneath. It can even explain systems with humans in the loop, like citizen science projects. Experiments on benchmark and real data show accurate, in-distribution explanations suggesting concrete actions.
arxiv-2510-14823:
Morreale and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a gentler way to shrink generative models until they fit on a phone. Big diffusion models generate striking images and text, but their memory and compute demands exceed handset hardware. Quantization lowers each parameter's precision, yet aggressive cuts to four bits usually damage output quality. Training that anticipates quantization helps, but a hard drop in precision is still a shock to the model.

Their method, FraQAT, reduces precision progressively from thirty-two bits down to four during training. Along the way it exploits fractional bit widths, easing the model through intermediate precisions instead of one cliff edge. Across several leading diffusion models, including SD3.5-Medium, Sana, and FLUX.1-schnell, FraQAT produced images with FID scores four to seven percent lower than standard quantization-aware training. The team also deployed Sana on a Samsung S25U phone, running on its tensor processor.
arxiv-2510-14923:
Baier-Reinio, Farrell, and Monroe present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a family of high-order finite element methods for simulating how electrolytes flow. Their target is the electroneutral Navier-Stokes-Onsager-Stefan-Maxwell equations, a coupled system describing momentum transport, multi-component diffusion, and charge effects inside the liquid. Such flows matter in batteries and electroplating, but they are delicate where the imposed boundaries meet the fluid's equation of state.

They handle steady and time-dependent problems, in two and three dimensions, under varied conditions. Material properties like viscosity, diffusivities, and density may depend on the solution, and the thermodynamics may be non-ideal, both common in devices. The authors work through the subtleties this creates at boundaries. Two demonstrations follow. One is fluid swirling around a microfluidic disk electrode. The other is flow in a Hull cell with a solvent electrolyte mixture used in lithium-ion cells.
arxiv-2510-15023:
Foroughi-Abari, Kelly, and Zhang explore, in a 2025 arXiv paper, an overlooked fingerprint of proposed new particles with a taste for neutrinos. These additions to the Standard Model are usually hunted directly, or through their tree-level effects on neutrino self-interaction. The authors point out that they also shift how neutrinos scatter off matter, through loop corrections. These loop effects persist even when it is never produced.

With a light enough mediator, these deviations could show up across a surprising range of experiments. They affect coherent elastic scattering off nuclei, deep-inelastic events, and electron scattering measured at Borexino. The effects also feed into the Z boson's decay width, a precision quantity. And they generate non-standard interactions for long-baseline oscillation programs. The paper works through each scenario in depth, mapping what loop-level thinking adds to the search program.
arxiv-2510-15123:
Douglas S. Bridges writes a short note in constructive mathematics, a style of proof that insists every claimed object can actually be built. His 2025 arXiv paper compares two ways of describing what lies outside a convex set inside a normed space. One is the metric double complement, the points safely away from everything outside the set; the other is its logical double negation.

Bridges proves that when the convex set has a nonempty interior, the inside of the logical double complement exactly equals the metric double complement. In finite-dimensional spaces he shows the interior assumption can be dropped altogether, broadening the result. He also shows a tempting strengthening fails: the interior of the original set cannot constructively replace that double complement interior. The note carefully separates notions that classical mathematics treats as identical but constructive logic pulls apart.
arxiv-2510-15623:
Knowledge graphs are incomplete, yet users ask multi-hop questions that go beyond stored facts. Parsa Abbasi and Stefan Heindorf work on explaining answers to such complex queries in this 2025 arXiv paper. Neural answering systems are black boxes, so users cannot see why an answer ranks first. Their framework CQD-SHAP computes how much each part of a query contributes to an answer's ranking. The scores use Shapley values from game theory, which fairly divide credit among cooperating parts.

The method satisfies all the basic Shapley axioms by construction. Automated tests check whether explanations are necessary and sufficient for the ranking produced. For most query types, CQD-SHAP explains answers more effectively than the baselines compared.
arxiv-2510-15723:
RR Lyrae stars are old pulsating stars, and almost none show heavy-element enrichment from slow neutron capture. V. D'Orazi leads a nineteen-author team reporting two such stars in this 2025 arXiv paper. Until now, TY Gruis was the only known example of this rare class. The team used high-resolution spectrographs in Australia and Chile to measure detailed abundances. Gaia data supplied motions and orbits, letting them classify each star's Galactic population.

Both stars show strong overabundances of barium and lanthanum compared with lighter s-process elements. The pattern fits pollution from a companion that once passed through its giant phase. Mismatches in dilution factors suggest low-metallicity giant models still need refinement.
arxiv-2511-00223:
Hussein Nassar and Andrew Weber study thin patterned sheets, such as corrugated or creased shells, that like to bend without stretching. Because the sheets are thin, stretching costs far more energy than bending, so their natural moves keep lengths fixed. The authors report a recent result that pins down exactly which bending moves are possible for surfaces with a repeating pattern.

The result ties how the sheet seems to stretch, while keeping true lengths fixed, to how it bends and twists. The link echoes a classic theorem of Gauss on curved surfaces. Worked examples and use cases show how designers might use the rule for flexible shell mechanisms.
arxiv-2511-00923:
Khushi Banthia and Rickmoy Samanta study vortex dipoles, pairs of swirling flows that propel themselves, moving on a catenoid, the hourglass shaped surface formed by rotating a hanging chain curve. The catenoid has variable negative curvature, so geometry itself steers the motion.

They build the full dynamical system, including how the two vortices interact and how each interacts with the curved surface. The Hamiltonian dynamics make dipoles follow the surface's geodesics, matching recent results, and a conserved momentum comes from the surface's rotational symmetry. Direct and exchange scattering are showed, along with rotating motion for chiral pairs. A finite size dipole model then shows self propulsion emerging to leading order, directed across the dipole axis.
arxiv-2511-01223:
Zahra Mehraban and colleagues ask how a self driving steering model trained in one country adapts to driving on the other side of the road. They adapt PilotNet, an end to end driving model, from United States right hand traffic to Australian left hand highways using real road data.

Four training routes were compared. One was the raw United States baseline. Others used flipped United States data, fine tuning on Australian data, or pretraining on flipped data followed by Australian fine tuning. Flipped pretraining alone hurt stability, because the learned features were misaligned. Followed by fine tuning, though, it gave the lowest prediction error. It also gave the strongest attention to left side road cues. A saliency analysis tracked where the models look, and repeating the study on ResNet confirmed the same pattern.
arxiv-2511-01323:
Jiabao Ji and colleagues benchmark whether language models with search tools give complete answers to ambiguous, multi step questions. A question like which actor from the film Heat won an Academy Award hides traps: several films share the title. The full cast must be reasoned over to gather every qualifying name.

Their data generation pipeline builds questions from text corpora linked to a knowledge graph, embedding name ambiguity and multi hop reasoning in a natural, verifiable way. The resulting data set holds thirty six hundred questions, half with explicit ambiguity. Even the strongest current model answered poorly, with low exact match scores on both ambiguous and unambiguous questions. The authors argue answer completeness is an under measured weakness of search augmented systems.
arxiv-2511-01723:
Maxime Dherbécourt, Joël Bellessa, Clémentine Symonds, Guillaume Weick, and David Hagenmüller settle a dispute about light scattering from molecules in an optical cavity. When a molecular vibration couples strongly to a cavity mode, the two form polaritons. Early reports claimed big changes to spontaneous Raman scattering from such systems. Later experiments mostly disagreed.

The authors build a microscopic quantum model that keeps the spatial shape of the polariton modes. In a cavity filled evenly with molecules, overlap between polaritons and cavity resonances enforces selection rules. Those rules suppress the claimed Raman peaks, which matches most experiments. In a thin, quasi-two-dimensional layer, the rules lift. Peaks at the polariton energies then return. The key factor is the spatial overlap of cavity and vibration. The model now makes that factor calculable.
arxiv-2511-01823:
Thiago Dias, José Roberto Iglesias, and Sebastián Gonçalves test the fairness of consumption taxes with agent-based simulations. Consumption-based systems, which tax spending rather than income, are often defended as simple and neutral; the authors examine whether they actually redistribute wealth in a socially fair way.

Simulating wealth exchanges among agents under flat consumption taxes, they compare universal redistribution of the revenue with optimal targeted redistribution. The regressivity is stark: the poorest 40 percent of households contribute over half of the total tax revenue at most tax rates, because poorer households spend nearly all they have. Even the better redistribution schemes struggle against this built-in tilt. The authors present the numbers as quantitative input for designing fairer fiscal policy.
arxiv-2511-02023:
