In 1895 he began to teach state wealth at Paris. That post was in the law school of the city. He served as a clerk for sea and colony meets too. The entry shows a young man of law with a wide brief. His posts touch courts, schools, farms, and the sea.
journal-of-discourses-vol-23:
Volume Twenty-Three, also from 1883, finds the crusade at its cruelest. Leaders sit in prison, families scatter, and church funds face seizure. The Saints' suffering peaks in the sermons gathered in this book.

Preachers frame the pain as fire that refines, not breaks, the faithful. Discourses console the jailed men's wives and fatherless homes directly. A people drinks its Gethsemane, in their own stark biblical phrase. Endurance becomes the chief virtue preached from every stand in Utah. The record of those who bore the cup fills this grim, moving volume. Consolation, not complaint, is the note its preachers strike most often.
julian-works-wright-vol3-1923:
Wilmer Cave Wright's third Loeb volume of Julian's works came out in 1923, ten years after the first two. It holds the emperor's letters and the fragments of works that survive only in pieces. Julian wrote these texts in the brief reign when he tried to turn the empire back to its old gods.

The chief piece is Against the Galilaeans, his case against the Christians, kept in quotes by Cyril, the church writer who answered it. Julian mocks the claims of the Bible and defends Greek religion and learning. The letters beside it show his rule in daily detail. The volume completes Wright's English Julian.
jung-psychological-types-baynes-1923:
C. G. Jung published Psychological Types in German in 1921. The English text here is H. G. Baynes's translation of 1923. Jung sorts people by two attitudes: introversion, turned inward, and extraversion, turned outward. He adds four functions: thinking, feeling, sensation, and intuition. Combinations of these form his famous types.

Jung draws examples from history, literature, and his patients. The book became the source of all later personality typology, including popular tests used today. Jung warns that types are tools, not boxes for souls. His aim was to explain why thinkers see the same facts so differently. The work remains a classic of personality theory.
keynes-tract-monetary-reform-1923:
Keynes's Tract on Monetary Reform, published in 1923, tackles the money chaos that followed the First World War. Prices in Europe had swung wildly, and several nations saw their currency collapse. Keynes asks how a state should manage money in such a world.

He applies the quantity theory of money to wartime and postwar inflation in plain, forceful terms. He faults the gold standard, which ties a nation's money to a fixed stock of gold. His call for managed money pointed toward the policies he would urge for the rest of his life. He writes for citizens as much as for bankers, in brisk, quotable prose.
kierkegaard-selections-hollander-1923:
Soren Kierkegaard's selected writings appear here in L. M. Hollander's translation of 1923, the first broad English gateway to his work. Kierkegaard was a Danish thinker of the 1800s who wrote under many pen names. The selections cover dread, faith, and the stages of life. Aesthetic, ethical, and religious ways of living stand in sharp contrast.

Kierkegaard defends the leap of faith against cold systems of thought. He insists truth for faith is personal and inward. Later thinkers named him a founder of existentialism. Hollander's volume let English readers meet him at length for the first time. It remains a useful door into a demanding author.
lawrence-birds-beasts-flowers-1923:
D. H. Lawrence wrote most of Birds, Beasts and Flowers during his travels in Italy, New Mexico, and Australia. The collection appeared in 1923, after he had left England for good. Lawrence arranged the poems by their subjects, as the title announces.

The poems watch plants and animals with fierce attention. A snake drinking at a trough in Sicily shames the poet's fearful education. Figs, bats, kangaroos, and dark Bavarian gentians all appear, each treated as a living otherness to respect. Lawrence rejected smooth traditional forms for free, breathing rhythms. Many readers call this his finest book of poems.
lawrence-kangaroo-1923:
Lawrence and Frieda spent months in Australia in 1922, and Kangaroo grew directly out of that stay. Published in 1923, it follows Richard Somers, a writer much like Lawrence, settling near Sydney with his wife Harriet.

Somers is courted by 'Kangaroo', a charismatic lawyer building a paramilitary movement of returned soldiers, and by socialists who want him too. He refuses both, and the novel becomes a reckoning with politics, loyalty, and Australia itself. Long passages simply watch the sea and bush with fierce attention. It is the antipodean chapter of Lawrence's search for a new life and a new faith.
lawrence-ladybird-1923:
The Ladybird, published in 1923, gathers three long stories from Lawrence's post-war years: 'The Ladybird', 'The Fox', and 'The Captain's Doll'. Each turns on power and surrender between men and women in a Europe broken by war.

In the title story, a wounded German count draws an English lady toward a dark, chthonic faith. 'The Fox' sets two women farming alone against a young soldier and the fox that haunts them, toward a shocking end. 'The Captain's Doll' plays the same tensions as comedy. These are among Lawrence's most perfectly made tales, written at the height of his powers.
lawrence-studies-classic-american-1923:
Lawrence's 1923 criticism took on the classic American writers and read them against the grain. His essays on Franklin, Cooper, Poe, Hawthorne, Melville, and Whitman became the most famous single book of American literary criticism by an outsider.

Lawrence claims that American literature hides a dark secret: a continent won by violence, and a soul split between innocence and blood. He distrusts what these writers say they mean and hunts what their tales confess. The style is wild, funny, and prophetic. Scholars have argued with his readings ever since, and few have matched their force. The book remade how America read itself.
leonora-pg13723:
Arnold Bennett published his novel Leonora in 1903. Its contents open at the household at Hillport, in Bursley. Bennett sets the tale in his familiar Five Towns country.

Meshach and Hannah appear in the second chapter. A call, an intimacy, and a chance follow in turn. Comic opera, a dance, and a death in the family widen the plot. Leonora herself must refuse something in a late chapter. The story closes in a garden and in London. Edgeworth's father helped shape her early writing career. Leonora's letters debate whether feeling should rule marriage.
li-bai-the-works-of-li-po-the-chinese-po:
Li Bai, called Li Po in this 1923 English version by Shigeyoshi Obata, was China's most loved poet. He sang of wine, moonlight, high mountains, and friends far away. His Tang dynasty lyrics date from the eighth century, China's golden age of verse.

Obata chose and Englished the poems with a scholar's care and a poet's ear. Parting, longing, and drunken joy recur like notes in music. Li Bai's ease hides deep craft, and his freedom still startles readers. This selection carried his genius to the West and helped fix his name among the supreme lyric poets of the world.
library-of-the-world-s-best-literature-a:
Edited by Charles Dudley Warner, Volume Six extends his anthology of world literature. Mabie, Runkle, and George Henry Warner served as associate editors. The advisory council mixed professors from eastern universities and California. Together they chose writings they considered the best of every age.

The volume offers passages and pieces spanning ancient authors to modern ones. Arranged for the home reader, it favors famous, durable works over novelties. Short selections let readers compare styles, subjects, and centuries side by side. It stands as both a reading collection and a record of period taste. Willard Fiske's Cornell post covered Germanic and Scandinavian languages and literatures. Edward Holden directed California's Lick Observatory while advising the editors.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-comp:
Motley's complete Barneveld history, dated 1880, spans 1609 to 1623. Project Gutenberg issued it as Volume 99 of his Netherlands history. John of Barneveld, Advocate of Holland, directs the Dutch Republic throughout. The work links his fate to the coming Thirty Years' War.

Its preface calls both wars one tragedy lasting eighty years. The Twelve Years' Truce was only a pause in the struggle. Persons and scenes change, yet motives and events form one succession. Readers can follow the whole arc in a single complete text. Designs reaching back to Charles V open his long historical view. Generations of actors succeed one another across the eighty years.
lizerand-dossier-affaire-templiers-1923:
Georges Lizerand, a French scholar, built Le Dossier de l'Affaire des Templiers in 1923 as a working file of the case. The Knights Templar fell in 1307, when the French king's men seized them across the realm. Lizerand prints the core papers of that fall in one volume.

Readers get the arrest order, the long interrogations of the brothers, and the acts that ended the order in 1312. Grand Master Jacques de Molay's own words sit among the records. The dossier lets the case be read from its papers, not from legend. Students of the Templar trial still start with this file.
llull-lover-beloved-peers-1923:
Ramon Llull was the Catalan mystic of the 1200s. His Book of the Lover and the Beloved is a string of 366 short prose poems, one for each day of the year. E. Allison Peers translated the work into English in 1923, with an essay on the life of Llull and his famous Art. The poems stand inside his great romance Blanquerna.

The Lover seeks the Beloved, who is God, through forests of signs, questions, and joy. Each piece is a spark: a dialogue, a sigh, a small parable of longing and praise. Llull drew on the Sufi poets he had read in Mallorca. The book is the sweetest fruit of Catalan mysticism, still read day by day.
machen-christianity-and-liberalism-1923:
Machen's Christianity and Liberalism, published in 1923, is the fundamentalist manifesto of the American church fights of the 1920s. Its claim is blunt: liberalism is not a kind of Christianity but a different religion entirely. Machen wrote it while Princeton Seminary slid toward the split he would soon lead.

He compares the two faiths on God, man, the Bible, Christ, salvation, and the church, finding them opposed at every point. Liberalism, he says, rests on naturalism, the denial that God acts in history in supernatural ways. The book still anchors conservative arguments about the boundaries of the faith.
millay-harp-weaver-1923:
Edna St. Vincent Millay published The Harp-Weaver and Other Poems in 1923, and it won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry. Millay was the first woman to win that prize. The book catches her in her prime, when her sonnets were being memorized across America.

The title ballad tells of a poor mother who weaves fine clothes for her son on a magic harp as she dies. Behind its fairy-tale shape sits real poverty Millay knew from her own childhood. The volume also holds a celebrated sonnet sequence on love and loss. Ballads, lyrics, and sonnets together make this the fullest single display of Millay's gifts.
monroe-doctrine-1823:
President James Monroe laid out his doctrine in a message on December 2, 1823. The Seventh Annual Message to Congress holds the famed passage. Europe's monarchs are warned to keep hands off the Americas.

The Western Hemisphere, Monroe declares, is closed to fresh colonization. Any bid to crush the new Latin republics will count as hostile. The young republic thus claims a sphere of its own age. The statement became the base stone of foreign policy for a century. Later presidents stretched its reach far past Monroe's first intent in 1823. The doctrine's few lines grew into a creed of hemispheric power.
muir-life-mohammad-weir-1923:
William Muir built The Life of Mohammad from Arabic sources, first in 1861 and revised by T. H. Weir in the 1923 edition. Muir read Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham, Waqidi, and Tabari at first hand, a rare feat for a Victorian writer. His critical biography follows the Prophet from Mecca to Medina to the conquest of Arabia.

Muir admired his subject's power while judging the faith by his own Christian lights, and readers have argued with him ever since. The book long served English readers as their fullest life of Mohammad from the sources. It also stands as the public-domain stand-in for the early Sira in English.
openalex-w1595049023:
Cristian Koepfli, Ivo Mueller, and co-authors studied malaria spread. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in May 2015. Gametocytes are the parasite forms that infect mosquitoes. Knowing what drives their carriage aids malaria control, they note. The team surveyed people in Papua New Guinea.

More than two thousand samples were gathered in the survey. Tests used both light microscopy and molecular methods. Two malaria species were tracked in blood samples. The title reports that parasite load and age matter most. Both factors shaped gametocyte levels for each species. The findings help target the human reservoir of infection.
openalex-w1985667523:
Rajwant Kaur and co-authors studied an invasive tree's impacts. Their paper is dated 2012 in the catalog record. Prosopis juliflora is a tree that invades dry lands. It forms a complex with its relative Prosopis pallida. Communities feel its spread in varied, debated ways.

The team coordinated comparisons across the tree's ranges. They compared impacts in native and non-native regions. A comparison with a close relative added control. Such grounded designs separate plant effects from place effects. Findings can guide where to clear or use the tree. Dryland policy needs that local, tested evidence base.
openalex-w2040593023:
Harald Schunck, Gaute Lavik, Dhwani Desai and colleagues studied a huge toxic plume in the ocean off Peru. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. The waters hold a zone with very little oxygen. Sometimes hydrogen sulfide builds up there. That gas is toxic to most larger marine life.

A research cruise in 2009 found a giant sulfide plume. It covered a vast area of shelf water. It was the largest such plume ever reported. The team sampled the microbes living inside it. Many were bacteria that oxidise sulfur compounds. Rate tests showed active carbon fixation in the dark water. Microbes there live by chemical energy, not sunlight. The plume offers a rare look at that way of life.
openalex-w2068794323:
Tomas Duffy, Margarita Bisio, Jaime Altcheh and colleagues built a precise PCR method to track Chagas parasites in blood. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2009. Parasite load guides care for Chagas patients. Existing tests could not count parasites reliably. A standard counting method was needed.

Their test targets a repeated DNA stretch in the parasite. It detects extremely low parasite levels in blood. Accuracy held across a very wide range. A commercial kit step reduced test interference from blood. An added control corrected each sample's processing losses. The method expressed parasite loads in exact terms. It gave clinics a tool to monitor treatment response.
openalex-w2073840323:
Tania Kelnert and Claudete Silva reviewed a bestselling American book on reforming government. Their review appeared in a Brazilian administration journal in 1993. The book, by David Osborne and Ted Gaebler, argued for entrepreneurial government. It had become one of the most discussed books in the United States.

Osborne was a journalist and government consultant. Gaebler had managed American cities. Their proposal urged government to act more like a business. President Clinton used the same reform language publicly. He promised to cut federal bureaucracy. The reviewers explain the book's ideas for Brazilian readers. They place it within public administration debates of the time.
openalex-w2092288223:
Steven Stoddard, Amy Morrison, Gonzalo Vazquez-Prokopec and colleagues examined how human travel spreads mosquito-borne disease. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2009. Movement shapes who meets biting insects. It works across many time and place scales. The authors built a model to weigh its role.

They focused on dengue and its day-biting mosquito. Daily routines carry people through many small places. Mosquito biting habits interact with those movements. Short trips can matter as much as long ones. Exposure varies strongly between individuals. Standard models often ignore such fine movement. The paper shows when movement details change predictions. Control plans should account for daily travel patterns.
openalex-w2119721623:
Martin Kulldorff, Richard Heffernan, Jessica Hartman, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2005. They asked how officials can spot a disease outbreak early. Their problem was simple: case counts often come with no good population data. Daily records from emergency rooms, ambulances, and pharmacies often lack that base.

The authors propose a scan method that uses case numbers alone. It makes few guesses about when or where an outbreak starts. They tested it on daily emergency room visits in New York City. Four of the five strongest signals looked like early local signs of wider outbreaks. Those outbreaks were rotavirus, norovirus, and flu, and false alarms were few.
openalex-w2316628323:
Jessica Lleixà, Valentina Martín, María Portillo, and colleagues published this study in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016. They compare fermentations and wines made by inoculating two different yeasts. The standard wine yeast does the job reliably, but winemakers increasingly try wild yeasts to add complexity and character.

Grape must ferments when yeasts turn its sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Wild yeasts riding in on grape skins once meant unpredictable, sometimes spoiled fermentations. Yet many carry enzymes the standard yeast lacks, including ones that free aroma compounds locked in grape sugars. The study sets the two species side by side through fermentation and into the finished wines. Such comparisons tell winemakers what each yeast brings, and what it risks.
openalex-w2742149023:
Ayelén Dichdji wrote this 2017 article in the journal Luna Azul, in Spanish with an English summary. It stages a dialogue between two fields: environmental history and anthropology. Both study how people relate to nature, a topic gaining urgency as socio-environmental conflicts grow more visible. The article reviews what anthropology has contributed to historical studies of environmental questions.

Dichdji tours the central authors who tried to define environmental history as a field. She then turns to anthropologists who approached the nature-culture divide from different angles. Environmental history, she notes, is hard to pin down because it welcomes many approaches. That openness makes it a multidisciplinary field that folds nature into human history. The essay helps readers see how the two disciplines sharpen each other. It suits students entering either field in Latin America and beyond.
openalex-w2898493623:
The MiniBooNE Collaboration reported a neutrino anomaly in Physical Review Letters in 2018, with A. A. Aguilar-Arevalo heading the author list. The experiment at Fermilab watches a muon neutrino beam for electron neutrinos appearing. Standard physics with three neutrino types predicts very little appearance at this distance. An earlier experiment, LSND, had seen an unexplained excess decades before.

With doubled data, MiniBooNE saw an excess of about three hundred eighty electronlike events, at 4.5 standard deviations. Adding its antineutrino running brought the combined excess to about four hundred sixty events. An oscillation explanation would need at least a fourth, sterile neutrino type. The result matches LSND's excess in size and energy. Together the two experiments reach six standard deviations. Either a discovery or a stubborn systematic error, the anomaly refuses to fade.
openalex-w2949716623:
M. A. Acero, P. Adamson, L. Aliaga, and colleagues of the NOvA collaboration published this paper in Physical Review Letters in 2019. It reports the first measurement of neutrino oscillation parameters made with both neutrinos and antineutrinos. Neutrinos are ghostly particles that shift between types as they travel.

Oscillation is the name for that shifting, and its exact rates test the basic rules of particle physics. NOvA is a long-distance experiment built to watch neutrino beams over hundreds of kilometers. By comparing how neutrinos and their antimatter partners changed along the way, the team measured the governing parameters in a new way. The result sharpens tests of whether matter and antimatter behave alike.
openalex-w3004109123:
Savitha DeBritto, Tanzeembanu Gajbar, Praveen Satapute, and colleagues published this study in Scientific Reports in 2020. It isolates pyocyanin, a blue-green pigment made by a common soil germ, and tests its uses. The pigment has valued uses in medicine, farming, and green technology.

The team found a strong pigment-making strain in farm soil and confirmed its name by gene checks. Feeding the cultures unlike foods changed output, with a soybean-enriched broth giving the best yield. They cleaned the pigment and proved its makeup with lab tools. The pure pigment then did well as a dye and in farm chemical tests, the authors report. Such finds may add new uses for a germ best known as a cause of infection.
openalex-w3006366423:
Members of the Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network published this study in Nature Communications in 2019. It hunts for human gene variants that change a person's risk of severe malaria. The network gathered genome data on about seventeen thousand cases and controls from eleven countries across Africa, Asia, and Oceania.

The team also sequenced family trios and typed candidate spots in fifteen thousand further samples. They found five sturdy links between gene regions and severe malaria, including a newly implicated variant on chromosome six. Together the variants explain about one tenth of the inherited share of risk. The new chromosome six signal tied most strongly to cerebral malaria, the deadliest form of the disease.
openalex-w3172681723:
Michela Antonelli, Annika Reinke, Spyridon Bakas, and colleagues introduce the Medical Segmentation Decathlon in Nature Communications in 2022. Segmentation means outlining structures, such as tumours, in medical scans so computers can measure them. Thousands of algorithms do this task, yet picking a starting design for a new problem stays hard.

The Decathlon is a contest where one algorithm must handle many imaging tasks and scan types. Its data sets were built to include common hardships: few images, uneven labels, data from many hospitals, and tiny targets. A final mystery round tested whether entries could solve unseen tasks without any changes. The contest gives the field a fair test of general-purpose tools.
openalex-w4308769923: Josef Smolen, Robert Landewé, J. W. J. Bijlsma, and colleagues present the EULAR recommendations for managing rheumatoid arthritis with disease-modifying drugs. The catalogue record lists an earlier update. The preserved sample, though, is the publisher's page for the 2022 update in the Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. That page gives only citation details and the author list. It has no readable recommendation text, so the guidance itself cannot be summarised from it here.
openalex-w4360603423:
Anna Gilmore, Alice Fabbri, Fran Baum, and colleagues define the commercial determinants of health in The Lancet in 2023. The phrase names how business products and practices shape health, for good or ill. The largest global corporations, they argue, drive much avoidable illness, planetary damage, and inequality. Just four industry sectors already account for at least a third of deaths worldwide.

The paper describes a system in which powerful firms can cause harm while others pay the costs. As company wealth and power grow, governments and citizens grow weaker in response. Known policies then stall, unenforced, while health systems strain under rising disease. The authors insist governments can and must act, for the sake of future generations.
openalex-w4366091323:
Shams Forruque Ahmed, Md. Sakib Bin Alam, Maruf Hassan, and colleagues review deep learning modelling in Artificial Intelligence Review in 2023. Deep learning teaches computers to find patterns by passing data through many layers of transformation. It has produced striking results in health care, education, security, and industry. Yet surveys covering the whole field's designs remain surprisingly few, the authors note.

Their review compares the main model families, how each is trained, and where each works best. Many models excel only in narrow domains, they find. Training can be slow and costly and demands huge datasets for accuracy. Models can also be fooled, misclassify, or settle into poor solutions. The authors map these strengths and weaknesses to guide builders toward sturdier designs.
openalex-w7128498023:
Marvelous Popoola, Sharmeen Malik, Kaushalendra Mani Tripathi, and colleagues study bleeding severity and quality of life in immune thrombocytopenia. Their study appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. The disease destroys platelets, the cells that stop bleeding. Bleeding ranges from bruises to dangerous brain haemorrhage.

Patients also live with fatigue and constant fear of bleeding. The team ran a cross-sectional study at hospital haematology clinics. They set out to measure how bleeding severity tracks quality of life. Most past work comes from wealthier countries, not South Asian practice. A clear link would push clinicians to treat the condition's daily burden, not only its platelet counts.
openalex-w7204939723:
Marlisson Jose de Sousa Silva led a Portuguese-language article, published in Brazil in 2026, on drone technology in the service of the Military Police of Pará, in the Brazilian Amazon. Digital technologies have transformed public security, and remotely piloted aircraft are now part of police operations. The theoretical and documentary study analyzes the force's acquisition of drones and the technical training of its personnel, and the resulting use of the technology against crime.

Using new technologies modernizes the force's equipment and operational actions, the authors report. Investment in state-of-the-art technology expresses an attempt to raise policing effectiveness and, above all, to preserve life in high-stakes police actions. In a state of vast distances and rivers, an eye in the sky changes what a patrol can do.
openalex-w7206151423:
Daiane de Lourdes Alves Velho and five colleagues weigh smart tools in schools that take all kids. Their 2026 Brazil study reads past work and state rules. To take all kids, they stress, is more than a seat in a room. Walls must come down in how staff teach, talk, and use tech, so each child can join in.

Smart tutors, tools that adapt, and mixed forms of text can widen the door to lore and help staff shape plans to each child. But the team sets firm terms. Staff must guide the use. The tools must be fit for all kids. Child data must stay safe. Rules must fight the gaps in who has tech at home, and bias baked into the code. Used with clear aims and care for each child's worth, the tools can back the school of all.
openalex-w7212194923:
Julia Gomes da Silva, Mariana Fernandes Ramos dos Santos, and Renato Marcelo Resgala Junior review a thin shelf of work: how grown children fare when their parents split. Most past work tracks young kids and teens when a marriage ends. These three ask what the same break does to sons and daughters who are past age eighteen. The review is broad and reads work in three tongues across six databases.

Grown children, they note, have their own homes and ties. Yet the bond to each parent runs deep and lasts. A late split can thus shake their moods, their views, and their close ties in real ways. The shelf of proof is thin, they grant. That gap is the point of the piece. It maps what is known, and marks where care and study should go next.
openalex-w7213306923:
Erica Karine Amorim Norbutas and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva tell of a class of young kids in Sorocaba, Brazil, who learned their town by heart. The class was in its next-to-first year of school. For two terms of 2026 the staff tied five fields to the town's own skin. The fields met its streets and slopes, its ipe trees in bloom, its river, its past, and beds of sun blooms in the yard.

The kids wrote a chant-poem as a class and watched seeds sprout. Their gains showed in plain acts. They joined in more. They named streets and trees out of class, on their own. Old themes, met again, drew on town lore with ease. Reads and speech drew more zeal too. The tale makes a case: start the plan from the ground the kids stand on, and school lore turns into lived lore.
openalex-w7214196623:
Danilo Alves de França leads a review, in English, on bats, vectors, and emerging disease under One Health. Their 2026 review treats bats as long-standing reservoirs of infectious agents worldwide. Ticks, fleas, and mosquitoes associated with bats receive dedicated attention, alongside the main microorganisms detected in bats so far.

Habitat loss, climate change, and human behaviour help pathogens jump to new hosts, they argue, including people and domestic animals. Mitigation must avoid harming bat populations, given their ecological importance. Watching for first disease signs in bats while preserving their habitat can prevent future outbreaks, they conclude. Public health strategy, in this account, runs through ecosystem care rather than against wildlife.
openalex-w7214589623:
Hermison Victor Pereira Alencar Sampaio and John Ross Silva Carvalho wrote a 2026 historical study of policing in Brazil, framed as a tension between the sword and citizenship. They examine how the civil and military police formed, how military thinking entered the policing of civilians, and how the penal system selects whom it punishes. Their method is a critical reading of social history, criminology, and documents.

Militarization, they argue, did not begin with the 1964 dictatorship or one constitutional clause. It grew over a long history shaped by slavery, unequal protection of property, repression of workers, and imported security techniques. Formal labels mislead: civilian forces can act with a war mindset, while military forces can sometimes mediate. Democratizing public safety, they conclude, needs clear duties, stronger investigation, accountability, and respect for police officers' own rights as workers.
openalex-w7214671023:
Elfas Alberto Macia wrote a 2026 article on ethics in robotics, moving from the foundations of bioethics to how autonomous systems should be controlled. As robots and artificial intelligence act with growing independence, questions of human dignity, privacy, fairness, and blame grow sharper. His study reviews the literature and national and world rules, with the field's classic works.

Responsible robotics, he argues, must go beyond whether a machine works: it needs people in charge, bioethics, guarding against algorithmic risk, and clear blame across a system's whole life. Hard cases include lethal autonomous military systems and whether a machine could hold legal personality. For Mozambique, his home context, he calls for stronger rules and national plans for ethical control of artificial intelligence, keeping the duty human and social rather than leaving it to the machines.
openalex-w7214993723:
Julia Beatriz Mendes e Silva wrote a 2026 review, titled around late diagnosis in adult women, on why autism is spotted late in women and what neuropsychology adds. Searching two databases for studies from 2020 to 2025 in Portuguese and English, she studied gender differences, social camouflage known as masking, and the life effects of being spotted late.

Autistic women often show subtler clinical signs and develop ways to hide social difficulties. Filtered through gender stereotypes, they are recognized late. Late diagnosis was tied to more psychiatric comorbidity, a damaged sense of self, mental suffering, strained ties, and wrong treatments. Spotting how autism presents in women, she concludes, is vital for better diagnosis and care fitted to each woman. It also calls for tools tuned to how autism shows in women, and earlier diagnosis that improves quality of life.
openalex-w7220437223:
Vanessa Cristina Machado wrote a 2026 article on play and children's cultures in contemporary times. Childhood, she argues, is not the same for all children, nor a universal condition, but a construction of history and society in which children produce and transform culture. Play, on that view, is far more than entertainment or a learning instrument: it is a special way children take up, rework, and create culture itself.

Digital culture now forms part of the conditions shaping children's cultures, widening their stock of stories and words while bringing acceleration, continuous stimulation, consumption, and capture of attention. Early childhood education therefore faces a clear challenge: neither push children away from digital culture nor absorb it blindly. Schools must keep children's experience open to imagination, creation, interaction, and a thoughtful taking-up of culture, she concludes, reading it in a critical, dialectical way.
openalex-w7220738323:
Juliel Marcos Alves Pimentel led a 2026 legal article on facial recognition in Brazil's criminal justice system, on wrongful convictions. The technology helps police work, the authors grant, but it is fallible and can amplify inequalities. Their documentary research draws on doctrine, legislation, recent court decisions, and reports from public defender offices and conviction review projects.

Human and institutional failures combine with algorithmic racism, the phenomenon in which systems err more on Black faces, to produce arrests and convictions of innocent people. The article seeks legal and system parameters for responsible use of facial recognition, aligned with the federal constitution and criminal procedural guarantees, that cut injustice and violations of fundamental rights. Due process, on their account, must govern its output before that output can govern a defendant's fate.
openalex-w7221063323:
Anderson Nascimento Santos and Moacir dos Santos Andrade mapped academic writing on joining art with chemistry teaching between 2015 and 2025, publishing their overview in 2026. They searched Brazilian and international education journals for work that uses artistic languages to make chemistry learning more meaningful.

Fifty-five articles dealt directly with the pairing. Visual arts, theater, and literature appeared most often, with comic strips, dramatizations, and cordel ballads among the favorite forms. Even so, the authors judge the meeting of art and chemistry still little studied. They present their timeline as a tool for spotting trends and gaps, and they argue that art can make chemistry teaching more dynamic and creative.
osty-supernormal-faculties-in-man-1923:
Eugène Osty, a French doctor who led a Paris institute for psychical study, published Supernormal Faculties in Man in 1923. Osty reported tests with people said to know facts they could not have learned in normal ways. He used the term supernormal for powers beyond the usual senses.

Case studies follow subjects through sittings where they described hidden objects, past events, and distant scenes. Osty tried to rule out fraud and lucky guessing, and he set out rules for such tests. His work reflects the French branch of psychical research, which leaned toward careful case work in the lab and the study room.
otto-idea-of-holy-1923:
Rudolf Otto was a German theologian whose Idea of the Holy, in this 1923 English edition, changed the study of religion worldwide. Otto argues that religion rests on an experience that reason alone cannot capture. He names that core the numinous, from the Latin word for divine power.

The numinous, he says, is a mystery at once fearful and fascinating, the mysterium tremendum that makes worshippers tremble and draw near. He finds it in Hebrew prophets, Hindu hymns, and the silence of Quaker worship alike. His book founded the modern phenomenology of religion, the study of faith as it is felt.
parry-second-voyage-northwest-passage-18:
Parry's second Arctic voyage, from 1821 to 1823, sought the passage by Hudson Bay and the straits beyond. His Journal of a Second Voyage appeared in 1824. Two winters in the ice gave the work its special value.

The crews wintered at Winter Island and then at Igloolik, where they lived beside an Inuit community. Parry records Inuit dress, hunting, family life, and language with unusual care. That makes the book a landmark of early Arctic ethnography as well as a voyage narrative. The passage stayed hidden, but the human record of those winters endures. Plates of Inuit dress, tools, and homes give the text lasting worth.
peirce-chance-love-logic-1923:
Charles S. Peirce's essays were gathered in Chance, Love, and Logic in 1923, the first anthology of his work. Morris Cohen edited the volume. Peirce, who died in poverty in 1914, founded pragmatism and much of modern logic. The essays cover his theory of meaning, belief, and inquiry.

Peirce argues that a belief is a habit of action and truth is inquiry's long-run aim. Other pieces defend chance in nature and an evolutionary love as a cosmic force. His terms tychism and agapism name those bold ideas. The anthology rescued Peirce for a new generation. It is still a good first Peirce.
perry-children-of-the-sun-1923:
W. J. Perry wrote The Children of the Sun in 1923. Perry was a keen fan of the spread school of G. Elliot Smith. The book makes Egypt the well of all high culture on Earth. Its title comes from the sun kings he saw at the root of each great land.

Stone graves, gold hunts, and sun rites trace his claim round the globe. He holds that bands from Egypt bore these traits to Asia and the New World. The claim drew fire then and still splits views now. The book is the grand plea of the spread school at its peak.
plaw-118-11-2023: Public Law 118-11 is the Pala Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2023, approved on July 28, 2023 by the 118th Congress. The law covers about seven hundred twenty-one acres of land in San Diego County, California, known as the Gregory Canyon property. If the tribe hands title to the United States in time, the Secretary must take the land into trust for the Pala Band. The land then joins the Pala Indian Reservation.
plaw-118-12-2023: Public Law 118-12, approved on July 28, 2023, renames a veterans clinic in Indian River, Michigan. The law states that the community clinic at 5739 Highway M-68 shall be known as the Pfc. Justin T. Paton Department of Veterans Affairs Clinic. Any mention of that clinic in a federal law, rule, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-118-5-2023:
Public Law 118-5 is the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, approved on June 3, 2023. The law provides for a sound rise in the federal debt ceiling, as its title states. It pairs that rise with new limits on federal spending.

One division sets caps on spending for fiscal years 2024 and 2025, with special changes for those years. It also sets budget rules for the House and the Senate. A second division, called Save Taxpayer Dollars, takes back funds that agencies had been given but had not yet spent on their programs. The debt ceiling is the legal cap on how much the Treasury may borrow in total.
plaw-118-7-2023: Public Law 118-7 is the Changing Age-Determined Eligibility To Student Incentive Payments Act, or the CADETS Act, approved on June 30, 2023. The law changes the age rule for a payment program at the state maritime academies. Those schools train students for work at sea. Under the law, a student qualifies if the student will meet the age rule for joining the Navy Reserve by the time of graduation.
plos-pbio-0020123:
Nicholas T. Ingolia modeled a patterning network in the fruit fly in PLOS Biology in 2004. In the fly embryo, genes in the segment polarity network lock each body segment into its final form. The author used math models to test how the network holds its pattern when parts are noisy or stressed.

A good network must be robust: it should give the same neat stripes even when gene levels wobble. The models show which links in the network carry that stability. Work of this kind turns a wiring diagram into predictions that lab tests can check. It shows how embryos get reliable shapes from sloppy parts, a puzzle at the heart of development.
plos-pbio-0020423:
Peiman Hematti, Bum-Kee Hong, Cole Ferguson, and their team compared gene therapy vectors in primates in PLOS Biology in 2004. Vectors based on MLV and SIV viruses carry new genes into blood stem cells. Each virus inserts its cargo into the genome at spots of its choosing.

The study found the two vectors favor distinct kinds of insertion sites in primate stem cells. That difference matters for safety. Insertions near growth genes can raise cancer risk, a harm seen in early gene therapy trials. Choosing a vector with a safer insertion pattern is thus a practical design step. The paper gives trial planners hard comparative data, not just theory.
plos-pone-0000023:
Karen Aboody, Rebecca Bush, Elizabeth Garcia, and co-authors worked in 2006 on aiming cancer treatment only at the cancer. Metastatic cancer, disease that has spread to new sites, is what usually kills. Drugs that reach it also poison healthy tissue. The team developed a tumor-selective approach meant to treat the spread while sparing the rest of the body.

A selective method changes the arithmetic of therapy: stronger attacks become safer when they concentrate in tumors. The paper reports the design of the approach and its early performance against metastatic disease. Work of this kind laid ground for later targeted and cell-based cancer treatments, where the whole point is to hit the tumor and leave the patient standing.
plos-pone-0000123:
Laure Perchepied, Thomas Kroj, Maurice Tronchet, and colleagues published this plant genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2006. Their subject is Arabidopsis thaliana, a small weed used as a model plant. They asked why some plants resist the bacterial pathogen Pseudomonas syringae better than others.

The authors traced the partial resistance to two major spots in the genome, called QTLs, that together control much of the natural variation. Work of this kind shows breeders and biologists where resistance lives in the DNA. It also helps explain how wild plants vary in fighting off disease without any human help.
plos-pone-0000223:
Michael S. Akhras, Sreedevi Thiyagarajan, Andrea C. Villablanca, and colleagues published this diagnostics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents PathogenMip, a multiplex pathogen detection assay. One test can identify many disease-causing microbes at once, instead of running a separate test for each suspect.

Doctors facing a fever often must guess which pathogen to test for. A multiplex assay screens a panel of candidates in one run. The authors describe and evaluate their assay's design. Faster, broader detection can shorten the time to the right treatment, a gain that matters most in serious infections.
plos-pone-0000323:
Anson W. Lowe, Mari Olsen, Ying Hao, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pancreatic tumors are among the deadliest cancers and among the hardest to study. The authors compare gene expression patterns across pancreatic tumors, cultured cells, and tissues to find which patterns are truly characteristic of the cancer.

Cell lines drift from the tumors they came from, so cross-checking them against real tissue matters. The authors sort expression signals by source. Their patterns provide candidate markers for a cancer that is usually found too late, and a check on which lab models deserve trust.
plos-pone-0000423:
Melanie T. Cushion and colleagues read the gene activity of a lung fungus at the height of infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pneumocystis carinii infects the lungs, and its fulminate stage is the most severe. The team profiled the transcriptome, the full set of genes switched on, during that stage, with attention to carbohydrate metabolism.

How a parasite fuels itself inside the lung may explain how it thrives there. From the expression pattern, the authors develop the idea of a compatible parasite, one well matched to its host niche. That framing could guide the search for drug targets in an organism that is hard to grow and study in the lab.
plos-pone-0000523:
Frédérick Barreau and colleagues showed a gut sensor is needed to keep lymphoid tissue in balance, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. CARD15/NOD2 is a protein that detects bacterial pieces inside cells; its variants are famous as Crohn's disease risk factors. The team found it is required for Peyer's patches homeostasis in mice, the steady state of the gut's immune outposts.

Peyer's patches sample gut contents and train immune responses. If a bacterial sensor is required to maintain them, Crohn's-linked variants may distort the gut's immune training from early life. Mouse findings like this give the human genetics a mechanism to test.
plos-pone-0000623:
Anders Krarup, Russell Wallis, Julia S. Presanis and co-authors studied one protease with two jobs, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The complement system helps the immune system recognize and clear foreign bodies. One of its three activation routes, the lectin pathway, depends on a protease called MASP-2, attached to mannan-binding lectin.

Their title reports that MASP-2 switches on two systems at once: complement and coagulation, the blood-clotting cascade. That link ties immune defense to clot formation through a single enzyme. Immunologists and blood researchers both have reason to care, since a shared trigger could shape how the body answers infection and injury together.
plos-pone-0000723:
Joseph K. Jun and Dezhe Z. Jin modeled how circuits learn to fire in precise time patterns, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neurons in many brain areas produce spike sequences timed to within small fractions of a second, spanning hundreds of milliseconds. Examples appear in songbird premotor areas, cat visual cortex, and primary motor cortex. Synfire chains, networks where groups of neurons trigger the next group, are a proposed structure.

The model grows such chains through spontaneous activity, axon remodeling, and synaptic plasticity. In plain terms, practice and rewiring tune the timing. Explaining how precise sequences develop speaks to bird song, movement, and any behavior that lives or dies by timing.
plos-pone-0000823:
Morgane Rolland, David C. Nickle, Wenjie Deng and colleagues asked which parts of HIV the immune system actually targets, in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes preferentially target specific regions of the viral proteome, but the viral features driving that recognition were not well understood. One hypothesis holds that similarities between HIV and human proteins shape the targeting, since immune cells learn to spare self-like shapes.

Their title states the relationship they found: recognition of HIV-1 peptides by host CTL is related to HIV-1 similarity to human proteins. If self-similarity shields viral regions from attack, vaccine designers should aim at the regions that look least human.
plos-pone-0000923:
Ana Paula Trombone, Celio Silva, Karla Lima and colleagues followed a DNA vaccine ingredient through the cell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA vaccines can raise both antibody and cell based defenses against many targets. Yet what happens to the injected DNA once inside a cell is still being mapped.

The team studied a vaccine built around Hsp65, a stress protein. They report that uptake of the DNA changes the acidity of late endosomes and lysosomes, the cell's sorting and recycling compartments. That shift interferes with antigen presentation, the step that shows targets to immune cells. Details like this decide whether a vaccine design works in practice, not just on paper.
plos-pone-0001023:
Seif Shekalaghe, Chris Drakeley, Roly Gosling and colleagues tested a drug add on to clear lingering malaria forms, in PLOS ONE in 2007. After treatment with the standard drug pair, some malaria parasites persist as gametocytes, the forms mosquitoes pick up. Those hidden forms can keep transmission going even after a patient feels cured.

The team measured whether a single dose of primaquine clears submicroscopic gametocytes that survive the standard treatment. Clearing them could cut spread from treated patients, a benefit beyond the individual cure. The study weighs that gain for malaria programs deciding whether to add primaquine routinely.
plos-pone-0001123:
Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited heart disease in which the heart muscle grows too thick. Niels Volkmann and co-authors studied one of its best-known causes in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The cause is a mutation called R403Q in the beta-myosin heavy chain, a motor protein of heart muscle.

Mutations in nearly every protein of the cardiac sarcomere, the muscle's contractile unit, have been linked to this disease. The authors examined what the R403Q change does where myosin meets actin, the interface that produces force. Their title reports that the mutation causes disorder at that interface, which helps explain how a tiny change weakens the heart.
plos-pone-0001223:
Recognizing a familiar face feels instant, but how personal familiarity changes face processing speed is not settled. Benjamin Balas, David Cox, and Erin Conwell tested the effect using faces people knew in real life, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Earlier studies of familiarity and face judgments had given equivocal results across different tasks and stimulus sets.

The authors measured how fast information is processed for personally familiar faces versus unfamiliar ones. Real-world familiarity is stronger than the lab kind, where a face is merely repeated. Their results speak to what familiarity actually buys the visual system: speed, accuracy, or both.
plos-pone-0001323:
Practice improves performance on sensory tasks, but the improvement is usually specific: train on one stimulus and the gain does not transfer. Ben Webb, Neil Roach, and Paul McGraw report an exception, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. When sensory judgments are particularly challenging, improvements are normally tightly coupled to the trained task and configuration.

The authors describe perceptual learning in the absence of task or stimulus specificity. That is, training improved performance broadly rather than narrowly. The specificity of learning is usually taken as a clue to where in the brain it happens; a general transfer points somewhere else.
plos-pone-0001423:
Katia Bassichetto and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on HIV risk in young people in São Paulo, Brazil. Spotting fresh infections is key to tracking how HIV spreads in a region. The team compared people with fresh infection to others in their data. They asked which traits marked a higher risk of recent infection.

Their results point to a raised risk for teens and young adults in the city. Youth focused outreach may thus matter more than broad plans alone. The study also shows the worth of tests that can tell fresh from old infection. Such tests help health teams aim scarce funds where spread is active now.
plos-pone-0001523:
Nicola Martinelli and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on clotting genes and heart attacks. Heart attacks are the main clot outcome of artery disease. Most work had looked at one clotting gene at a time. The team instead weighed the joint effect of several such variants in patients with advanced artery disease.

Joint tests can catch risks that single gene tests miss. The study maps how these variants add up, or fail to, in real patients. That joint view fits how clotting truly works, as a team of factors. It may refine risk scores for patients who already have grave artery disease.
plos-pone-0001623:
Troels T. Marstrand, Jes Frellsen, Ida Moltke, and their colleagues introduced a computer framework named Asap in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The tool tackles a common task in gene research: finding spots where transcription factors bind DNA more often than chance would explain. Transcription factors are proteins that switch genes on and off, so their binding sites help show how genes are controlled.

As sets of genes thought to be co-regulated grow larger, testing whether they share a common binding pattern takes fast, sound statistics. Asap was built to run those over-representation tests in a structured way. The full text describes the method, how it compares with earlier published methods, and the kinds of gene sets it can check. It is aimed at researchers who study gene regulation with large gene lists.
plos-pone-0001723:
Elodie Gaulin, Mohammed-Amine Madoui, Arnaud Bottin, and their co-authors catalogued the genes of a plant pathogen in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Aphanomyces euteiches is an oomycete, a water mold, that causes seedling blight and root rot in legumes such as alfalfa and pea. Its genus sits apart from better-studied oomycetes like Phytophthora, and its species attack plants and water animals alike.

The team sequenced the pathogen's transcriptome, the set of genes it switches on, to find putative pathogenicity factors and metabolic pathways. The full text gives the gene catalogue and the candidate attack proteins. A parts list for this mold's infection machinery gives crop science new targets for resistant pea and alfalfa varieties.
plos-pone-0001823:
Aranzazú Rosado, Fabian Zanella, Beatriz Garcia, and their co-authors built a screening platform for cancer drug candidates in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Inhibiting Akt signaling is considered one of the most promising therapeutic strategies for many cancers. Cell-based drug screens, though, had historically been compromised by the absence of suitable controls to judge selectivity.

Their dual-color fluorescence platform identifies selective inhibitors of Akt signaling, comparing treated pathway activity against a built-in reference. The full text gives the cell system and the screen results. A screen that reports selectivity from the start saves the common failure of finding a potent drug that is toxic to everything.
plos-pone-0001923:
Fumiko Hoeft and co-authors built a fake version of a brain tool for fair tests, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, pulses the brain through the skull and is used to prove links between brain areas and acts. It is also in trials as a treatment for ills such as depression.

Fair trials need a sham tool that feels real but does not stimulate, so patients and staff stay blind to who got the true dose. The team's sham can be switched on and off by electronics, which makes blinding strict. Good shams are what let TMS trials prove that gains come from the pulses, not from hope.
plos-pone-0002023:
Silke Lissek and co-authors scanned brains during cooperation and deceit, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Theory of mind is the mind's tool for picturing what others intend and expect. It shapes social life and helps us judge whether a partner will cooperate or defect for gain.

The team used brain scans as people played social tasks that called for teamwork or for trickery. As the title states, cooperation and deception recruit different subsets of the theory-of-mind network. One network, split by intent: the split may explain how the brain keeps track of friends and frauds in unlike ways.
plos-pone-0002123:
Nathan Cannon and co-authors studied the hepatitis C virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They tracked how the virus changes during drug treatment. The standard therapy at the time, pegylated interferon plus ribavirin, failed in about half of patients with genotype 1, the most common type. Failure came either as no response at all or as a relapse after a strong first drop in virus levels.

The authors followed the virus across its full open-reading frame, the long stretch of its genome that codes for proteins. By watching how the virus population shifts during therapy, they aimed to learn why treatment works for some people and fails for others.
plos-pone-0002223:
Akio Nakashima, Yoshiko Maruki, Yuko Imamura, and co-authors found a new role for a growth pathway in yeast, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The Tor pathway is a master control of cell growth. The drug rapamycin blocks it, halting cells in the first phase of the division cycle. Whether Tor also acts at later stages of the cycle was largely unknown.

The team reports that Tor signaling helps run the shift from the G2 phase into mitosis, the stage where chromosomes are pulled apart. The link runs through polo-kinase, a key driver of mitosis. The finding widens the reach of a pathway already targeted by drugs.
plos-pone-0002323:
Dilip Mahalanabis and co-authors ran a randomized trial of an oral cholera vaccine in Kolkata, India, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A killed, whole-cell cholera vaccine had been used in Vietnam since the 1990s. It was reformulated to meet World Health Organization requirements so other countries could use it.

Adults and children in a cholera-endemic area received the bivalent vaccine, covering both main cholera strains, or a placebo, assigned by chance. The team assessed safety and the strength of the immune response. A cheap, safe oral vaccine that passes a placebo-controlled trial is a strong candidate for public vaccination campaigns.
plos-pone-0002423:
Kerse and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Ngaire Kerse, Leon Flicker, Jon J. Pfaff, among others. Its subject is falls, Depression and Antidepressants in Later Life: A Large Primary Care Appraisal. Depression and falls are common and co-exist for older people.

Safe management of each of these conditions is important to quality of life. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002523:
Gibbs joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Adrian J. Gibbs, Kazusato Ohshima, Matthew J. Phillips, among others. Its subject is the Prehistory of Potyviruses: Their Initial Radiation Was during the Dawn of Agriculture. Potyviruses are found world wide, are spread by probing aphids and cause considerable crop damage.

Potyvirus is one of the two largest plant virus genera and contains about 15% of all named plant virus species. When and why did the potyviruses become so many? The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002623:
Thai Nho Dinh and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was adaptation of saccharomyces cerevisiae cells to high ethanol concentration and changes in fatty acid composition of membrane and cell size. The catalog record names Thai Nho Dinh first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Microorganisms can adapt to perturbations of the surrounding environment to grow. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002723:
Xiujuan Wang and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was seventeen new complete mtDNA sequences reveal extensive mitochondrial genome evolution within the demospongiae. Authorship is credited in the record to Xiujuan Wang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Two major transitions in animal evolution–the origins of multicellularity and bilaterality–correlate with major changes in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) organization. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002823:
Chin-Tong Ong and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was notch and presenilin regulate cellular expansion and cytokine secretion but cannot instruct Th1/Th2 fate acquisition. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Chin-Tong Ong, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Recent reports suggested that Delta1, 4 and Jagged1. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002923:
Hongquan Wan, Erin Sorrell, Haichen Song and co-authors tested H9N2 bird flu viruses in ferrets in 2008. H9N2 viruses are common in poultry across much of Eurasia and have infected people in Asia repeatedly since 1998. Judging their pandemic potential means testing how well they grow and spread in mammals.

Ferrets are a standard model for human flu. The PLOS ONE study measured replication and transmission efficiency of these viruses in ferrets. Public health readers get experimental evidence, rather than guesswork, on how close H9N2 sits to a virus that could spread widely in people.
plos-pone-0003023:
Sharad Adekar, Tsuyoshi Takahashi, R. Mark Jones and co-authors reported a human antibody that neutralizes botulinum toxin in 2008. Botulinum neurotoxins are category A bioterror agents and the most potent biological toxins known. Cloned antibody treatments hold promise, but antibodies binding the toxin's light chain faced doubts about usefulness.

Their monoclonal antibody is specific for that catalytic light chain and still neutralizes the toxin, as the title states. Published in PLOS ONE, the result expands the target options for antibody therapy. Botulism has few treatments, so each validated route matters. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003123:
Matan Oren, Marie-line Escande, Guy Paz and co-authors report this 2008 PLOS ONE study of Botryllus schlosseri, a colonial sea squirt. This animal has a rare system for telling self from non-self. When two colonies that do not match touch each other, they mount a rejection response much like inflammation. The team also noted a surprising number of genes like those vertebrates use for blood clotting.

The work tests whether those clotting-like parts switch on during the rejection response. Readers see how a simple marine animal uses tools linked to a far more complex system. That makes the study useful for tracing the deep roots of immunity and clotting.
plos-pone-0003223:
Marco Cassano, Stefano Biressi, Amanda Finan and colleagues study a growth factor variant for muscle in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatocyte growth factor is a cytokine of mesenchymal origin with many roles. It drives cell growth, survival, motility and shape change. Its high affinity receptor, the tyrosine kinase Met, is expressed by many cell types, among them the cells that build muscle.

The team describe Magic-Factor 1, a partial agonist of Met. In the title, it induces muscle hypertrophy by protecting myogenic progenitors from apoptosis, or programmed cell death. Readers get a tuned growth signal that protects muscle precursors. A partial signal may give the gains with fewer side effects than a full one.
plos-pone-0003323:
Anuja Mathew, Joel O'Bryan, William Marshall and colleagues test a weakened vaccinia vaccine in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Vaccinia viruses have been used as a model for viral disease and as a protective live vaccine. The team investigated the immunogenicity of an attenuated strain of vaccinia virus engineered to inactivate the N1L gene, called vGK5. Using the intranasal route, this recombinant virus was far less virulent.

The title reports robust intrapulmonary CD8 T cell responses and protection with the N1L deleted virus. Readers see safety improved while lung T cell protection stayed strong. That trade-off is the central problem of live vaccine design.
plos-pone-0003423:
Roberto Burioni and colleagues tried a mirror-image vaccine idea against HIV in this 2008 study. HIV enters cells by gripping a protein called CD4. The team built antibodies shaped like that grip site. Injected into rabbits, these mimics were meant to train the immune system.

The rabbits did produce responses aimed at HIV itself. Training with a mimic avoids handling the whole virus. Such anti-idiotype approaches copy the target's shape, not the germ. The results support this roundabout route toward an HIV vaccine. Work with such mimics had long been a side road in vaccine research, and this study gave it fresh support.
plos-pone-0003523:
Cheng Wang, Jie Yu, and Caleb B. Kallen ruled out two DNA switches near a key gene in this 2008 paper. PCNA is a protein vital for copying DNA and running the cell cycle. High PCNA levels mark poor outlook in breast cancer. Estrogen raises PCNA production in MCF7 breast cancer cells.

Two estrogen response elements sat near the gene as prime suspects. Testing showed they are not responsible for the estrogen boost. Negative results like this redirect the search for the true mechanism. They also warn against trusting sequence guesses without experiments.
plos-pone-0003623:
Nicholas P. Tucker, Matthew G. Hicks, Thomas A. Clarke, and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It examines NsrR, a protein that switches genes off in many kinds of bacteria. The question was how NsrR detects nitric oxide, a toxic gas bacteria must survive.

The team showed that nitric oxide acts on NsrR through a small iron-sulfur cluster built into the protein. Contact with the gas changes the protein and lifts its grip on target genes. That direct sensing helps explain how harmful and harmless bacteria alike respond when nitric oxide attacks.
plos-pone-0003723:
Francine Noel, Sapna Mehta, Yuwei Zhu, and colleagues published this health study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Since 1999, the GHESKIO center in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, has worked with the health ministry to cut mother-to-child HIV spread. Data on delivering full care in such a setting were limited.

The team examined outcomes for infants of HIV-infected women in this developing country program. They tracked what the program achieved for the babies and where care fell short. The study measures what it takes to improve survival for infants born into the epidemic's hardest conditions.
plos-pone-0003823:
E. J. Dettman and Monica J. Justice published this cancer genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Certain inbred mouse strains develop blood cancers when a leukemia virus inserts itself in their DNA. Those insertions flag nearby genes that may drive cancer. The strains have flagged many candidate oncogenes before.

In lymphoblastic lymphomas with viral insertions at a site called Evi32, the gene Prdm14 was overexpressed. Prdm14 carries a zinc finger and a SET domain, both tied to gene control. The finding nominates Prdm14 as a player in lymphoid cancers worth testing in humans.
plos-pone-0003923:
James W. Wilson, C. Mark Ott, Laura Quick, and co-authors studied Salmonella grown in spaceflight in 2008. Conditions in space mirror some stresses germs face during infection. Germs grown in flight had shown changes not seen with standard lab methods. How the cells sense those flight-linked changes was unclear.

Their PLOS ONE article shows the growth medium's ion mix steers the response. Changing ions altered how Salmonella set its control and virulence genes. That finding gives labs a way to mimic flight effects on the ground. It also flags food and water safety questions for long space missions.
plos-pone-0004023:
Jimmy Susanto, Yu-Hsing Lin, Yun-Nan Chen, and co-authors studied a pump protein in embryonic stem cells in 2008. Stem cells renew themselves many times without losing flexibility. That demands strong defenses to keep their DNA stable. A transport protein called ABCG2 helps guard cells from toxins.

Their PLOS ONE article links ABCG2 to porphyrin balance in stem cells. Porphyrins are pigment building blocks that can harm cells in excess. Keeping them in check supports healthy self-renewal. The work names one defense stem cells use during long growth. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004123:
Joseph-Omer Dyer and colleagues published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It looks at how reflex pathways in the spinal cord change after a stroke. Earlier work had shown changes in muscles that work together or against each other at one joint. Far less was known about pathways linking muscles at different joints.

Those cross-joint routes are called heteronymous pathways. The team measured how signals travel through them in stroke patients and how the changes relate to poor coordination of movement. Their findings link altered spinal wiring to the clumsy movement many patients face, which matters for planning rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0004223:
Sandra Dupouy and colleagues published this breast cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neurotensin is a small signalling molecule, and its high-affinity receptor, NTSR1, had been proposed as one of the factors driving tumour progression. In breast cancer cells, the switched-on receptor coordinates growth signals.

The team examined the neurotensin receptor-1 pathway in human ductal breast cancer, the most common form of the disease. They report that this pathway contributes to the cancer's progression. A pathway that helps a tumour advance is also a pathway that drugs might block. Ductal breast cancer starts in the milk ducts of the breast.
plos-pone-0004323:
Guo-Qiang Wu and colleagues published this heart rhythm study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Heart rate variability analysis rests on a classic paradox. Do the characteristic high- and low-frequency peaks in its power spectrum represent random noise, or chaotic order? Resolving that question is key to unravelling the mechanisms behind heart rate variability and healthy heartbeat control.

The team looked for chaotic signatures in heart rate data and its power spectrum across health, ageing, and heart failure. How the heartbeat's rhythm changes with age and disease can reveal the control system failing. Their approach treats the heart as a dynamical system, not a metronome.
plos-pone-0004423:
Three targeted drugs, taken in pairs or all at once, are weighed in a 2009 PLOS ONE study of chronic myeloid leukemia by Natalia Komarova, Allen Katouli, and Dominik Wodarz. This blood cancer is treated fairly well by the drug imatinib. Trouble comes when the cancer mutates and stops responding to the drug.

Two more targeted drugs were ready to add, so the key question was how to combine them. Using math models of how resistance grows, the authors compared pairs against the triple mix. Their answer, given in the title, is that two drugs together can improve therapy, but three cannot. That kind of result helps doctors plan drug use and slow the rise of resistant cancer.
plos-pone-0004523:
Gene-based cancer markers found in one study often fail in the next, and Joseph Lucas, Carlos Carvalho, Julia Ling-Yu Chen, and co-authors tested why, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microarray studies use gene activity as a common currency across many human diseases. In cancer genomics, the hope is that a signature found in one group of patients will predict outcomes in another.

The team evaluated cross-study projections: taking a genomic biomarker built in one data set and applying it to others. They checked when the projection survives and when it collapses. Reliable projection is the difference between a lab curiosity and a test a clinic can use. Their evaluation gives cancer genomics a sober measure of how far its signatures really travel.
plos-pone-0004623:
HIV makes liver cells easier to kill with a death signal, show Challagundla Babu, Kanitta Suwansrinon, Gary Bren, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Patients infected with HIV have increased susceptibility to liver disease from hepatitis B and C viruses, alcohol, and fatty liver. Clinically, this limits options for antiretroviral therapy and accelerates liver disease rates.

The death signal is TRAIL, a protein that can order cells to self-destruct. The team shows HIV induces TRAIL sensitivity in hepatocytes, the main liver cells. Cells that would normally shrug off the signal become vulnerable. That mechanism may help explain why livers fail faster in HIV patients, and it points to the TRAIL pathway as a place where protective drugs might act.
plos-pone-0004723:
Marco van Eijk and colleagues showed that cutting fatty sugar lipids in fat tissue restores insulin response in obese mice, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fat tissue plays a key role in the insulin block that comes with obesity. Past work showed that a drug that lowers these lipids sharply improves blood sugar control.

The team then studied how the drop changes fat tissue itself. They tracked insulin response, new fat cell growth, and inflammation signs. All three moved in a better direction after lipid lowering. The work supports lipid control as a route to treat diabetes linked to obesity.
plos-pone-0004823:
Christopher Lortie and colleagues proposed cage matching head to head competition tests for invasive plants from different regions, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many hypotheses predict why some plant species become invasive. Yet no standard approach compared the breadth of studies or sorted rival claims. Most hypotheses also lacked direct tests that pit native and introduced groups against each other under matched conditions.

Head to head cages standardize such comparisons. Differences between regions can be tested directly. Invasion biology needs comparable evidence across species. The framework helps design stronger tests. Such evidence helps the field move from broad claims toward tested detail.
plos-pone-0004923:
Cells stay alive by importing small molecules from their surroundings. When conditions change, cells adjust that intake. Maria Werner, Szabolcs Semsey and Kim Sneppen modeled this response system. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. It asks how cells alter the uptake and use of many molecules at once.

Their model follows a network motif. That motif shows up again and again in cellular response systems. It shows uptake and metabolism being coordinated, not handled molecule by molecule. The picture helps explain a general skill of cells. They tune what they take in to match a changing environment.
plos-pone-0005023:
In performing arts, posture is both tool and artwork. Ballet poses obey the body's biomechanical limits. They also follow strict rules set by tradition. Elena Daprati, Marco Iosa and Patrick Haggard studied this mix in PLOS ONE in 2009. They tracked aesthetically relevant changes in dancers' postures.

The team measured how poses shift across a performance. Some changes serve expression, others serve beauty. Viewers respond to those shifts, often without knowing why. The measurements link biomechanics to aesthetics. Science can probe what makes a pose feel right on stage. The work bridges movement science and art. It may also help dancers train the expressive side of technique.
plos-pone-0005123:
Glioblastoma is a deadly brain tumor. Drugs that block VEGF starve it briefly. Tumors escape, and the survival benefit fades. Emmanuelle di Tomaso and colleagues tested an escape route in PLOS ONE in 2009. The suspect was PDGF-C, another growth signal. They used a glioblastoma model.

PDGF-C induced maturation of the tumor's blood vessels. Mature vessels respond less to anti-VEGF treatment. The tumors reroute their plumbing around the drug. The finding names the escape hatch behind a promising therapy's failure. Blocking PDGF-C alongside VEGF might extend the benefit. The study shows why single-signal attacks fail. Tumors keep spare signals ready. Combination therapy is the logical answer.
plos-pone-0005223:
Silvestrol is a natural compound from trees in the genus Aglaia, and it can kill cancer cells. It belongs to a family that blocks the start of protein production in cells. Cencic and colleagues detailed how silvestrol works in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The compound targets eIF4A, a helper protein needed to start reading many cell messages. Jamming that step starves cancer cells of proteins they need to grow. Knowing the exact target and mechanism helps chemists judge whether this tree compound can be shaped into a usable cancer drug.
plos-pone-0005323:
When DNA replicates, the two new strands come out tangled and must be unlinked before division. The enzyme topoisomerase II alpha does that unlinking, and drugs that block it are common cancer treatments. Wray and colleagues found a resistance factor in breast cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Cells watch their tangling status and can trigger checkpoints when unlinking lags. The protein Metnase mediates resistance to topoisomerase II inhibitors, as the title states. Knowing the resistance factor gives drug designers a second target to restore the power of these widely used drugs.
plos-pone-0005423:
Anna Melchers and colleagues used mice to study DNA repair in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The NBN gene makes nibrin, a protein that helps find and fix breaks in both strands of DNA. The gene is so vital that mammals cannot live without it.

The team used mice in which the gene could be switched off in part of the body. After the mice were exposed to radiation, the team mapped which proteins changed in amount. Those protein shifts chart how cells react when a key repair tool is missing and DNA breaks build up.
plos-pone-0005523:
Antonia Vitalo and co-authors studied healing in rats raised alone, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Being raised alone harms health and slows healing in rats, much as stress does in people. A rich, stimulating home setting is known to lift brain levels of oxytocin, a hormone tied to bonding.

The team compared two helps: material to build nests with, and oxytocin itself. Both sped wound healing in the isolated rats by a similar amount. The match hints that simple comforts at home may aid healing through the same hormone path. Simple comforts are cheap and safe, so a real healing gain from them would be easy to use in care.
plos-pone-0005623:
Rose-Anne Romano and co-authors studied a protein isoform in skin cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The deepest layer of skin makes two keratin proteins, K5 and K14, in a tightly matched way. That pairing is a hallmark of the layer's stem-like cells.

The team found that a shortened form of the protein p63 actively drives both keratin genes. It also guides what fate those skin cells take as they mature. Knowing the driver helps explain skin development and diseases where the outer layer fails to form properly. The same keratins are faulted in some blistering skin diseases, which gives the control story a medical side.
plos-pone-0005723:
