Iris Pit and co-authors audited Europe's monitoring records for freshwater invertebrates, the small animals that signal river health. Rivers and lakes hold a rich share of species but face pollution, water extraction, and habitat loss. Their 2026 study gathered millions of records from twenty-eight countries for the early twenty-tens.

Records clustered in central Europe and England, leaving other regions and river types thin. Countries differed in sampling methods, reporting units, and how finely species were named. Those differences block clean Europe-wide trend estimates. Pit and colleagues argue that shared standards for naming and methods, plus better data exchange, are needed before biodiversity trends can be judged fairly across the continent.
plos-pone-0354823:
Xinyu Tian and co-authors developed a structured support programme for family caregivers of autistic children in China. Caregivers carry heavy, many-sided strain that can harm their health and the child's progress. Earlier structured programmes for this exact burden were scarce. Their 2026 development study blended family stress theory with evidence review and the team's own prior findings.

Expert panels refined the draft over two consultation rounds. The finished programme has three core modules covering stressors, how caregivers appraise them, and coping. Inside sit seven themes and twenty-two components, including teaching and mindfulness elements. Tian and colleagues present the programme as ready for formal outcome testing with caregiver groups.
plos-pone-0355223:
Deborah Kilday and colleagues compared delivery outcomes for mothers with and without COVID-19 across successive virus variant periods in the United States. Earlier work tied infection in pregnancy to serious harm, but whether risk changed as variants shifted was unclear. Their 2026 study drew on a national hospital database covering more than two and a half million deliveries.

About two percent of mothers had a COVID-19 diagnosis. Infection came with sharply higher odds of dying in hospital in every variant period studied. The Delta period showed the starkest elevation, while the first Omicron phase showed the smallest, though still raised. Severe maternal illness, early birth, and intensive care use were also tracked. Kilday and colleagues say variant era belongs in obstetric risk planning.
plos-pone-0355623:
Amy K Johnson and colleagues present the protocol for EUPHORIA, a trial aiming to raise use of HIV prevention medication among Black women in Cook County, Illinois, published in 2026. Black women face high HIV rates yet are rarely first in line for pre-exposure prophylaxis, the daily or on-demand medicine that blocks infection. The study works through eight family planning centers.

Clinics will adopt a bundle of support strategies at staggered times, so each center serves as its own comparison. The team will measure prescriptions, continued use, and what helps or blocks progress at patient, provider, and system levels. Because family planning visits are a trusted, routine contact point, success here could offer a model for closing a stubborn prevention gap.
plos-pone-0355723:
Matthew Johnson and colleagues extended an electrical method for reading the resting voltage across a cell membrane. That voltage guides muscle and nerve cells, but it is usually measured with fine electrodes. Their 2026 study adapted dielectrophoresis, which moves cells in an electric field, so it could estimate the voltage in excitable cells too.

The adapted model treats part of the voltage as sitting in the charged layer just outside the membrane. With that fix, estimates for nerve-like and heart-like cells matched values reported in earlier work. The method also tracked how estimates shift when the fluid around cells grows very dilute. Johnson and colleagues say it could help study ion channels without piercing cells.
plos-pone-0356623:
Marcus White and a mixed team of designers, clinicians, and stroke survivors tackle a long hospital design argument in their 2026 paper. Wards must choose between single rooms, which offer privacy and rest, and shared rooms, which offer company and watchful eyes. For stroke recovery, each option fails in its own way, so the team designed mixed rooms that borrow from both.

Working in a shared design lab, the group built four mixed layouts and showed them in virtual reality. Twenty experts and people with lived experience scored the designs against values such as activity, safety, control, and access to green space. Two mixed layouts won clear support. White and colleagues argue that flexible rooms can fit recovery needs better than either extreme.
plos-pone-0356723:
Yuchuan Yang, Qiang Hao, Jun Wen, Wei Zhao, and Chi Zhang reconstructed how phosphorus, life's limiting nutrient, flooded the oceans around 540 million years ago when complex animals were emerging. Their 2026 geochemistry study analyzed rock layers from phosphate mining country on the edge of China's Yangtze Plate, dating to the boundary between the Ediacaran and Cambrian periods.

Their reading: rising atmospheric oxygen supercharged chemical weathering on land, while tectonic grinding set how much rock was exposed to erode, together sending phosphorus seaward. Ocean upwelling then carried it into shallow water, where physical sorting, microbes, and possibly hot vents concentrated it into rich phosphate rock. The work ties the era's biological explosion's fuel supply to mountain building and air itself.
plos-pone-0356823:
Eman Salamah Albtoush, Keng Hoon Gan, and Saif Addeen A Alrababah studied whether deceptive Arabic news headlines betray themselves through style alone. Their 2026 cross-corpus study assembled five headline collections. It added translated English sets, prepared to preserve stylistic flavor. It measured wording and number patterns that differ between fake and genuine headlines.

Modern Arabic language models beat classical text classifiers consistently. They read sub-word patterns that capture both meaning and style. Adding hand-built features on top helped only where fakes leaned on flashy numbers or dates. It added nothing on the combined corpus. Still, the authors value the visible features for explaining a verdict. Pure neural scores cannot do that for editors deciding what to flag.
plos-pone-0357023:
Ramesh Shrestha and colleagues test a simple idea for preventing diabetes-related blindness in Nepal: teach schoolchildren, and let them teach their families. Eye damage from diabetes can be prevented when adults act early, but awareness is low. In one municipality, a school nurse ran a short education program for early secondary students, who then held sessions at home for a co-resident older family member; matched schools served as controls.

Student knowledge jumped after the program with a large measured effect, and family members also gained knowledge and better habits. Shrestha and colleagues gathered discussion evidence alongside the scores to judge how the child-to-family route felt in practice. They present nurse-supported school teaching as a cheap channel into homes that clinics rarely reach.
plos-pone-0357123:
Mai Tuyet Do and five colleagues surveyed 384 LGBTQ+ people aged eighteen to twenty-four across Vietnam in early 2025. They asked about suicidal thoughts, plans, and attempts. The questions covered their lifetimes and the past year. Their 2026 cross-sectional study also measured depression, anxiety, and stress with a standard questionnaire. It tested which background and mental health factors tracked with each outcome.

More than half reported suicidal thoughts at some point. About a third had made a plan, and roughly one in six had attempted. Stress and anxiety were the strongest companions of thoughts and plans. Anxiety alone predicted attempts. Higher income and living outside cities linked to lower risk. The authors call for routine anxiety and stress screening and affirming care for this group.
plos-pone-0357923:
Can Colakoglu and Sefa Levent Ozsahin published a 2026 clinical study in PLOS ONE on inflammation in advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Doctors often read a simple blood ratio, neutrophils divided by lymphocytes, as a sign of body-wide inflammation. They compared stable patients on long-term oxygen therapy with those not on it, checking that ratio against standard markers such as C-reactive protein and white cell counts.

Patients on oxygen had markedly higher ratios, driven by lower lymphocyte and eosinophil counts, yet their standard inflammation markers were no higher than the other group's. Statistical modeling confirmed the ratio moved with blood cell counts rather than with oxygen levels or lung function. This discordant pattern, they argue, means a high ratio may mark a distinct immune state, not simply more inflammation, so clinicians should read it in context.
plos-pone-0358323:
Mieko Tsuruoka and Kenji Inoue published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on people applying for visual disability certification at a large eye hospital in Japan. Officials rate impairment using scores computed from eye-chart results, but those scores say little about whether a person can actually read. The authors compared three official scores against real reading tests in a small group, most of whom had glaucoma or other non-macular eye disease.

One score, based on visual sharpness, tracked reading performance closely: it lined up with the smallest print size people could read and with a standard index of reading accessibility. Scores based on visual field, by contrast, showed weak or inconsistent links to reading. The sharpness-based score, they suggest, can stand in for reading ability when direct tests are unavailable. They caution that very few participants had macular disease, so the finding may not extend there.
plos-pone-0358423:
Tapon Kumar Roy and four colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on rice farming in Bangladesh. For six years the team ran a light trap in Gazipur, catching insects to count them. They study how weather shapes the numbers of rice insect pests, and of the natural enemies that prey on them.

Light trap records over six seasons show pest numbers rising and falling with weather patterns. Knowing which weather favors pests, and which favors their enemies, helps farmers time control measures. Agricultural extension services in Bangladesh can turn these long-run patterns into warnings that protect the country's staple crop.
plos-pone-0359323:
Mateusz Kukla and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on wheelchair performance. It offers a preliminary model for estimating how much oxygen, per unit of body mass, a person uses while pushing a manual wheelchair. The estimate is built from two signals: mechanical power, the work the arms produce, and heart rate.

Oxygen uptake is the standard measure of aerobic effort, but measuring it directly needs laboratory gas equipment. A model that infers it from power and pulse could work courtside during training or testing. Sports scientists and rehabilitation clinicians who train wheelchair athletes are the audience for a lighter-weight estimate of effort.
plos-pone-0359423: Ouyang and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a steroid-like compound called dioscin and eye aging. In their tests, a sugar-based aging trigger made pigment cells at the back of the eye grow old and change type. The title reports that dioscin softened both effects, acting through a named chain of signals. Slowing such cell aging could one day help protect sight in older eyes.
pmc-13196923:
Shu-Xian Lin and Kuang-Sheng Yeh published a 2026 study of a drug-resistant germ strain in pets. The strain is a type of E. coli, a common gut germ that can infect the bladder. They checked samples from dogs and cats treated for bladder infections in Taiwan.

The team studied 400 germ samples from a teaching animal hospital, gathered over nine years. Gene tests confirmed 26 samples as the ST131 strain, known for resisting many drugs. Those samples carried many harm-linked genes. All resisted two common drugs, but all still responded to one strong reserve drug. Some resistance genes could pass between germs. The spread in pets matters for both animal and human health.
pmc-13197423:
Rym Baccouch and colleagues ran a 2026 trial on music paired with exercise for teens with poor vision. Teens born with visual impairment often have lower fitness and less daily independence. Music has boosted drive in other groups, so the team tested it within strength and body-sense training.

Fifty-nine teens split into three groups: training alone, training with music, and no training. After eight weeks, both training groups improved on all fitness tests. The music group scored higher than the plain group on sit-to-stand counts, a wall-sit hold, and one-leg balance. Reach distance did not differ. The control group showed no real change. Music may add gains for daily autonomy.
pmc-13201323:
Wolves shift where they roam as the seasons change, and a 2026 study led by Nathaniel H Wehr tests whether those shifts track the movements of their prey. The research article follows gray wolves, moose, and white-tailed deer in Minnesota, plus wolves and moose on Isle Royale in Michigan.

The team analyzed GPS collar records gathered from 2008 through 2021 and used cluster analysis to define seasonal patterns of space use. Mainland wolves changed their ranges in step with deer migration, while island wolves and moose kept steadier patterns. The results link predator movement to prey movement and argue for managing several species together.
pmc-13202823:
Research on blood and tissue markers for lung cancer screening is expanding fast, and a 2026 bibliometric analysis led by Huange Zhu maps the field's shape. The study retrieves publications from the Web of Science Core Collection and visualizes trends, collaboration networks, and emerging topics with several analysis tools.

The analysis covered 3,636 publications and found output growing exponentially since 2014 across the field. Collaboration formed a dual core around China and the United States, with Chinese volume high and American work more cited. Topic modeling grouped the literature into five directions, and burst analysis pointed to DNA methylation, liquid biopsy, and artificial intelligence platforms as future priorities.
pmc-13202923: A short correction notice from Tao Liu and co-authors, published in 2026, amends their 2025 BMC Plant Biology article on cotton PLATZ transcription factors and drought resistance in tomato. The notice states that a paragraph was duplicated by mistake in the introduction and must be removed, and it confirms the error does not affect the article's conclusions. Only the correction notice itself survives here, so the underlying experiments and results are not described.
pmc-13203023:
The gut talks to the skeleton, and a 2026 review by Alba Rodriguez-Bryant surveys that talk for ways to protect bone. The article studies the gut-bone axis in osteoporosis, on how gut microbes and their products influence nutrient uptake, gut leakiness, acidity, and immune control.

Rodriguez-Bryant and co-authors review diet plans meant to steer the microbiome toward bone protection. Options include butyrate and other postbiotics, chosen probiotic strains, prebiotic fibers, synbiotic mixes, and dietary patterns such as Mediterranean and vegetarian diets. The review also maps microbe product pathways and flags gaps that must close before these plans become standard osteoporosis care.
pmc-13203423:
Making art may measurably lift mental health, and a 2026 meta-analysis led by Xu Song pools the randomized evidence for painting-based interventions. The study gathers trials of painting activities for outcomes such as depression and anxiety, across age groups and types of art practice.

Forty-five randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria and passed a formal risk-of-bias assessment. The pooled effect was significant and large, indicating better scale-measured mental health after painting interventions in the combined data. Effects looked similar across intervention lengths, art forms, and gender mixes, while older adults appeared to benefit the most from taking part.
pmc-13207923:
Glowing carbon specks are too small to reach tumors well alone, and a 2026 review led by Xiaowen Xu examines hiding them inside membrane vesicles. The article surveys carbon dots and their hybrid carriers, which range from natural extracellular vesicles to laboratory-made liposomes, for biomedical delivery.

The review first covers how carbon dots are synthesized and why they fluoresce, then details strategies for loading them into vesicles. Hybrid systems are being tried for targeted drug delivery, imaging, tumor therapy, antibacterial work, and wound care in the literature surveyed. Loading efficiency, burst release, and what the dots do to vesicle stability remain open problems for clinical translation.
pmc-13240923:
Li and colleagues in Luoyang linked the stress hyperglycemia ratio to delirium risk across two thousand ninety-three intensive care patients. The ratio compares acute blood sugar against a patient's usual level. Logistic models, curve fitting, and threshold analysis probed the shape of the link. Subgroup checks tested whether severity scores modified it.

Risk stayed flat until the ratio passed roughly two-thirds, then climbed steeply. Beyond that bend, delirium odds nearly doubled with each step upward. The association strengthened in patients with higher severity scores and inflammation markers. Li proposes the ratio as an early flag for targeted glucose management.
pmc-13241423:
da Silva and colleagues in Rio de Janeiro asked how little enlargement root canal retreatment can get away with. Fourteen extracted lower molars with severely curved canals were filled, then retreated. A paired design tested conservative and conventional protocols inside the same roots. Micro-CT scans gauged leftover filling at three stages.

The conservative protocol cleared more material early, removing ninety-five percent at the first pass. After final shaping, both approaches ended near complete removal. Less than five percent of filling stayed either way. The authors endorse the smaller preparation for sparing root dentin.
pmc-13242323:
Terui-Kohbata's team in Tokyo let five lay reviewers rewrite a survey about children's genomic data before fielding it. Japanese teens re-consent at sixteen for new samples, while earlier data stay usable regardless. Four involvement stages structured the public feedback. Every change was logged under the GRIPP2 standard.

83 percent of first-round comments were adopted, then 87 percent in round two. Wording, opt-out notes, and parent-child framing all sharpened. The five disagreed productively on allowed side uses of data. The report ranks among Japan's first ordered accounts of structured patient input.
pmc-13242423:
Pureum Sun and co-authors asked whether extracts from three traditional herbs could help mice resist Toxoplasma gondii, a widespread parasite. Their paper appeared in Acta Parasitologica in 2026. One extract came from Gypsophila oldhamiana, a plant long used in herbal medicine. Mice received the extracts by mouth before and after infection, and the team tracked parasite loads and immune responses in the spleen.

Only the Gypsophila extract clearly limited the infection, leaving treated mice with far fewer parasites than the other groups. It pushed dendritic cells to mature and release interleukin-12, which in turn expanded killer T cells that produce interferon-gamma. At the same time it raised checkpoint proteins that keep the response from overshooting. The authors present the plant as a preventive candidate worth further study.
pmc-13242623:
Yu Rao wrote a short piece marking the first approval of a PROTAC drug. It appeared in Cancer Innovation in 2026. On May 1, 2026, United States officials approved vepdegestrant, sold as Veppanu, for some advanced breast cancers with ESR1 changes. Arvinas built the drug with Pfizer after more than twenty years of work.

Most drugs block a protein only while they sit on it. A PROTAC instead tags its target so the cell destroys it. Rao argues the approval proves this event-driven idea can pass review and reach the market. It also gives the many degrader drugs now in testing a path to point to. He sets degraders beside antibodies, gene therapies, and RNA drugs as one more small-molecule tool. For Rao, a lab idea has become a real treatment.
pmc-13247423:
Chen and co-authors record a complication they believe is the first of its kind in this 2026 Case Reports in Critical Care article. Intraosseous access, drilling a needle into bone to deliver emergency fluids and drugs, is considered safe and routine in resuscitation. A sixty-seven-year-old woman, however, crashed with severe heart failure on both sides shortly after such a line was placed and resuscitation began.

Scans showed a new, large fat embolism in her lungs, fat forced from the bone marrow into circulation, which had not been present a day earlier. Emergency heart-lung support and suction removal of the clot improved her circulation dramatically. Tragically she had already sustained anoxic brain injury and care was withdrawn. The authors urge awareness of this rare, lethal possibility.
pmc-13248323:
Bektas-Dag and colleagues analyzed personal memories written by people with anorexia nervosa, in a 2026 qualitative study. Participants answered cue words linked to disgust toward themselves or moral disgust. The team compared forty-three adults with anorexia against twenty healthy adults, coding one hundred eighty-nine short memory accounts in all.

Three themes emerged: wounds dealt by other people, constant watchfulness in relationships, and a disturbed sense of identity. Memories in the anorexia group told of betrayal, shame, and harm from treatment itself, and the feelings stayed unresolved. The authors suggest therapy should rebuild trust in others and a steadier sense of self.
pmc-13249423:
Gao and a large Chinese team report that capsaicin, the heat in chili peppers, can shield the stomach from alcohol damage, in a 2026 eLife study. Alcohol burns the stomach lining partly through oxidative stress. Using binding assays and cell tests, the team showed capsaicin slips into the KEAP1 protein and loosens its grip on NRF2, the master switch for antioxidant defenses.

Freed NRF2 switched on protective genes in stomach cells, and the effect vanished in cells or mice lacking the relevant gene. Rats given capsaicin, including a nanoparticle version that dissolves better, suffered far less inflammation after alcohol dosing. The authors propose capsaicin as a gentler template for antioxidant drugs, since it does not bind permanently.
pmc-13249923:
Son and an international team printed a living graft that grows its own blood vessels, in a 2026 Angiogenesis study. Blocked circulation starves limbs of oxygen, and injected cells usually wash away. Their graft combines a printed microvascular pattern with stem cell spheroids placed in a planned layout, tuned so the balls of cells release more vessel-growing signals and invite host capillaries in.

In mice with critically starved hind legs, the grafts doubled host vessel infiltration compared with simpler designs. Sixty percent of treated limbs were saved, a four-and-a-half-fold improvement over conventional grafts, and the new vessels joined smoothly with the animal's own. Muscle damage shrank accordingly. The authors propose the design for ischemic disease therapy.
pmc-13250323:
Ari Solomon, Laura Roberson, and Karim Jreije describe an unusually large pancreatic tumour in this 2026 case report. The tumour type, acinar cell carcinoma, makes up only about one to two percent of pancreatic cancers, and most are five to ten centimetres wide.

Their patient, an 82-year-old man, had the mass spotted on a scan done for another cancer. It measured 15 centimetres and sat against the stomach. Surgeons removed it whole, together with the tail of the pancreas and the spleen, and the patient went home four days later. Lab tests confirmed the type, with clean edges and no spread to lymph nodes, and no return was seen at two months.
pmc-13250623:
Musab Hamed Saeed and a large team test dental filling materials in this 2026 lab study. Dentists sometimes use bonding glue as a shaping liquid on soft fillings, but whether that changes how germs stick to the finished surface was unclear.

Five filling materials were made with and without the glue layer, seven samples each. The main cavity germ was grown on them, and surfaces were viewed under a powerful microscope. Glued surfaces were rougher and more uneven. Germ counts rose with glue for three materials but fell for two. Since the effect cuts both ways, the authors urge caution with the shortcut.
pmc-13250723:
Henrik Åberg and co-authors test a precise way to track broken hip bones in this 2026 study. Flat X-ray pictures can understate how far fragments of a hip fracture have shifted in three dimensions, which matters when judging a repair.

Fifteen patients with fractures near the top of the thigh bone received CT scans before and after surgery and at follow-up; twelve had complete sets. The CT-based motion analysis repeated measurements to within less than a millimetre. It showed the initial shift was large, surgery cut it sharply, and fragments then moved only slightly as they healed, mostly by shortening. The method looks reliable for follow-up checks.
pmc-13250923:
Xiao and co-authors review how an aging immune system may drive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a scarring lung disease of older adults. Their 2026 Journal of Inflammation Research paper treats the disease as age-related, with worn-out cells and a tired immune system feeding steady low-grade inflammation. The authors searched the literature through October 2025 for the clearest studies.

The review walks through recent findings on immune aging in this disease and the roles of specific immune cell groups. It also gathers candidate blood markers that might help doctors diagnose and track the condition earlier. Treatment ideas aimed at immune aging get surveyed as a fresh direction beyond current drugs. The authors call for deeper mechanism work and better tools to turn these leads into care.
pmc-13251023:
Kim and a large team are the authors of this 2026 Publisher Correction in Genome Biology, attached to their whole-genome study of lung function and COPD. The original paper analyzed sequences from more than forty-four thousand participants of many ancestries. A typesetting error dropped several figure legends from the published version.

The missing legends belonged to figures one, two, three, and five, covering fine-mapping summaries, ancestry comparisons, regional association plots, and the analysis workflow. The correction prints the four legends in full so readers can interpret the figures as intended. The journal confirms that the original article has been corrected. No data, results, or conclusions are altered by this notice.
pmc-13251223:
Xiaoming Shi and colleagues introduce a special journal issue on climate change and infections in this 2026 article. A warming world is shifting where germs spread and how they pass between people, animals, and food, yet turning that evidence into action has lagged.

The editors sum up new findings on climate-sensitive diseases and propose four strategies. They call for stronger health adaptation, fresh and combined control measures, health systems that are both climate-proof and low-carbon, and fairer global governance. Policy makers, researchers, and clinicians must work together, they argue, if the growing disease burden from climate change is to be cut.
pmc-13251823:
Chloe Bird and Hamad Al Ibrahim argue that precision medicine has a blind spot in this 2026 commentary. Care tailored to each person's biology still rests on evidence built mostly from male bodies, a legacy of decades of excluding women from early research.

The authors trace policy milestones, from a 1977 rule that pushed women out of early drug trials to later laws requiring their inclusion. Even so, only about nine percent of United States federal research funding from 2013 to 2023 targeted women's health. Women made up about 41 percent of trial participants in a recent large sample. They demand reforms in funding, design, and sex-split reporting.
pmc-13252723:
Amera Al-Amery and co-authors review simulation studies of targeted vaccination in this 2026 paper. Who gets vaccinated first can decide how an outbreak unfolds, and computer models that track contact networks or single agents let planners test targeting before acting.

The review gathered 39 simulation studies published between 2018 and 2025 from major databases. It compared how network shapes, from household clusters to wide mixing, changed the payoff of targeting strategies. The authors find modelling practice still leans on simplified networks that miss real contact patterns. They call for more realistic networks and for testing hybrid plans that combine targeting with other measures.
pmc-13253023:
Le Shang Teo and colleagues review how children's ankle fractures are classified in this 2026 paper. Many competing systems exist for sorting these injuries, and doctors lacked consensus on which are reliable and which actually guide care.

The review covered 42 studies of eleven systems, searched to October 2025. Two systems, one based on injury mechanics and one standard surgical scheme, agreed best between and within readers. The most used system, based on the growth plate's anatomy, best predicted early growth plate closure, while the mechanics-based one better foresaw crooked healing. The authors suggest pairing an anatomy system with a mechanics system for sharper forecasts and planning.
pmc-13253723:
C Meyer and colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, which patients with endometriosis face lower egg supply and embryo quality. Endometriosis is tissue like the womb lining growing outside the womb. The team reviewed 205 patients having egg collection for IVF care, sorting them by disease type found at surgery.

Patients with ovarian disease had the lowest follicle counts, at 10.85 on average, versus 16.43 for surface disease. They also gave fewer eggs, 8.14, and their embryos scored lowest on day five. The authors propose early egg freezing for this group, since harm was already present at treatment time.
pmc-13253923:
Bhavesh Kevadiya and a large team create a new CT scan contrast agent in a 2026 study. CT imaging uses X-rays, and contrast agents help tell soft tissues apart. Their agent places gold particles on bismuth sulfide nanorods, made by a heat-based method.

Tests showed the rods were stable, uniform, and well formed. Stem cells tolerated them at lower doses, with lower survival at higher doses. In small animals, the agent brightened soft tissues on CT scans and caused no local swelling. The authors call it proof of concept and plan versions that also carry treatments.
pmc-13254323:
Maurício Garcia and co-authors describe a new fossil reptile in a 2026 study from southern Brazil. The fossil comes from Middle Triassic rocks and belongs to the archosauriforms, the wider group that later gave rise to dinosaurs and crocodile kin. They name the new form Silescelida acristata.

Family tree analyses place it possibly within Euparkeriidae, a debated early group, though its position shifted with different data sets. The find is the first record of this grade of archosauriform in Brazil's Triassic. The authors say it helps trace where these early reptiles lived and how the group began.
pmc-13254823:
Sarah Hardcastle and co-authors explore exercise barriers in pulmonary hypertension in a 2026 interview study. Pulmonary hypertension is a rare lung and heart disease causing breathlessness and fatigue. Twenty-one patients in the United Kingdom, with a mean age of 57.4 years, gave virtual interviews.

Four themes emerged: fear of breathlessness and overdoing it, low motivation with a wish for monitoring and targets, keeping up appearances, and little activity advice from clinicians. The appearance and identity angle was new, the authors say. They propose programs that ease fear, set goals, and widen what counts as activity.
pmc-13255323:
Rozerin Kevci and colleagues study brain pressure signals after bleeding in the cerebellum in a 2026 study. Spontaneous cerebellar hemorrhage is severe because the rear skull space is tight. The team analyzed high-resolution monitoring data from 94 adults treated in intensive care in Uppsala, Sweden, between 2008 and 2024.

Very high pressure inside the skull and poor pressure control showed trends toward worse outcomes but were not statistically firm. Blood flow pressure below set levels tied to worse outcomes, while higher pressure tied to better ones. Falling below the computed best pressure also hurt. The authors say targets here differ from other brain injuries and need larger studies.
pmc-13256223: A short 2026 retraction notice in Open Forum Infectious Diseases withdraws an IDWeek conference abstract by Monirujjaman Biswas comparing Xpert and Xpert Ultra tests. Its subject was diagnosing lung tuberculosis from stool samples of children in India. The journal says the abstract overlapped significantly with a previously published abstract, without giving credit to it. It also says the authorship of the publication cannot be verified. The notice gives no test results, so the retracted work is described here only by its subject and the reasons for withdrawal.
pmc-13256923:
Costin, Marcu, and Marcu evaluated an artificial intelligence contouring tool for head and neck radiotherapy, focusing on the smaller organs at risk that reports usually skip. Fifty patients had treatment plans built from both manual contours and the commercial auto-segmentation tool. Agreement was scored geometrically and by dose differences across ten primary organs, then extended to twenty-nine secondary ones.

Auto-contouring with adjustment took under half the manual time, with mostly small dose differences. Across fifteen hundred dose values for secondary organs, about eight percent breached constraints. The constrictor muscle exceeded its limit in over half of cases, and organs without set constraints raised concern. The authors argue validated auto-segmentation enables fuller toxicity checks.
pmc-13257923:
Raquel Moreno-Díaz and a working group from four Madrid hospitals built a tool for comparing cancer care costs fairly. Drug spending varies hugely by tumor type, stage, and treatment plan, which makes hospital comparisons misleading. Their 2026 system, called PATONCOS, sorts patients into like-for-like groups first.

Groups were defined by tumor location, treatment goal, and key biomarkers, covering over three thousand six hundred patients. For each group the team computed average drug cost per patient per month. Costs differed sharply between hospitals even inside the same group, exposing different drug choices. The authors say such benchmarking can guide fairer spending decisions.
pmc-13258123:
Yong Zhang and Runming Zhao wrote a 2026 engineering article on TL-DETR, a computer vision model for spotting defects on power transmission lines. Edge deployment means running the model on small devices near the lines, with limited computing power. Defects vary hugely in size and sit against cluttered backgrounds, which makes detection hard. Their design adds multi-scale feature tools and a dynamic sparse attention system to focus on small defects while cutting computation.

On the CableInspect-ADs dataset, TL-DETR reached precision of 91.4 percent and a detection score called mAP50 of 86.0 percent, both clear of the baseline RT-DETR model's marks. The gains over that baseline were 3.2 points on precision and 2.9 points on the detection score. Further tests showed the model also generalized well to insulators, vibration dampers, and bolts. The authors say it balances accuracy with efficiency well enough for real field use.
pmc-13259423:
Roger Dias and colleagues test whether wearable signals can betray how hard military medical teams are working. Air Force critical care crews flew twenty-six simulated transport missions while chest straps logged heart rhythms and body motion. Seventy-two clinicians took part in their 2026 study, rating workload after each run.

The straps kept almost all heart data and every motion trace, and crews found them comfortable. A heart variability measure, once adjusted to each person's baseline, tracked self-rated workload faithfully. Motion data added separate clues about physical strain. Together, the pair could flag overload during real evacuations without stopping anyone to ask.
pmc-13259623:
Rowyda Salman and co-authors hunt pancreatic cancer in a blood draw. The disease is usually found too late, so circulating RNA signals that betray it early are prized. Their 2026 case-control study compares sixty-five patients with twenty-five healthy volunteers.

Two RNAs moved in opposite directions in patients: the long RNA MIR22HG fell, while a small RNA named miR-10a-5p rose. Each alone separated patients from controls with striking accuracy, and adding them sharpened the classic blood markers. Low MIR22HG also tracked with cancer that had already spread. The pair could anchor earlier diagnosis and better staging, the authors argue.
pmc-13260523:
Vishwajit Kumar and co-authors present a 2026 review of recent progress in turning plant biomass into green bioenergy. The review takes a conversion-centered, systems-level view, asking how feedstock choice, pretreatment chemistry, enzyme breakdown, and microbe metabolism jointly govern output. It weighs how pretreatments change the chemical mix released from biomass, the inhibitors formed, and the balance that microbes need. That sets limits on how well enzymes work, on fuel yields, and on emissions.

Enzyme progress is weighed for bond-specific action and synergy, alongside lasting bottlenecks from mixed feedstocks and lignin blocking. Strategies for microbes range from single bred strains to built communities and cell-free systems. The review highlights AI and multi-omics data for picking the best pretreatment strength, enzyme cocktails, and reaction routes. Carbon capture is covered as part of an integrated fuel pathway.
pmc-13261123: Jialing Zhang and co-authors publish a 2026 correction to their study of a KAP1-associated complex in mouse muscle cells. The original paper appeared in Cell Death & Disease in 2020 and examined C2C12 myoblast differentiation and mitochondrial biogenesis. In Figure 1C, two representative images for the 4-day and 6-day culture conditions were inadvertently misplaced during figure assembly. A corrected figure is provided. The authors state the error does not affect the results, interpretation, or conclusions of the study.
pmc-13262223:
Raha Abedini and colleagues grow gut bacteria from dromedary camels in a 2026 journal article, using a method called culturomics. Rather than only reading DNA from samples, they cultured living microbes so their functions can be tested later. The camels graze on desert plants, and their guts must handle dry, poor forage.

Using six growth media, the team isolated 97 bacterial species across 42 genera and four phyla. One medium family, based on a yeast and fatty acid mix, recovered 88.6 percent of that diversity. Four species may be new to science. The rumen, the first stomach chamber, held the richest mix, while the small intestine held more Gram-negative types, some with disease potential.
pmc-13262623:
Taole Liu and colleagues build a time-of-day atlas of the zebrafish testis in a 2026 journal article. The testis, the organ that makes sperm, was long thought to lack strong daily rhythms. Using single-cell gene reading across the day, they mapped cell types in the adult fish testis and tracked how gene activity rose and fell.

Support cells, early sperm-forming cells, and late sperm cells showed strong swings in core clock genes. Other cell types showed rhythms mainly in genes tied to their jobs, and cell-to-cell signaling also varied by time. Sperm formation clearly favored the night. Constant light cut germ cell numbers and fertility, and disabling a clock gene halted early sperm cell development.
pmc-13262723:
Emma Waight and colleagues test whether strengthening daily body rhythms helps recovery after stroke in mice, in a 2026 journal article. Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability, and few treatments aid recovery. The team targeted circadian rhythms, the body's 24-hour cycles, and the glymphatic system, the brain's waste-clearing fluid network, which those cycles control.

Four rhythm-boosting steps each improved waste clearance in mice: a clock-tuning drug, high-dose melatonin, light pulses, and feeding limited to active hours. Starting the drug or the timed feeding three days after stroke still helped. Treated mice moved better, had smaller brain lesions, and carried fewer inflammation signals. Clearance flow also rose, linking rhythm repair to recovery.
pmc-13263623:
Jutta Pikalo and colleagues report a tapeworm's larval cysts in Austrian roe deer for the first time. Meat inspectors spotted Taenia krabbei cysts in muscle from two Carinthia hunting districts. Their 2026 report confirms the species by sequencing a mitochondrial gene fragment.

The adult worm's final host went unidentified, but grey wolves returning to the region are prime suspects. Deer are the parasite's intermediate host, carrying the cyst stage in their flesh. Visually tainted carcasses are commonly rejected, costing hunters and venison producers. The authors call for mapping the parasite in both hosts and teaching hunters habits that break its life cycle.
pmc-13264623:
Julia Jelitzki, Alexandra Reichenbach, and Alexander Windberger wrote a 2026 study on whether brain scan AI models decide for the right reasons. Deep learning can sort schizophrenia from MRI scans, but its choices are hidden. The team used saliency maps, which highlight the scan areas a model leaned on, to judge seven common models.

All seven models scored much alike at sorting the scans. Yet only two based their choices on brain areas that make medical sense. The other five leaned on areas with no clear link to the illness. The team also turned the maps into shared anatomical markers and found regions that match known schizophrenia markers. They argue that explanation tools must sit beside deep learning in medical imaging.
pmc-13264823:
Angelo Lamadrid and colleagues wrote a 2026 scoping review of how the COVID-19 pandemic changed hepatitis C care. Hepatitis C is a liver virus with a step-by-step care path: testing, linking to care, treatment, and cure. Reports of pandemic harm existed but were scattered, so the team mapped them all.

They kept 28 studies, most from Europe and North America. Declines showed at every step. Diagnosis fell in 15 of 21 studies that checked it, treatment starts or completions fell in 18 of 27, and cure fell in 6 of 13. Linkage to care was the step most often reported as disrupted. The authors urge stronger tracking and tougher services to protect the 2030 goal of ending hepatitis as a public threat.
pmc-13266623:
Hatice Betigul Meral, Sena Tolu, and Zeynep Noyan report a 2026 study adapting a muscle-loss risk scale for Turkey. Sarcopenia is the slow loss of muscle mass and strength with age. Their scale asks older adults how at risk they feel, an area with no Turkey-specific tool before.

The team translated the scale and tested it on 323 adults aged 60 to 93. Expert review supported the content of the Turkish version. Statistical tests found two parts: how likely people feel they are to get sarcopenia, and how serious they judge it. Scores were steady on repeat testing. The authors say the scale can support screening and health teaching.
pmc-13266723:
Scott Young wrote a 2026 introduction to a special section of The Permanente Journal on access to health care. He argues that being able to get timely, fitting care is basic to health itself. Gaps persist across places, groups, and stages of life despite steady gains in medical treatment.

Young previews themes the collected papers take up. Access matters most at key moments such as early childhood, pregnancy, and mental health care. Culture, language, and trust shape whether people seek care at all. New tools like video visits and AI add reach but also confusion. Coverage alone is not enough when costs and paperwork block use, so systems must be designed for real access.
pmc-13267823:
Mengqi Huang and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of hormone therapy and womb growths during the menopause transition. Uterine fibroids are common non-cancer growths that react to hormones. Whether menopausal hormone therapy makes them grow was unclear. The team followed 83 women at a Nanjing hospital who took a standard two-hormone sequence from 2016 onward, with repeat ultrasound scans.

Fibroid area shifted slightly during the first four years, in ways the team judged too small to matter in practice. By year five no difference from the start could be detected. Side effects were mostly brief and faded on their own. Unexpected bleeding affected about 18 percent, breast discomfort about 11 percent, and stomach symptoms about 2 percent. The authors call the therapy a safe option with regular checks.
pmc-13267923:
Jiangchuan Liu and colleagues wrote a 2026 perspective on smoking, vaping, and osteoarthritis. This joint disease was long blamed on wear and tear, but inflammation now looks central to it. Population studies of smoking and joint damage disagree, yet smoke clearly disturbs immune function. The authors map several linked paths by which cigarette and e-cigarette exposure may harm joints.

Smoke may stir immune cells in the joint lining and set off alarm signals from damaged tissue. Those signals switch on inflammation pathways and a protein complex called the inflammasome. Helper and regulator T cells may fall out of balance, and small gene-control molecules may shift. Together these changes could poison the joint's inner setting. The authors flag weak points in the field, including few joint-specific studies.
pmc-13271123:
Junrui Chen is lead author of a 2026 multicentre study linking a blood fat ratio to osteoarthritis, the wear-related joint disease. The ratio, triglycerides divided by the protective HDL cholesterol, is a combined marker of metabolic problems whose link to joint disease was unclear.

With 6,570 participants, each unit rise in the ratio carried an 11 percent higher odds of osteoarthritis after adjustment. The link was not a straight line: risk rose more steeply at lower levels in women and in people with diabetes. In a machine-learning model the ratio ranked second only to age in importance. The team also built an interactive web tool that shows estimated risk by age, sex, diabetes, and ratio.
pmc-13271423:
Tom Lapidus is lead author of a 2026 pilot study on how the chemotherapy drug irinotecan changes immune checkpoints on neuroblastoma cells. Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumour outside the brain in children, and only about half of high-risk patients survive, making combined chemo-immunotherapy a central strategy.

Two neuroblastoma cell lines were exposed to low doses of irinotecan and an immune signal. The drug shifted several immune markers, including GD2, CD47, PD-L1, and MHC class I. It reduced eating of cancer cells by immune scavenger cells, but an anti-CD47 antibody reversed that. T cell killing improved after irinotecan treatment, and in mice the drug plus immune cells shrank tumours more than either alone.
pmc-13273023:
Hirut Basha leads a 2026 small field trial of a plant extract that kills snails carrying schistosomiasis, a parasitic disease. The plant, Hagenia abyssinica, grows in Ethiopia, and its female flowers were extracted with alcohol and chloroform. Biomphalaria snails, which host the parasite, were exposed for up to 72 hours, and fish toxicity was also tested.

Both extracts killed snails, with the chloroform form stronger at 24 hours. For fish, the alcohol extract's lethal level was lower than for snails, meaning fish were more sensitive than the target snails. Fingerlings showed no harm up to 16 milligrams per liter. The authors flag this gap as an ecological concern for wider use.
pmc-13273523:
Luiz Felipe Azevedo Marques leads a 2026 profile of five patients in Brazil hospitalized with COVID-19 who had one of two rare genetic syndromes. Berardinelli-Seip syndrome involves near absence of body fat and metabolic problems, while Silver-Russell syndrome involves poor growth before birth and other abnormalities. Such features were feared to worsen COVID-19.

Two patients had Berardinelli-Seip syndrome and three had Silver-Russell syndrome. Most had breathing symptoms and low oxygen at admission, two needed intensive care, and two needed noninvasive breathing support. Four were discharged, while one unvaccinated 19-year-old with Berardinelli-Seip syndrome and multiple other conditions died. The authors found no consistent link between these syndromes and severe COVID-19.
pmc-13273623:
Kristine Marie Vege leads a 2026 study of medical problems during rehab for children with brain or spinal cord injury. Children aged 2 to 17 were treated at a tertiary center. Data came from charts and surveys on admission and discharge, for a set list of problems.

Of 64 children, 59 had problems, with 183 instances across 19 types. Sleep problems, pain, constipation, anemia, infections, spasticity, and poor nutrition were most common. No clear link appeared with age, sex, or diagnosis. Most problems, 74 percent, did not affect rehab. But poor nutrition, infections, and spasticity could prolong stays and worsen outlook.
pmc-13273923:
Gangapersad and colleagues track how often lithium is dispensed to young people in the Netherlands. Their 2026 paper uses a national community pharmacy database covering 2011 to 2022. Lithium is the first-choice long-term treatment for bipolar disorder, which often begins in the teens, yet its use has fallen as other psychiatric drugs have risen.

The study included 567 people aged 6 to 25 who received lithium in that period. Yearly prevalence stayed roughly flat, between about 30 and 35 per 100,000 young people, and ran higher in females than males. New starts shifted with age: incidence fell in 13 to 19 year olds but rose in 20 to 25 year olds. About half of patients also received other psychiatric medicines, most often antipsychotics and antidepressants.
pmc-13275123:
Caroline E Terry wrote a 2026 commentary highlighting a new hormone test for tracking rhino pregnancies. Black and white rhino pregnancies run well over a year with few outward signs, leaving zoo managers guessing. The study she describes, by George Mason University researchers with thirty-seven North American rhino facilities, measured the hormone DHEA in blood.

The team first tuned their extraction method for rhino serum, then took monthly samples from forty black rhinos and seventy-one white rhinos for a year. DHEA rose with age until about fifteen years, matching peak breeding ages. Crucially, it also climbed during pregnancy, especially from the middle onward, compared with non-pregnant animals. One white rhino that miscarried never showed that rise.
pmc-13276223:
Sk Injamamul Islam and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on mining a workhorse bacterium for hidden antibiotic potential. Corynebacterium glutamicum is famous for making amino acids in factories. Whether it also carries genes for natural antimicrobial products had never been checked across the whole species.

The team compared thirty-six complete genomes and catalogued their gene clusters for making secondary compounds. Strains differed in cluster content, and some carried mixed clusters. Alongside known terpene pathways, they found clusters tied to polyketides, a rich drug family, never before reported in this species. Machine learning models then scanned small gene fragments for likely antimicrobial peptides. The best model flagged eighteen strong candidates after duplicates were removed. The authors say these leads need lab testing.
pmc-13276723:
Giulia Pollice and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on the social exclusion of people with mental disorders. Inclusion means joining social, economic, and cultural life, not just being present. Evidence using proper measuring tools, rather than rough population statistics, had never been pooled.

Ten studies qualified, and six entered the pooled analysis covering about nineteen hundred people. Those with mental disorders scored far lower on inclusion than the general population, a large gap by statistical standards. The review found weaker relationships, less support, and reduced community participation. Disadvantages stacked up in jobs, income, education, and housing, including money hardship and unhappy neighborhoods. Several studies showed people could take part in activities yet still not feel they belonged. The authors note class, gender, and ethnicity deepen the exclusion.
pmc-13277823:
Kara Saiki leads a 2026 survey study of a media campaign in Hawai'i that urged adults at risk for type 2 diabetes to join a prevention program. The state campaign, called Beat Diabetes, ran from July to October 2024, with a focus on Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander, and Filipino communities, which face high diabetes rates. A survey of 860 at-risk adults followed.

Forty percent of respondents recalled the campaign. Those who had seen it gave higher ratings for how likely they were to join a prevention program. They also scored higher on believing diabetes may be unavoidable, a belief the campaign may need to address. The design is a one-time survey, so it shows links rather than proof that the campaign caused the difference.
pmc-13278023:
Xiaoyi Bai leads a 2026 cohort study of survival factors in the most common type of womb cancer, endometrioid endometrial cancer, in China. The team followed 142 patients diagnosed from 2009 to 2013 for up to ten years. They sorted patients into no recurrence, recurrence with survival, and death groups, and tested which features predicted each path.

Advanced stage and larger tumors predicted shorter survival, and the highest tumor grade also worsened outlook. For recurrence, advanced stage and tumors of three centimeters or more mattered most. Hormone receptor positivity and absence of vessel invasion looked protective in simple analyses but faded in adjusted models. Tumor size and stage remain the core guides for personal risk planning, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278623:
Vicky Bennett leads a 2026 mouse study of a new bacteria-killing compound for skin infections caused by MRSA, a drug-resistant Staphylococcus strain. The compound, epidermicin NI01, is a bacteriocin, a natural antimicrobial made by bacteria, with a novel mode of action. Infected skin on immunosuppressed mice was treated daily with the compound or with standard antibiotic creams.

No adverse effects appeared from infection or treatment. A single-dose group showed no benefit, but repeated three percent dosing cut bacterial counts about as much as the standard creams. The dose needed to kill the test strain stayed unchanged after treatment. Further development is warranted, the authors say, and clinical use could spare standard antibiotics for severe infections.
pmc-13279723:
Xin Lai and colleagues report a 2026 dog study of nerve cutting to aid heart repair after heart attack. A heart attack, or myocardial infarction, scars the heart and warps its left pump chamber. Nerve balance loss makes the warp worse. Heart nerve hubs called ganglionated plexi drive that imbalance. The team cut sensory nerve input with a nerve toxin called resiniferatoxin, shot in a front nerve hub.

Thirty one beagle dogs split in three groups: heart attack alone, heart attack with nerve cut, and sham surgery. After four weeks, the nerve cut group showed lower nerve hub activity and less hub warp. Left pump dilation eased and pump function rose versus the attack alone group. Scar linked tissue change in the pump also eased. Calm nerve tone may guard heart shape after attack.
pmc-13281923:
Ying Wang and colleagues hunted brain signs that foretell failed face pain surgery in a 2026 study. The surgery lifts a blood vessel off a pinched face nerve. It is the standard fix when drugs fail, yet up to three in ten patients gain little. The team enrolled sixty such patients and thirty healthy peers. Before surgery all had brain scans of links and wiring. Patients were split by their relief three months after surgery. Pain levels before surgery were alike in both groups.

Those who fared poorly had gentler vessel pressure found in surgery. Their brains showed tighter links between rest and movement networks and deep feeling hubs. Those hubs govern memory, reward, and fear. A learning model fed the top links called the outcome right in most cases. The authors say lasting pain can rewire the brain itself. Such rewiring may cap what surgery can give back.
pmc-13282323:
Freddy H Marin-Dett and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on how a fungus changes a bacterium's effect on mouth cells that may precede cancer. The fungus Candida albicans and the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus often live together in biofilms, slimy microbial layers. The team treated human immune cells with fluid from single-species and mixed biofilms, then exposed precancerous mouth lining cells to the immune cells' output.

Bacterial fluid alone stirred strong inflammation signals in immune cells. Fluid from the mixed biofilm suppressed those signals. Bacterial treatment also shifted two cancer-related genes in mouth cells in a risky direction, lowering a protective gene and raising a survival gene. The wild-type fungus reversed that shift. The authors say cross-species teamwork can shape immune signals tied to early oral cancer change.
pmc-13282423:
Mingjue Jian and co-authors report a 2026 study on a lower-dose protocol for CT scans that check for lung artery clots. Such scans, CT pulmonary angiography, use contrast dye and radiation, both of which carry risks. Patients with suspected clots were randomly split between a dual low-dose method and routine scanning. The low-dose method used a mixed dual-flow dye injection tracked automatically, plus dual-energy imaging.

Low-dose scans at a chosen energy setting showed much stronger vessel brightness and a better quality-per-signal measure in the main lung artery. Contrast against noise was comparable, and small branch visibility was preserved. Artifacts in a large chest vein fell. Radiation dose dropped by more than half versus routine scans, and dye volume also fell, while clot detection did not differ clearly. The authors judge the protocol feasible for routine clot checks.
pmc-13284023:
Robot help erases the handedness penalty in partial knee replacement in a 2026 analysis by Shujun Chen and colleagues. Hand dominance can skew implant alignment when surgeons operate on the non-dominant side. The Mako robot system guides cuts with planned precision for each knee.

A total of 391 patients had medial partial knee replacement by five right-handed surgeons. Robot cases took longer but lost less blood and left hospital sooner. With robot help, left and right knees matched on every alignment measure. Without it, left-side implants landed less precisely than right-side ones. Function scores also favored robot cases with no side gap.
pmc-13284323:
Reem Ghonaim and co-authors report a laboratory study, published in 2026, on wound dressings made from chitosan cryogels loaded with a phenothiazine dye. The team made a chalcone form of the dye and mixed it into sponge-like chitosan gels. They then tested how well the gels killed bacteria linked to wound infection.

Growth tests, leakage assays, and a Microtox test showed strong killing of six bacterial species, with clear zones near 33 mm for Escherichia coli in the best gels. The gels also showed good heat stability and no harmful effects in the safety test. Docking work pointed to binding with CDK6 and CDK2 proteins. The authors present the gels as low-cost, multi-use dressings that could help infected wounds heal.
pmc-13284423:
Sasan Radfar and co-authors give a systematic review, published in 2026, of electrochemical immunosensors for tuberculosis detection. The review covers 19 studies that target key proteins and markers of the TB bacterium, such as Ag85, ESAT-6, CFP-10, and MPT64. These sensors aim to offer fast, portable tests where lab diagnosis is slow or hard to reach.

Sensor surfaces fell into three groups: metal nanoparticles, conductive polymers, and carbon-based mixes. Carbon materials were still used least, despite strong traits for sensing, the authors report. Most new work favors label-free formats. The review calls for better use of advanced materials and nanozymes to lift sensitivity, stability, and repeat results before wide clinical use.
pmc-13284823:
Rei Takeichi and co-authors present a 2026 case report where a small brainstem bleed mimicked Bell palsy. A 75-year-old man with poorly controlled blood pressure, diabetes, and a smoking history developed left face weakness over four days. The slow onset and lower motor pattern first pointed to Bell palsy, the usual cause of such weakness.

MRI showed a dark spot in the left pons, and CT confirmed a small hemorrhage pressing on the facial nerve. Care stayed conservative, with clotting support, rest, and rehabilitation. Signs began to ease by day four in hospital, scans showed shrinkage by day seven, and he left after fifteen days. The authors urge selective imaging for atypical cases.
pmc-13285323:
Rudi Campo pens an obituary, published in 2026, for Stephan Gordts, a founder of modern fertility care in Belgium who died on May 22, 2026. Gordts helped deliver the first baby born through in vitro fertilization in Belgium in 1983. A year later he set up the Leuven Institute for Fertility and Embryology, leading its science work until his death.

World fame came from his skill in gentle fertility surgery and from a viewing method through the vagina that first filmed normal egg release. His early microsurgery courses in Leuven drew wide praise, and he taught at many meetings with patience and warmth. The European endoscopy society gave him its top honorary rank in 2024.
pmc-13286223:
Umanath R Poojary and co-authors tie steel microstructure to machining ease in a 2026 study of AISI 1040 steel. Shops heat-treat this workhorse steel for strength, yet the same heating can chew through cutting tools and rough up finished faces. Bars annealed, normalized, or oil-quenched went under the lathe in a planned grid of speeds, feeds, and depths.

Heat setting, cutting speed, and feed rate each steered tool life in the analysis, while feed alone ruled surface roughness in every condition. Annealed bars, with their soft two-phase grain, gave the longest tool life and the cleanest overall cutting. Quenched bars hardened into a tough phase that wore tools fastest, and normalized bars landed between the two. Formula models forecast both outcomes well inside the tested range, handing machinists a map for pairing heat treatment with cutting settings.
pmc-13286523:
Jair Camargo Ferreira and colleagues test ozonated sunflower oil as an antibiotic-free womb treatment for fresh cows in a 2026 veterinary study. Womb infections after calving drain fertility, and drug residues plus resistance push the search for alternatives. Eighteen first-time mothers received a single infusion of ozonated or plain oil ten days after calving, with tissue samples before treatment and fifteen days later.

Ozonated oil left the womb lining richer in glands, roughly triple the count of the plain-oil group, with narrower, less swollen glands. pmc-13287223:

pmc-13287323:

pmc-13287823:
Danladi C Husaini and co-authors surveyed health students in 2026 at the University of Belize about infections picked up during care, a problem hitting about four in ten patients locally. pmc-13288723:

pmc-13289223:

pmc-13289423:

pmc-13289823:

pmc-13290123:
How far a lab-grown airway lining can stand in for the real thing is assessed by Nuria Roldan and colleagues in 2026. Their paper builds the case for reconstructed human respiratory epithelium, focusing on the MucilAir model, as a test system for substances people breathe in.

pmc-13290523:
Pairing eye-tracking with neurofeedback lifted young women footballers' skills in a small 2026 study by Sílvio Carvalho and colleagues. Eight youth players from a FIFA-certified centre, aged 15.6 years on average, trained for six weeks.

pmc-13290823:
Climate change will reshuffle South America's malaria mosquitoes, Janderson Batista Rodrigues Alencar and colleagues project in a modeling study from 2026. Malaria still burdens the continent, yet how warming will move its Anopheles mosquitoes around has been unclear.

Several secondary species may also spread. Alencar and colleagues warn control programs should plan for new vector mixes, not just less malaria.
pmc-13291023:
Junlin Zhao and colleagues build a simple allergy burden score in a 2026 study of children with asthma, then ask whether a higher score tracks with worse lung function. pmc-13291123:
Ambulance heart tracings may predict heart attack risk by sex. L. E. Sams and colleagues study that gap in a 2026 paper. Finding attacks that need vessel reopening is harder in women. Patients with suspected attacks and early tracings were studied.

The group held 1,963 patients from 2014 to 2021. Men showed ischemic tracings more often than women. Men also needed vessel treatment more often. pmc-13291223:
A blood score may warn which fatty liver patients face the worst path. Mohammad S Siddiqui leads a 2026 study of the metabolic vulnerability index. The score reflects inflammation and amino acid upset. The liver disease studied covers a wide range of tissue harm.

The group held 1,613 patients, followed for about four years. Each rise in the score linked to higher death risk. Liver death, organ failure, and kidney decline also rose. Pairing the score with scarring stage beat scarring alone. Gains held for death, failure, and liver cancer calls. The team backs wider testing of this score. pmc-13291323:
Motor cortex can speak straight to the brain’s gate for action. William Scott Thompson leads a 2026 mouse study of this direct line. The target sits in the substantia nigra, a basal ganglia output hub. Its cells normally hold back movement signals.

Textbooks can add this shortcut to the classic loop.
pmc-13291423:
Captive breeding may not save a rare rainforest duck alone. Peri E Bolton leads a 2026 study of the white-winged wood duck. This bird is among the world’s rarest waterfowl. Captive flocks suffer badly from bird tuberculosis.

Wild birds kept more diversity in immune genes. Long past declines predated human pressure. Inbreeding adds strain in closed captive flocks. Fresh wild immune diversity may be key to survival plans.
pmc-13291723:
Iman Taghizadeh Firoozjaei and co-authors detail a 2026 case-control study from Iran on gestational diabetes and thyroid problems in pregnancy. They compared 176 women who had gestational diabetes with 177 who did not, checking how often hypothyroidism appeared in each group. The study covered 353 pregnant women in total.

Women with gestational diabetes faced a risk of hypothyroidism roughly 2.8 times higher than the comparison group, and a history of other diseases also raised the risk. First-pregnancy age, parity, and breastfeeding showed no clear link. The authors suggest regular thyroid screening for pregnant women who have gestational diabetes or other conditions, whatever their reproductive history.
pmc-13292023:
Aseel Awad Alsaidan wrote a 2026 review perspective on how lipid disorders drive cardiovascular deaths in Saudi Arabia. Heart and vessel disease causes about 45 percent of deaths in the Kingdom, and abnormal blood lipids are a major contributor. Genes, city living, inactivity, and a shift toward Western-style eating all feed the problem. Current care leans heavily on lowering LDL cholesterol, which Alsaidan argues leaves HDL and triglyceride risks undertreated. The review calls for early screening, prevention programs fitted to local culture, registries, and large national studies.
pmc-13292323:
Tine Claeys and colleagues present a 2026 machine learning tool, MLMarker, that guesses which tissue a proteomics sample came from. It also sorted a pan-cancer cohort with high accuracy and picked out brain and pituitary origins hiding in body fluids. pmc-13292823:
Ayla Macyelle de Oliveira Correia leads a 2026 lab study on fillings for worn spots near the gum line, called non-carious cervical lesions. Such spots bond poorly, so gaps at the edges can shorten the life of a repair.

A light microscope and optical coherence tomography checked edge and inner gaps before and after heat cycling. Shape and material made no clear difference, and heat aging did not widen gaps. Either shape or material thus seems workable for these repairs.
pmc-13293623:
Bertille Mohring and a large team compare, in a 2026 study, hormone profiles in common eider ducks breeding at two nearby colonies with opposite risks. One site has few people but many predators, while heavy tourism at the other scares predators away.

pmc-13294423:
Adnan and coauthors model microbe-laden hybrid nanofluid squeezing through a stretchy channel under magnetism and heat input in a 2026 math study. Walls expand or contract while swimming microbes drift with the flow, a setup tied to lab and medical devices. Similarity transforms shrank the governing laws, and an iterative scheme solved the reduced system with good convergence.

pmc-13295223:
Djifahamaï Soma and colleagues pool what is known on drug-proof Klebsiella pneumoniae in Burkina Faso in a 2026 review. pmc-13295823:

Epilepsy touches about one percent of Americans, and many harms shrink when patients hold a clear emergency plan. A record template carrying that plan will be built into routine neurology visits.

Providers will be randomised to the plan plus general health teaching or to teaching alone, with ten patients each followed for a year. Quality scores, seizure counts, and service use will be compared before and after the change. pmc-13295923:

pmc-13299323:

pmc-13301723:

pmc-13301823:

pmc-13302623:

pmc-13303723:

pmc-13305523:

pmc-13306523:

pmc-13306723:

pmc-13307523:

pmc-13308823:

pmc-13311023:

pmc-13311323:

pmc-13312023:

pmc-13312823:

pmc-13313223:

pmc-13314423:

pmc-13314923:

pmc-13315523:
