Lasting drops in fitness matter for work, daily life, and care planning, and objective wearable data can show limits that self-reports alone may miss.
pmc-13316223:
Yannic Volz and colleagues traced surgical care in 2026 for male stress incontinence in Germany, using the nationwide GRAND inpatient register from 2005 to 2023. Leakage after prostate treatment burdens many men, and care splits between the gold-standard artificial sphincter and sling procedures for chosen patients.

In total, 24,234 men had surgery, with the artificial sphincter making up 63 percent of cases in the reported split. The study charted long-term trends, in-hospital complications, death, and stay length, plus reasons devices were removed or replaced, adjusted for age, other illness, prior radiation, and surgery year.
pmc-13316423:
Rana Salah and co-authors introduce DeepTaxa in a 2026 methods paper, a hybrid deep learning tool that names bacteria from their 16S gene reads down to species level. Older tools lean on exact matching or word-count tricks and suffer when reference lists are incomplete.

DeepTaxa pairs a multi-scale pattern network with a transformer built for DNA text, giving calls at all seven ranks of the classic naming ladder. On a held-out Greengenes2 test set it reached species accuracy of 92.96 percent in the reported runs, ahead of DADA2 and QIIME 2, with near-perfect scores at broad ranks. A short-read version still hit high accuracy. Code, trained models, and data are public for reuse.
pmc-13317123:
Jue Wang, Fumihiko Ino, and Alia Benkahla present RAM-MSA in a 2026 computing paper, a method for aligning many DNA or protein sequences exactly without blowing up memory. Exact aligners give provably best answers but eat memory as sequences pile up, while fast shortcuts sacrifice accuracy.

Their recursive method bounds memory, returns a first alignment quickly, then keeps improving it until the exact answer lands. Tests cut memory use to 62.51 percent of a leading exact method's footprint in the reported comparison, and the first output scored near heuristic speed with a quality score of 0.96 in the benchmark. It also handles the more realistic affine gap costs that older path methods skip.
pmc-13317423: Jun Jiang and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to a 2024 study of targeted exosomes carrying gene-silencing cargo against lung cancer spread to the brain. The notice is a correction only: a Ki67 fluorescence image in Figure 7D was duplicated by mistake during assembly, and the corrected figure is shown. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13318123:
Jianan Wang and a Dutch team report a sobering 2026 gene therapy study on TBX18, a developmental switch once hailed as a way to grow a biological pacemaker in the heart. Early short bursts had produced pacing in animals, raising hopes of replacing hardware devices.

Long-lasting virus-delivered TBX18 scarred mouse hearts badly at full strength. At gentler, safe levels it still rewired cell identity genes but never switched on the pacemaker program or its signature current, and cells beat oddly with stretched recovery. In rats with complete heart block, a rival channel gene, Hcn2, paced robustly with stimulation while TBX18 added nothing. The authors close the case: Hcn2, not TBX18, deserves development money.
pmc-13318723:
Shikhar Kumar and colleagues report a 2026 pair of user studies on robot politeness and mistakes. They asked whether polite behaviour can offset error-prone performance. Two non-humanoid robots were tested: a mobile robot and a manipulator arm. Participants were 59 young adults with engineering backgrounds, aged 24 to 28.

Politeness followed a classic three-rule scheme, present or absent. Correctness was varied by adding deliberate errors or none. Correct and polite robots earned the best ratings overall. Crucially, politeness never made up for errors. A correct but strict robot beat a polite but mistaken one. The polite, error-prone robot could even frustrate users more. The authors stress testing across robot types and tasks.
pmc-13319423:
M. A. van Bree and co-authors report a hands on study from 2026 on fully plant based meals for hospital patients. Hospitals want meals that cut climate harm yet still give sick people enough protein and taste good. Few ready options give a full mix of the building blocks found in animal foods, so a mixed team of staff and food firms built new menus from scratch.

Thirty recipes were shaped into seven day plans giving 90 to 97 grams of protein a day, drawn from soy, lentils, grains, and nuts. Extra pea protein and soy drinks lifted breakfast and lunch without bigger plates. Day costs stayed near ten to twelve euros, though trade offs with taste and cost remain.
pmc-13319923:
Linxi Wang and co-authors review cage like nano carriers for cancer immune drugs in a 2026 article on metal organic frameworks. Immune care has changed cancer treatment, yet side harm, tumor escape, and a hostile tumor setting still cap its reach. Tiny cages built from metal joints and carbon links can carry large drug loads and free them in a timed way, which makes them a fresh delivery route.

The review weighs cage strengths for safety, aim, and load, then maps joint delivery of immune drugs with tumor bits that train the immune system. Pairings with heat, light, and chemical attack therapies are also covered. Hurdles for clinic use, such as scale up and long term safety, close the survey with paths for next work.
pmc-13320423:
Francesca Vedovo wrote a letter in 2026 on a trial of music during prostate biopsy, the VIVALDI trial by Basadonna and co-authors. Music is a cheap, safe, drug free way to ease pain and worry during the through skin biopsy, and the trial found gains worth noting. The letter holds that music, once tested as care, must meet the same reporting rules as any other care step.

In the trial arm, patients picked their own music, played on speakers from the wait room to the end of the biopsy. Free choice aids comfort but makes the dose a moving target, since genre, beat, words, and volume all shift the effect. Set guides for music care ask for full detail on content, chooser, delivery, and checks that the plan was followed.
pmc-13320523:
Huining Gu and a large team report a 2026 study on how the liver regrows after injury. A protein piece called immunoglobulin kappa, made by liver cells, had earlier been tied to cell survival during harm. The team asked how it guides regrowth and whether it could anchor the whole repair process.

Kappa levels rose in liver samples from patients with drug caused liver injury and in mouse injury models. Mice lacking kappa in liver cells regrew poorly, with disordered cell scaffolding and fewer new cells. Lab work showed kappa binds directly to a protein called MYLK that supports cell structure. The results place an unlikely immune protein at the heart of liver repair.
pmc-13321023:
Prashant Sharma, Awanit Kumar, and Harsh Verma comment in a 2026 letter on a review of prediction models for atrial fibrillation after heart bypass surgery. The review, by Eini and others, pooled machine learning and regression models for this common rhythm problem. The writers argue that how the outcome was defined shapes what the pooled scores really mean.

Studies set episode length cut-offs from 30 seconds to over 5 minutes and used anything from constant heart monitoring to spot checks, which miss brief episodes. A pooled specificity of 0.83 may thus reflect monitoring intensity more than model skill. The letter also flags missing calibration and decision curve proof as the bridge to clinic use.
pmc-13321223:
Yi Hao and co-authors warn that plant water saving under rising carbon dioxide may be overstated in a 2026 study. Higher carbon dioxide makes leaf pores narrow, which should cut water loss and ease land drying. The team shows an indirect feedback that works the other way.

As plants change, surface energy balance shifts, making air warmer and drier, which in turn raises water loss from land. That feedback offsets about half of the water saving in northern mid to high latitudes, yet most assessments leave it out. Ignoring it may understate future drought risk for farms and ecosystems that depend on soil moisture.
pmc-13322823:
Yifan Luo, Jiarong Wang and Jichun Zhao review the enzyme MMP-12 and its mixed roles in artery disease, in work published in 2026. MMP-12, also called macrophage elastase, sits where inflammation meets breakdown of the tissue that holds artery walls together.

Across diseases such as atherosclerosis and aortic aneurysm, MMP-12 can break down matrix, draw in immune cells, switch on other enzymes, or at times help calm inflammation. Which role dominates depends on the inflammatory setting, the stage of disease and the material present in the wall. That context shapes whether blocking MMP-12 could help, and the authors urge care when moving findings from models to patients.
pmc-13323023:
Shanshan Li and co-authors ask who stays up to date with lung cancer screening in the United States, in a 2026 analysis of the 2024 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. Their weighted sample held 6,234 adults aged 50 to 79 years who were eligible for screening.

Only about a fifth were up to date with screening in the weighted figures. Fourteen social and health measures were grouped into four components, covering resources, physical health, psychosocial health and work and neighbourhood. Only socioeconomic resources linked clearly to screening after full adjustment. Cluster and SHAP analyses showed differing barriers by subgroup, and the authors argue that outreach should be tailored rather than uniform.
pmc-13323223:
Shengqi Zheng and co-authors evaluate negative-pressure therapy for children whose concealed penis returned after surgery, in a 2026 retrospective study. They reviewed 126 patients who finished a standard 20-session, pressure-titrated course between September 2022 and June 2025.

Visible, flaccid and stretched lengths plus diameter all rose significantly after treatment in their records, and gains held at three months without clear regression. Older age, higher body mass index and smaller starting size each predicted larger gains. No serious side effects appeared. The authors present suction-based treatment as a non-surgical salvage option that uses mechanical stretch to loosen fibrotic restriction, pending stronger controlled evidence in children.
pmc-13323623:
Kelly Marriott-Statham and colleagues study how care home settings shape shared decisions between older residents and nurses, in a 2026 qualitative study from an Australian residential aged care home. Shared decision-making is widely promoted, yet routine, rigid rules and scarce resources often block it in practice.

Emotional touchpoint interviews with five older people and six nurses, eight practice observations and development methods fed a joint interpretive analysis. Seven components shaped how connected residents and nurses felt and how fully decisions were shared, led by affirming personhood and mutual trust in the reported themes. The authors argue that the wider practice environment, not goodwill alone, decides whether residents hold a real voice.
pmc-13325123:
Wenyi Sun and colleagues read the fluid history locked in calcite veins of the Ordos Basin in a 2026 geology study. The veins sit in the subsalt fourth member of the Ordovician Majiagou Formation, a target for gas search.

Microscopy, isotope ratios, trace elements, and fluid inclusions were combined to date the vein fluids. Most veins grew in a single stage from burial fluids buffered by the host rock. Trapped droplets record three hydrocarbon chapters: light early charging, wide oil charging from the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, and later cracking of that oil to gas in the Early Cretaceous. The story guides where mature gas may sit today.
pmc-13327923:
Eva Karaskova and colleagues review heart risk in inflammatory bowel disease in a 2026 article. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are now seen as body-wide illnesses whose vessel risk runs above what standard factors explain, above all in younger patients and during gut flares. The authors gather the shared mechanisms.

Chronic inflammation harms vessel linings, speeds clotting, and feeds plaque growth, aided by a leaky gut barrier, shifted microbes, and troubled belly fat. Lipids mislead in this setting: blood levels can look low while risk stays high, because inflammation warps lipoprotein quality, a pattern dubbed the lipid paradox. Tight control of bowel activity and care with steroids anchor the prevention advice.
pmc-13328423:
Rana Abdelaal and co-authors map skin microbes in Egyptian acne patients in a 2026 study. Acne ties to the bacterium Cutibacterium acnes, yet diversity shifts may matter more than sheer growth, and Middle East data are scarce. Swabs from 45 patients, 37 urban and 8 rural, plus 25 healthy urban controls, underwent gene sequencing.

In city patients, worse acne came with richer, more even microbe mixes rather than more species, and village patients showed their own distinct, diverse patterns with different metabolic leanings. Surprisingly, the namesake bacterium's types thinned as acne worsened in both groups, hinting that only certain strains misbehave. Future treatments might spare friendly strains and target only harmful ones, tuned to local environments.
pmc-13330523:
Lizhi Liu and colleagues show new uses for a bacterial Argonaute enzyme in handling lab-made RNA in a 2026 study. Argonaute cutters can be guided to chosen sequences without the strict site rules that limit Cas enzymes. The team used a DNA-guided enzyme from Mucilaginibacter paludis that cuts RNA.

Uses shown include polishing the tail end of messenger RNA made in vitro. Paired with mass spectrometry, the cutter helped grade cap quality at the head end and tail length and makeup at the other end. One-pot cutting with many guides aided RNA sequencing, change detection, and fingerprint checks. The authors present the enzyme as a flexible quality tool for RNA production.
pmc-13330623:
Erdenebat Bulgan and a large team give first national data on drug-resistant gut bacteria in Mongolian animals in a 2026 study. E. coli from eight animal species, spanning livestock and pets, served as an indicator bug. Resistance patterns varied sharply by how animals are raised.

Resistance stayed very low in camels, goats, and sheep under nomadic herding, and low in cattle in the reported findings. Intensively raised chickens and pigs carried far more resistance, with high multi-drug shares in both. Horses and dogs also carried high rates. Worryingly, high-threat resistant types appeared only in owned dogs. Close human contact tracked with higher carriage. Joined human and animal action is urgent, the authors argue.
pmc-13332323:
Raffaele Epis and co-authors review treatments targeting the downstream damage pathways of Duchenne muscular dystrophy rather than the missing protein itself. Loss of dystrophin remains the root cause with no definitive cure, so most strategies aim to slow progression. Their 2026 narrative review covers more than one hundred articles, most from the last fifteen years, spanning forty different approaches.

Each approach was judged on whether it promoted regeneration or limited degeneration. Calcium- and mitochondria-targeted interventions overwhelmingly preserved muscle structure and slowed regeneration cycles. Fibre stability approaches split evenly between regeneration and delaying wasting. Cell therapies aimed at the muscle stem cell pool mostly enhanced regeneration, while anti-inflammatory strategies more often slowed degeneration than built new fibres. The authors argue the field is shifting: limiting chronic degeneration and its exhausting repair cycles may preserve muscle better than chasing regeneration alone.
pmc-13333523:
Xingwei Zhao and colleagues propose in 2026 that stray mitochondrial DNA acts as an amplifier inside the inflammation of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The condition is increasingly read as a multi-organ inflammatory state, and the puzzle is how stresses, ageing, obesity, diabetes, kidney trouble, fuse into a self-sustaining network.

Their framework gives mitochondrial DNA the messenger's role. Stressed cells oxidize and shed it, free, packaged in vesicles, or caught in neutrophil traps. Sensors such as TLR9 and cGAS-STING read it as danger. They trigger inflammasomes and waves of IL-6, TNF, and interferon signals across endothelium, heart muscle, and organs. The authors are careful with the claim. They position the DNA leak as one amplifier among phenotype-dependent mechanisms, not the cause. They admit evidence cannot prove it drives the disease. Longitudinal and intervention studies, they say, must settle where it sits in the causal chain.
pmc-13333623:
For newborns with a rare heart defect, Shuo Chen and co-authors asked in a 2026 retrospective study whether gestational age at birth predicts short-term recovery after biventricular repair surgery. The defect is pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum.

The study covered 97 children treated at one referral center between 1999 and 2024, including 21 born preterm and 76 born at term. Each extra week of gestation cut the risk of a poor outcome by roughly half in adjusted analysis. A threshold appeared near 37.6 weeks, beyond which risk fell sharply compared with earlier births. The findings help surgical teams judge risk and counsel families when a baby with this rare heart defect is born early.
pmc-13333723:
Yongfu Wang, Li Yang, and Qiang Shi compared two ways to treat femur fractures that occur after surgery for developmental dysplasia of the hip in children, in a 2026 study. The options are elastic stable intramedullary nailing and hip spica casting.

From 396 children treated for hip dysplasia between July 2012 and July 2018, the team identified 18 with fractures after proximal femoral osteotomy. Ten received nailing and eight received casting, and the groups differed clearly in age and fracture pattern, which usually drives the choice. Hospital stay, surgery time, and complications were compared between groups. The small head-to-head series helps surgeons weigh an operation against casting for a rare but troublesome complication of dysplasia treatment.
pmc-13335023:
Calum Lindsay and co-authors designed a package of interventions for 'missingness' in healthcare in a 2026 study. Missingness means a repeated pattern of not taking up offered care, which tracks with multiple illnesses, precarious lives, and poor outcomes, while services often respond punitively.

The work braided three strands: a realist review of 253 documents, interviews with 61 informants who know missingness personally or professionally, and co-design with affected people. Together these produced a suite of interventions aimed at the specific, tangled causes that keep people from care, rather than at the missed appointments themselves. The authors argue that engaging with causes, instead of penalizing absence, is the only route that will not widen access inequalities for the patients who most need care.
pmc-13337123:
Jiaying Zhang leads a large 2026 team trapping an intermediate gas inside catalyst pores to make two-carbon products from carbon dioxide. Tandem catalysts split the job: silver sites make carbon monoxide, copper sites couple carbons. Letting the gas escape wastes it, so their silica framework confines it near copper instead.

Composition formed a volcano pattern, peaking at the version with 15 wt.% silver and 40 wt.% copper in the catalyst series. That version reached a top C2 Faradaic efficiency of 75.4% at −1.4 V in half-cell tests and kept 63.5% efficiency at high current in a full membrane device during the reported runs. Spectra and calculations confirmed spillover and confinement raise surface coverage and coupling speed.
pmc-13337423:
Emily Jones and Kiki Cano-Gamez review loose DNA as both driver and marker of lupus in a 2026 article. In systemic lupus, the immune system attacks self-DNA. Dying cells release cell-free DNA, normally cleared by the nuclease DNASE1L3. Its fragment lengths, end patterns, jaggedness, and chemical marks can signal disease activity.

When DNASE1L3 is missing or blocked by cross-reacting autoantibodies, DNA fragments grow more provocative. They fire interferon signaling through plasmacytoid dendritic cells, pushing B cells to make anti-DNA antibodies and worsening inflammation. The review ties these mechanisms to therapies targeting interferon and those dendritic cells, while warning that large-scale validation and standard tests are still needed for precision care.
pmc-13337523:
Wenyan Wang and colleagues profile 30 Chinese children with Gitelman syndrome, a salt-losing kidney tubule disorder, in a 2026 study spanning cases from 2015–2025. Onset came at a mean age of 7.9 years in the cohort, with muscle weakness in 50% of children and limb numbness in 40% of children in the symptom tally. Every child had low potassium, and 90% had low magnesium in blood tests.

Girls showed more limb numbness and lower calcium. Very low potassium tracked with tetany, blood fat changes, and higher urinary potassium loss. Genetic testing found 55 variants in the SLC12A3 gene, 6 of them novel, led by two frequent changes. Which protein domain a variant hit did not predict symptoms, so the authors urge early screening and long follow-up.
pmc-13338723: Keda Cao and co-authors issued a 2026 correction. It covers only the funding note of a study on jaw deformity care. The note was wrong as printed. Support had in fact been received. Three named programs in Shaanxi and China gave the grants. The corrected note lists them. The rest of the study stands unchanged.
pmc-13341423:
Tracking electric fish in three dimensions without disturbing them is the goal of a 2026 methods study by Reynaldo D. Pinto and colleagues. Weakly electric fish are nocturnal, so filming light can distort the natural behavior neuroethologists want to observe.

Working with Gymnotus carapo in a deep tank, the team combined a multi-camera setup with an electrode array around the tank. Deep learning rebuilt skeletal paths from video with accuracy near 0.8 mm per coordinate. The authors then simulated the fish's self-made electric field under three charge models and compared the output with real recordings, a first step toward locating fish from their own signals alone.
pmc-13341523:
Natural products for childhood psoriasis are reviewed by Zitong Wang and colleagues in the 2026 paper focused on the immune microenvironment. Standard systemic drugs raise safety worries in children, motivating interest in plant extracts, active components, and compound formulas.

These products appear to reshape lesion immunity by adjusting T cell subsets, cytokine networks, innate immune cells, and skin barrier integrity. The authors carefully separate evidence from pediatric studies, adult studies, and lab models, since much of the promise still rests on the latter two. Their roadmap points to trials designed for children rather than borrowed adult dosing.
pmc-13343223:
Hasan Ünver and co-authors examine childhood trauma, discomfort with uncertainty, and symptom severity in obsessive-compulsive disorder in a 2026 study. Trauma is common in OCD, yet its link to how bad symptoms get has been uneven, so the team tested whether intolerance of uncertainty carries part of that link.

Eighty-two patients and 82 matched healthy controls completed trauma, uncertainty, and severity scales. Patients scored higher on every trauma type and on uncertainty measures, and physical abuse was the only trauma type tied to severity inside the patient group. Path analysis showed uncertainty partly carried the trauma effect: once it entered the model, the direct trauma link faded. Easing uncertainty fears may personalize OCD care.
pmc-13345823:
Shalander Kumar and co-authors map the groundnut value chain of Senegal through group model building in 2026. Peanut farming covers about 1.25 million hectares and feeds rural livelihoods, yet weak seed supply, price swings, and idle processors drag it down, so the team paired a 503-farmer survey with stakeholder workshops in Dakar.

Survey answers flagged poor seed access for 86.77 percent of farmers and climate losses for 75.88 percent, alongside unstable prices. Workshop diagrams exposed traps: a low-productivity seed loop, processors squeezed by foreign traders while the national firm runs near a third of capacity, and tangled subsidy and export rules. Fixes range from breeder seed investment to price stabilization and smarter export timing.
pmc-13346323:
Vincent Vander Poorten and a large review team assess ways to help people with head and neck cancer stop smoking, in a systematic review from 2026. Continued smoking after diagnosis worsens treatment results and survival, so the team searched five databases for trials of quitting support in this patient group.

Eleven studies with 1,593 patients in total met the entry rules, covering counselling, drug aids such as varenicline and nicotine replacement, and digital or service-level tools. Quit rates ranged from 23.9 to 74 percent across studies, with combined counselling, drugs, and follow-up doing best, especially near diagnosis. Differences among studies blocked a pooled analysis, so tailored combined care is the main message.
pmc-13348023:
Xuhui Lin and colleagues propose judging orbital diagrams in place rather than in isolation, in a concepts account published in 2026. Classic diagrams line up frontier orbitals of lone reactants and products. Yet neighbours and fields can shift orbital energies sharply before any bonding starts, which leaves some reactions poorly explained by a few lone orbitals.

Their in situ view uses a block-localised wave method, the simplest form of valence bond theory, to price each molecule orbitals while other species sit nearby with push, pull, and crowding included. Worked cases show levels reshuffling under those physical effects alone, giving chemists a truer start point for reading reaction paths and molecular traits.
pmc-13348823:
Kiersten S Bell and colleagues trace when daily clock rhythms appear in the developing mouse brain, in a study from 2026. Male and female pups on a set light cycle were sampled from day 1 to day 24 for three clock genes in the master clock, memory. Control brain areas, plus immune tissues and blood hormone pulses.

Rhythms showed in hormone levels and every brain area, growing stronger and settling toward adult timing by day 24 in the reported pattern. Two immune border tissues showed clock swings by mid development. While isolated microglia showed no clock swing yet still ate particles on a daily rhythm, so function can tick before genes visibly do.
pmc-13349923:
Yihao Cui and colleagues mapped 20 years of research on Suaeda, a salt-tolerant plant genus, in a 2026 bibliometric study. They compared Chinese-language and international literature from 2005 to 2025 using databases from both spheres and CiteSpace software.

Publication counts rose overall with periodic dips, and China ranked first in output and in network centrality. Keyword and collaboration patterns traced how topics such as salt marsh ecology and use of the plant as a resource grew and shifted. Suaeda thrives on salty coasts and inland soils where crops fail, so the field matters for land restoration. The study shows where Chinese and world research meet and diverge.
pmc-13350323:
Sarah Parry and a large team set out a study protocol in 2026 for evaluating a joint crisis response for young people in mental distress. The service pairs police officers with mental health practitioners, aiming to answer rising and complex crises better than either service alone.

Their evaluation blends realist methods, which ask what works for whom and why, with cost analysis, immersive theatre, and co-production with families. Children aged 5 to 18, carers, and practitioners across five areas will contribute surveys, interviews, and service records. The goal is a full programme theory that other regions can use when designing crisis care for the young.
pmc-13350523:
Eric Biney and colleagues reviewed seaweed-derived sugars as salt helpers in coated frozen foods in a 2026 systematic review of work from 2005 to 2025. Battered fish, nuggets, and fried potato items carry much of the salt in processed diets, driving blood pressure and heart disease worldwide.

Alginate fragments from brown seaweed can shape batter structure, hold water, and support flavour perception when salt is cut. Most studies found used ordinary alginate gels rather than the smaller fragments, leaving the specific evidence thin. The review sorts mechanism from marketing so food makers can judge whether these ingredients truly ease sodium reduction.
pmc-13351523:
Qingbin Guo and fellow editors introduced a 2026 research collection on new vaccine strategies against parasitic diseases. Parasites cause immense harm around the world. Malaria alone brought an estimated 263 million cases in 2023, with nearly 597,000 deaths that year. Neglected diseases and livestock infections add heavily to the toll. Drug resistance keeps eroding standard treatments.

The collection holds ten pieces, nine research articles and one review. Older vaccines used single surface proteins or killed organisms, and they rarely gave lasting protection across strains, beaten by complex life cycles and immune evasion. The editors back carefully designed next-generation approaches as the lasting route to control.
pmc-13351623:
Mingxue Zhang and co-authors share early experience from 2026 with oral drugs that raise platelet production in children with immune thrombocytopenia. Newer agents such as hetrombopag have little real-world data in children whose illness returned after first treatment. Records for 18 children treated at Qingdao Women and Children's Hospital from January 2023 to June 2024 were reviewed.

Platelet counts rose after treatment began, with clear gains at week 1 and at months 1, 3, and 6. Bleeding scores, though, did not improve in a clear way for the group. Most side effects were mild or moderate. Given the small size and mixed drug use, the authors treat the results as early signals that need prospective testing.
pmc-13352623:
Jan Luxa and colleagues pattern graphene oxide with a focused copper ion beam in 2026. Ion beams offer a clean, mask-free way to tune graphene oxide in chosen spots, unlike chemical reduction. Free-standing foils were blasted with copper ions, then checked by microscopy, spectroscopy, and electrochemical scanning.

Bombardment partly reduced the oxide, lowering oxygen content and raising graphitic character. Electrochemical activity jumped in and around the struck stripes when probed with a ruthenium redox marker. Local thinning and fresh reactive edges, rather than surface sticking, best explain the gain. Element signals confirmed the pattern's structural origin. The method writes active zones at nanoscale without reagents, a useful tool for custom sensors.
pmc-13353223:
Mohmmed Tauseef Sharip leads a 2026 real-world cohort study of mirikizumab in ulcerative colitis, split by prior ustekinumab use. Trial data excluded patients who had taken ustekinumab, leaving a practical gap. Treatment persistence at 3 months was 72 percent, with no clear gap between groups. Symptom scores fell from 5.8 at baseline down to 3.3 at the 3-month review visit. Faecal calprotectin dropped from 1094 to 586 micrograms per gram over the same span. Scope scores improved from a mean of 4.4 before induction down to 2.7 after induction had ended. Prior ustekinumab did not blunt response in adjusted models.
pmc-13353823:
Dillon C Mobasser, Alex N Kerendi, and Foad Nahai review clonidine for preventing blood collections after aesthetic face surgery in 2026. Bleeding under the skin is the top major complication of face and neck lifts, driven by pressure spikes and sympathetic surges after surgery. Clonidine, a central alpha-2 agonist, has entered facelift routines to steady pressure and blunt those surges.

Drug action, bleeding biology, and clinical evidence are reviewed alongside dosing plans, contraindications, and safety notes from practice. Within a full pressure-control routine, clonidine looks safe and helpful for bleeding prevention. Support, though, rests mostly on retrospective series and expert views at Level IV evidence, so the authors counsel measured use.
pmc-13355023:
Jon G Dean and co-authors set out a 2026 trial plan on how mindfulness meditation eases long-term low back pain in the brain. Such pain is a top cause of disability and often resists drug care. Earlier work hints that meditation calms self-focused and emotional brain circuits, but the direct brain path was unclear.

The trial enrolled 120 adults with back pain who had never meditated, split among real mindfulness, sham mindfulness, and book listening groups. Sessions ran over two weeks, with brain blood flow scans before and after during a leg raise that triggers pain. The team will compare brain and pain changes to single out effects tied to true mindfulness.
pmc-13355723:
Qianzi Wang and co-authors modeled in 2026 how worker movement softens the economic harm of workplace heat stress in China. Heat cuts worker output, and losses ripple through supply chains, but yearly models miss daily detail and worker flows. Their model used daily movement data across 313 Chinese cities to trace these ripples.

Yearly heat stress cost China about 2.6 percent of GDP, with supply chain spread driving most losses. Worker inflows to hot, industrial southeast regions offset local output drops, saving billions directly and more through the chain. Under a 2030 warming path, losses grow sharply, but paired industry and work-hour changes could cut them by about 30 percent.
pmc-13358523:
Hongjiang Liu and co-authors compare two ways to mark small lung spots before surgery in a 2026 study. Doctors must find tiny nodules deep in the lung so surgeons can remove them. One method steers a scope with magnetic guidance; the other uses a robot. The team asked how fast one surgeon learns each method.

They reviewed 120 patients treated from 2024 to 2025, half with each method, all by the same surgeon. Using a tracking method that charts case times in order, they found the point where each technique became smooth and steady. Such learning curves help hospitals plan training when they bring in costly new gear.
pmc-13358623:
Lucas Wilhelm and co-authors present a 2026 study on forecasting lung power after a partial lung operation. When surgeons remove one segment of lung for a nodule, patients lose some breathing strength. A scan that maps blood flow through the lungs helps predict that loss after larger removals, but its worth after segment removal was unclear.

They studied 51 patients who had the blood flow scan before planned segment surgery. Six months later they compared the real drop in a key breathing measure with what the scan and other methods had forecast. A sharper forecast helps patients weigh surgery against other options and plan recovery with open eyes.
pmc-13358823:
Dennis Aliev and co-authors test a training body for chest nerve surgery in a 2026 study. Cutting a chain of nerves in the chest can cure severe sweating and related disorders, but the surgeon must know the chain's exact layout and its variant side paths. Practice on real tissue is ideal, yet costly and often poor in quality.

The team dissected one female body donor preserved with a special fluid called Modified Larssen Solution. The fluid kept tissues lifelike, and the nerve chain, its branches, and side paths showed clearly. They also weigh cost and pitfalls. A cheaper, faithful training body could help more surgeons learn this delicate operation safely.
pmc-13360623:
Federica Lina Salamone led a 2026 cell study on quercetin, a plant compound found in common foods. Cells can age early when stress damages them, a process tied to aging and brain disease. The team used nerve-like cells grown in the lab and stressed them with hydrogen peroxide to force early aging. Some cells then received quercetin at two low doses.

Quercetin is known for fighting cell stress and calming inflammation, so the team checked whether it could protect the nerve-like cells. They tracked signs of aging such as cell-cycle halt, lasting DNA damage, and the release of irritating signals aged cells send out. Work like this tests whether a common food compound might one day help slow brain cell aging. The authors treat it as an early lab step, not a treatment.
pmc-13362323:
Kuluve Chotso and co-authors read the whole genome of a little-studied Indian cattle breed in a 2026 study. The Arunachali mithun is a semi-domesticated bovine central to the culture and economy of tribal communities in Northeast India. It is among the least mapped large farm animals, leaving conservation without genetic grounding. The team sequenced 11 animals and kept nearly five million high-quality gene variants for analysis.

The breed showed moderate genetic diversity, clearly lower than in commercial cattle. The animals carried fewer mixed gene copies than chance predicts, a deficit pointing to inbreeding. Several independent measures put inbreeding at a moderate level. These numbers give conservationists their first firm base for breeding plans that protect this culturally prized animal.
pmc-13362723:
Marek Szołtysik and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on why high-protein dairy powders cake, clump, and lose their easy mixing during storage. These powders, from whey and milk protein lines, fill sports and medical foods. Their protein-rich glassy grains shift with heat and moisture, and once grains stick, lumps grow and the powder no longer dissolves well in water.

The review ties the slide from sticky surfaces to hard cakes to grain mobility, water uptake, and protein and mineral links between grains. It separates clumping done on purpose at the factory from unwanted storage clumping, which follows other rules. Gaps remain in tracking surface change under real warehouse conditions, and the authors propose a mobility-based map to guide makers.
pmc-13363823:
Gabriele Fassina and colleagues present a 2026 validation study of the Azure Kinect camera for tracking arm and shoulder movement in rehab settings. Marker-free cameras promise cheap, quick motion checks versus lab systems with body markers. Sixteen healthy adults performed ten upper-body tasks in three setups: ideal, seated with a table blocking the view, and a longer camera distance, while a gold-standard light system recorded the truth.

The camera tracked movements in its own plane well, with error staying low even in the awkward setups. Movements toward or away from the camera fared poorly. Range of motion reads were solid and repeatable, but timing and smoothness scores strayed. The authors advise care with camera placement and further tests in patients.
pmc-13364323:
Sai Wan and co-workers present MSA-DET in 2026, a net for finding ships in radar images from space. Radar views carry speckle noise, messy coasts, and ships of vastly unlike size. Their design adds focus blocks that scan in two ways at once and a head that blends scale views by learned weights.

On two ship data sets the net beat its base model by clear gaps on both strict and loose scores. The cost was a larger model and more compute. The trade may suit coast watch work, where missed small ships carry real risk.
pmc-13374023:
Helena R. Loan and co-authors read tin signals to probe a lone pair of electrons in a 2026 study. The frames in view hold tin in a state that keeps a spare pair, which warps its space. That warp shows as a wide spread in magnet reads.

Six tin frames were read with new spin tricks that can catch very wide spreads. Sums from first rules were set next to the reads. The sums matched the core read well but fell short on the spread each time. That miss tells sum makers where their models of the lone pair need work. Truer sums would help design new frames.
pmc-13378023:
Jacob A Orkwis and co-authors read worm takes on a human fire part in a 2026 study. Gut worms make kin of a human part that fans fire, and they use them as arms in the host. Such arms could be hit to lift worm loads, a wide ill.

The team found a wide set of the kin in worm code banks and checked their shapes. A picked set then faced man-made tests: work acts, grip to the part's own port, and talk through two more ports. The kin kept the core shape yet gave wide acts from small shifts. That spread is the tale of how worms tune man's fire.
pmc-13380723:
S Brown, E Best, and A Kirby wrote a 2026 letter on drug-resistant gut bacteria found in waste water inside a hospital building. Resistant bacteria living in patients are linked to hospital drains and sink traps, which can release them back onto wards through blockages or fine sprays. Most earlier work followed outbreaks in intensive care units.

Their study, at a large teaching hospital trust in Leeds in July 2024, looked beyond intensive care. Samples were taken throughout one hospital building to check for bacteria resistant to commonly used antibiotics, not only the most feared types. Finding such bacteria matters because routine prevention may be missing routes by which they reach patients.
pmc-13380823:
Claire C Russell and colleagues describe a 2026 case where a special stain revealed the cause of gut bleeding in a woman with amyloidosis. In this disease, misfolded protein chains deposit in organs and can make gut vessels fragile. Their patient was a 65-year-old woman whose disease already affected her heart and kidneys.

She arrived passing blood from the bowel. An early camera examination found a large clot but no active bleeding. Days later the bleeding returned heavily, and samples taken from an ulcer at the clot site were examined. The title refers to the Congo Red stain used to prove amyloid in tissue. The case shows why this disease belongs on the list of bleeding causes.
pmc-13382523:
Vanessa Vento, Luis Cabeza-Osorio, and Erika Esperanza Lozano-Rincon present a 2026 case series, written in Spanish, on infections that follow BCG therapy placed directly into the bladder. That treatment is the standard add-on for bladder cancer that has not invaded muscle. Infections from it are uncommon but can be severe and take many forms.

Four cases treated at their centre between 2019 and 2025 illustrate the range. Diagnosis is hard because standard cultures and DNA tests detect the organism in only a minority of cases. The first case involved a 77-year-old man who developed testicle pain and low fever after his second treatment, with all cultures negative. The series underlines clinical suspicion as key.
pmc-13383223:
Yuzhou Zhang and colleagues hunt blood proteins linked to future cataract in a 2026 UK Biobank cohort study. Nearly 49,581 adults without cataract at the start took part, and 2,920 plasma proteins were tested against later disease. Genetic methods then probed which links might be causal rather than mere markers.

Fifty-eight proteins tied significantly to cataract risk, led by a lens protein, beta-crystallin B2, with the strongest signal. Genetic analyses supported causal roles for four proteins, with the lens protein backed by shared genetic evidence. Pathway results pointed to immune activity, cell fate choices, and tissue remodeling as routes worth targeting for early prevention.
pmc-13385423:
Bao Q. Thai and colleagues trace how WNT signals prepare stem cells to form hormone-responsive gut-layer tissue in 2026 work. Human pluripotent stem cells can supply immune cells for therapy, but only through the right early tissue steps. Early WNT activation pushed cells toward a marked mesoderm type needed for later T cell growth.

Single-cell gene and chromatin maps charted the path, and network models fingered the regulator HDAC2. Removing HDAC2 blocked the key step, adding more of it boosted yields, and blocking it with drugs had the same blocking effect. The findings suggest practical ways to raise lymphocyte output from stem cells.
pmc-13385723:
Ayesha Kafeel and colleagues examine how a desert shrub copes with salt and drought across sites near Sargodha, Pakistan, in 2026 work. Capparis decidua thrives in arid lands, but populations face differing local stress mixes. Samples from Shahpur faced the strongest salinity, while Chak 48 NB offered richer soil organic matter.

Shahpur plants grew tallest with the longest roots, thicker skin layers, and more support tissue for holding water. Their light-protecting pigments ran higher while chlorophyll stayed stable under stress. Grouping analysis split Shahpur cleanly from the other sites, which the authors read as a stress-adapted trait suite worth probing at molecular level.
pmc-13387423:
Ankita Shrivastava and a large team map selective protein production under mutant KRAS control in 2026 work. Mutant KRAS drives many cancers, yet how it steers which messages get translated stayed poorly defined. The team charted KRAS-dependent translation programs and how they remodel fast when KRAS is blocked.

A chosen message subset, including messages for the protein-making machinery itself, answered to KRAS in their data. Those messages share short, weakly folded leader regions and low-energy sequence motifs. Ribosomes piled up on the selected messages, which the authors read as a distinct control route apart from known mTOR and initiation factor paths.
pmc-13388423:
Stefania Morelli and colleagues present a careful sequencing workflow in 2026 for naming species from tiny amounts of badly damaged DNA. The method was built for hard cases in ecology, wildlife crime work, museum study, and efforts to protect rare species, where old material often leads to false matches.

The workflow combines very small sampling, special library preparation, removal of duplicate reads, mapping against a chosen set of reference genomes. A final check then separates reads unique to one species from reads shared across close relatives. Tests on collagen-rich material showed correct identification from pieces as small as one square millimetre, even in mixtures. Readers gain a cautious approach that favours accuracy over speed.
pmc-13391223:
Dave K Garg and Jeffrey Wei report, in 2026, substantial weight loss with a daily diabetes injection in a young man with a rare genetic obesity syndrome. Smith-Magenis syndrome drove excessive hunger and rapid weight gain despite portion control and behaviour support over five years.

With prediabetes, abnormal lipids, and fatty liver emerging, the team started liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, and raised it gradually to the maximum dose over five months. The patient tolerated it without severe stomach side effects and, with lifestyle support, lost a large amount of weight over eleven months. Endocrine readers gain a single-case signal that appetite-targeting drugs can work even when obesity has a strong genetic driver.
pmc-13392423:
Dimakopoulou and colleagues test whether virtual reality can soften food avoidance in anorexia nervosa, in 2026 neuroscience research. Women with anorexia, 29 patients, and 31 controls completed sessions: a baseline plus illusion sessions in VR where they embodied avatars slimmer or larger. Each session measured responses to food images in a binocular rivalry task, and approach-avoidance behavior toward high- and low-calorie foods. It measured body-size guesses and questionnaires.

At the start, patients showed salience of, and stronger avoidance toward, high-calorie foods than controls, matching the disorder's pattern. Embodying a larger avatar attenuated that bias in patients, while controls shifted the reverse way under the same trick. The manipulation transiently rewired implicit food biases in opposite directions depending on group. Dimakopoulou suggests body-illusion therapy might loosen the automatic bias that sustains it, a possible adjunct to treatment worth testing.
pmc-13392623:
Mengying Xiao and co-authors describe a 70-year-old woman whose slipped lumbar disc was treated with a hook-shaped needle worked beside the spine under local anaesthetic. She had lived with on-and-off back pain for more than ten years, then developed leg pain and numbness over two weeks. Scans showed herniations at two low levels plus a loose fragment pressing the nerve.

After the needle procedure her pain scores fell sharply, walking returned to normal, and leg strength recovered fully over follow-up. Later imaging showed the loose fragment had vanished, and no relapse appeared within a year. The authors are careful to note that such fragments often shrink on their own, so one case cannot prove the needle caused the change, and controlled trials would be needed.
pmc-13393523:
Hiram H Plata-Huerta and five colleagues watched for patulous Eustachian tube after bariatric surgery. In this ear condition the pressure tube stays open. Rapid weight loss has been blamed for it in earlier reports. Fifty-two patients having bypass or sleeve operations were examined before surgery, just after, and at three months, using Japanese diagnostic criteria plus a standard symptom questionnaire. Average weight loss by three months was substantial.

No patient met the bar for definite disease at any visit. Possible cases crept up from about a tenth before surgery to just under a quarter at three months, a shift that did not reach significance, and symptom scores stayed flat. Weight loss size did not track ear outcomes. The authors suspect earlier high rates reflect loose diagnostic standards, and they recommend symptom-driven checks over routine screening early after surgery.
pmc-13393723:
Rafael Hortêncio Melo and Chiara Robba argue that transcranial Doppler ultrasound, a bedside probe of blood flow speed inside the brain, can personalise blood pressure targets after acute brain injury. Standard care chases fixed perfusion pressure thresholds, yet the right pressure likely differs by patient and hour as vessel resistance and self-regulation shift. Doppler measures such as diastolic flow velocity and the pulsatility index expose how the brain's circulation answers each pressure change.

Watching those signals while clinicians adjust arterial pressure in controlled steps could reveal the range where an individual's brain perfusion looks healthiest. The authors insist Doppler never be read alone: cardiac output, fluid responsiveness, and the cause of low pressure belong in the same picture, inside multimodal monitoring. They present the piece as a viewpoint mapping rationale, uses, and current limits.
pmc-13394723:
Yi Zhen Bao and colleagues review, in 2026, a young method for testing the lining of brain blood vessels in people. The method watches the neck artery widen when extra carbon dioxide raises brain blood flow. That widening reflects nitric oxide from the vessel lining, much like a known arm test. Early studies have tried the method after exercise, in heat and cold, and across ages and sexes.

Some results match the arm test, while others break away, such as with smoking or long sitting. The review weighs the two ways of raising gas levels and the hitches in each. The authors sketch next steps toward clinic use.
pmc-13395423:
Lisa A. Niemann leads a 2026 account of how bedside nucleic acid tests for HIV were rolled out in Seattle. Such tests catch infection earlier than antibody kits and give virus counts on the spot. The study ran at a hospital clinic and a community centre from 2022 to 2024. People seeking tests or prevention drugs, and people living with HIV, joined different arms.

More than seven hundred people completed study visits. Each got standard care plus a bedside test and lab checks for comparison. Subsets answered surveys and interviews on how the tests felt. Staff also timed clinic flow. The authors lay out the full protocol as a model for wider rollout studies.
pmc-13396423:
Prateek D. T. and co-authors compared the prices of branded and generic creams for skin fungal infections in India, in a 2026 pharmacoeconomic study. These infections, called superficial mycoses, are common in tropical climates, need long treatment, and often return, so the price of each tube matters to households.

The authors gathered prices for the same antifungal drugs across many brands and measured the spread between the cheapest generic and the costliest branded twin. Wide gaps for identical medicine mean doctors can cut a patient's bill sharply by prescribing choice alone. The study frames antifungal pricing as a resource question for clinics as much as a shopping question for patients.
pmc-13396623:
Junaid Younus is the lead author of a 2023 RSC Advances study on tuning nickel sulphide films with zinc for solar uses. The Royal Society of Chemistry wholly retracted that study in a 2026 notice. The publisher states that concerns over the reliability of the data forced the withdrawal.

Two microscope images in the paper had already appeared elsewhere, described there as a different material. Two pairs of light-absorbance charts also looked strongly alike across figures that should have shown separate results. The authors replied and supplied new data, but the response did not settle the concerns. The original raw data could not be produced, so the retraction covers the whole article.
pmc-13396723:
Yanjiao Liang and co-authors fed a Chinese herbal mixture to chickens infected with H9N2 bird flu and measured whether the blend fights the virus and calms the inflammation it causes. Their 2026 study uses specific pathogen-free chickens, a clean test population for a virus that costs poultry farms heavily and can infect people.

Vaccines lose ground as the virus surface keeps drifting, so alternatives are in demand. Birds given the Siji antiviral mixture carried far less virus in liver, spleen, lung, kidney, brain, and windpipe than untreated infected birds. The mixture also turned down the excessive inflammatory response the infection provokes, a dual action the authors back with tissue-level measurements.
pmc-13396923:
Jiaxin Zheng and co-authors review how labs measure acylcarnitines, a family of molecules that ferry fatty acids into mitochondria, in a 2026 article. Best known from newborn screening for inherited metabolic faults, these markers now show promise in heart disease, diabetes, and drug injury.

Measuring them well is hard: family members span a wide range of water-loving and fat-loving behavior, their levels differ by orders of magnitude, and near-identical isomers hide among them. The review tours sample preparation and detection platforms, with liquid chromatography at the center, and weighs where each method strains. A closing section maps clinical uses that better measurement could unlock.
pmc-13397523:
Jessica Berns, Justin L Anderson and Detlev Erdmann reviewed the portal messages sent to one plastic surgeon at Duke University Hospital. Their 2026 study spans 18 months, from July 2023 through December 2024. Secure messaging helps patients stay in touch, but each note adds work, and plastic surgeons also face pressure from public ratings.

Every message was logged by topic, timing and patient details, then stored in a secure REDCap database for study. Patterns in the inbox show what patients most often ask before and after surgery. Spotting the common themes points to clearer handouts and pre-visit guidance, which could trim message load while keeping patients informed and doctors less strained.
pmc-13397823:
Jianqing Li and a large team scan the protein-coding genome for genes that shape the retina and its diseases. Their 2026 study uses whole-exome data from 356,982 UK Biobank participants. The retina is a reachable outpost of the brain, yet the coding variants behind its structure, its function and its blinding diseases were only sketchily known.

Gene-level tests of rare variants found 22 strong links across 16 genes, 12 of them new, with most backed in a second cohort of 245,388 people. Common variant scans added 243 independent signals in 126 genes. Three genes (CFI, C3 and RIOX1) touched structure, function and disease alike, and a new gene, FYB2, was picked for lab follow-up.
pmc-13399323:
Pattara Kanoksing and colleagues genotyped adults with asthma to see which cytokine gene variants track with the disease's inflammatory patterns, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Asthma driven by type 2 inflammation depends heavily on interleukin-4, interleukin-5, and interleukin-13. These proteins drive allergy responses and eosinophil production. Inherited changes in their genes influence asthma, but links to specific patterns needed clarifying.

The study enrolled 125 adults and tested seven variants across the IL33, IL4, IL5, and IL13 genes. One IL5 variant, rs2069812, stood out. Each extra copy of its T version raised eosinophil counts in a dose-like pattern and lowered post-bronchodilator lung function. Carriers faced more than double the prevalence of blood eosinophilia in the reported analysis. An IL13 variant, rs1800925, was tied to higher Th2 cell counts and fixed airflow obstruction. The authors propose both variants as markers for sorting asthma patients into precise treatment groups.
pmc-13399523:
Haein Kim, Seungwon Shin, and Kuo-Cherh Huang analyzed a decade of national insurance claims to show how South Korea's long-term care hospitals have quietly become end-of-life settings, in a 2026 study. The team built three views from claims filed between 2014 and 2023: yearly inpatient trends, profiles of newly admitted patients, and the final trajectories of patients who died.

Deaths involving a long-term care hospital stay climbed from 68,357 in 2014 to 112,157 in 2023. New patients typically arrived in their early eighties, at a median age of 81, and 62.1 percent were women in the admission profile. Those who died had spent a median of 79 days as inpatients, and 68.5 percent of them died inside the hospital itself. The authors call for palliative care and advance planning to be built into these hospitals.
pmc-13400223:
Hidemasa Yoneda and colleagues built a planning method that lets surgeons, without an engineer's help, measure the three-dimensional twist in a child's elbow that healed crooked, in a 2026 methods study. Their framework mirrors the healthy humerus from CT and superimposes the proximal segments. It defines coordinate systems from a centroid plus anatomical landmarks, then computes the deformity three ways: as a wedge osteotomy rotation, as a full 3D rotation, and as a coronal-plane-only correction.

Validation used CT scans from five patients with extra-articular malunion. The full 3D methods barely cared which landmarks were picked: across all twenty-one landmark pairings from seven candidate points, median within-patient ranges stayed below 0.02 degrees for every rotational component. The coronal components matched the simple single-plane method within three degrees in all patients. The authors conclude the method is robust enough for routine surgical decision-making.
pmc-13400423:
Mohammad Iqbal Nouyed and colleagues test, in 2026, how well ChatGPT handles mental health warning signs hidden in skin complaints. People with skin disease often face anxiety or depression, and some beliefs about infestation reflect psychosis. An overly agreeable chatbot might miss danger or even reinforce false beliefs.

The team fed the chatbot 50 short patient stories, section by section, and repeated each run three times. Psychiatrists had judged which stories needed referral. Focusing on 28 clear cases, the chatbot voiced concern in most chats yet advised mental health follow-up in only about half. It almost always advised skin follow-up instead. In some delusional cases it even suggested collecting specimens, which could entrench false beliefs.
pmc-13400523:
Abdulmohsin J Alamoudi reviews, in 2026, plant compounds that may calm overactive NMDA receptors in the brain. These receptors help learning and memory, but overstimulation floods nerve cells with calcium. That excitotoxic process drives damage in stroke, epilepsy, brain injury and degenerative disease.

Compounds from several plant families are surveyed, including vitexin, ginsenosides, quercetin, resveratrol, huperzine A and bilobalide. Studies suggest they can block the receptor directly, target one of its subunits, or lower its production. Many also ease inflammation, oxidative stress and cell death pathways downstream. The author presents these natural products as a rich source for future brain-protective drug design, while noting most evidence is early and experimental.
pmc-13400723:
Ulrich Schreiber, Ivan Bobkov and Marc Nowaczyk report, in 2026, unusual light responses in isolated photosystem II complexes from a heat-loving cyanobacterium. Photosystem II is the water-splitting core of photosynthesis. A new fluorometer let them watch chlorophyll glow changes during ultra-short bright flashes in two ways at once.

Freshly prepared complexes showed exceptionally high fluorescence ratios, near the theoretical ceiling. Regular oscillations with periods of four and two flashes appeared under certain chemical conditions, reflecting the stepwise cycle of the water-splitting machinery. A fast quenching process briefly lowered the glow and relaxed within microseconds. The authors dissect that quenching into donor-side and pigment triplet parts, refining how such signals should be read.
pmc-13400923:
Elizabeth Y X Leong and colleagues report, in 2026, a difficult case of orbital apex syndrome caused by several microbes at once in a woman with a weakened immune system. The syndrome strikes the nerves passing the eye socket tip, threatening vision and eye movement. Causes range from tumors to infection, and fungal disease is easy to miss.

The 70-year-old arrived with one-sided eye pain, headache and an early nerve palsy, then worsened over two weeks to complete eye paralysis and vision loss. Investigation found skull base bone infection reaching the orbital apex and cavernous sinus. Cultures grew four organisms, including a fungus and three bacteria. Six to eight weeks of targeted antimicrobial drugs followed, and the authors stress early imaging and tissue diagnosis.
pmc-13401323:
Ann-Christin Eliasson and a large team of co-authors present a 2026 study protocol called Full Speed Ahead, testing Frame Running plus goal-directed training for young children with cerebral palsy. Frame Running uses a wheeled support frame that lets children with limited walking move fast and train hard.

Early, intensive intervention matters while gross motor skills are developing, but solid evidence for early mobility programmes is still thin. The protocol uses a repeated-measures design with baseline, intervention, and follow-up phases. At least 18 children aged two to five years with cerebral palsy will take part. Outcomes centre on mobility in everyday life and cardiovascular health. The study aims to show whether combining the running frame with goal-directed gross motor practice improves daily activity at this young age.
pmc-13401523:
Seguchi and co-authors ask, in 2026, whether being treated by a board-certified medical oncologist improves survival in metastatic colorectal cancer, using Japan's SCRUM-Japan MONSTAR-SCREEN genomic screening cohort from 2019 to 2022. Among 2,184 patients overall, standard treatment uptake was nearly identical between the two physician groups, at 97.0 and 96.9 percent, setting up a test of what specialist care adds beyond protocol.

In the 358 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer, enrollment by a certified oncologist was associated with median survival of 36.5 months against 30.7 months for the others, a hazard ratio of 0.66 before fuller adjustment. The advantage persisted after adjusting for clinical factors, metastatic burden, and RAS and BRAF mutation status. They used molecular targeted therapy more often, in 89.5 percent of cases versus 80.4 percent for the others. The platform overall has enrolled over 10,000 patients across roughly 29 institutions.
pmc-13401723:
İbrahim Vasi and co-authors measure interleukin-40, a recently identified immune signal made mainly by activated B cells, in systemic sclerosis. B-cell dysfunction is central to this disease, yet this marker's behaviour in it was undefined. Their 2026 study compares blood levels in 41 patients and 29 matched healthy controls.

Levels differed significantly across three groups. Patients receiving immunosuppressive treatment had markedly lower interleukin-40 than both untreated patients and controls, while untreated patients resembled controls. The marker showed no significant link to skin subtype, lung involvement, swallowing problems, or disease activity, and the treatment pattern held regardless of activity status. The authors conclude interleukin-40 reflects treatment exposure and immune modulation rather than how active the disease is, while cautioning that only longitudinal studies can prove cause and effect.
pmc-13402023:
Meihan Guo and David Montero report in 2026 that whether raising the head during sleep boosts red blood cell production remains unknown, despite a plausible theory. More red blood cells raise oxygen delivery and endurance performance, and the authors had proposed that low chest blood volume during head-up sleep might trigger the hormone erythropoietin.

They tested twelve weeks of sleeping with the bed head raised forty centimetres, combined with increased water drinking, against increased drinking alone in healthy adults. Night-time heart rate rose in the early sleep hours for the head-up group, suggesting the intended reflex was engaged. Yet blood volumes, total red cell volume, and haemoglobin mass did not change in either group. Resting stroke volume rose in both groups. The authors conclude the intervention did not enhance red cell production under these conditions, so the question in their title stays open.
pmc-13402723:
Ting Xie and a large team survey the microbes living on tossed cigarette butts in city parks across 35 Chinese cities, treating the litter as a new urban habitat. Butts are everywhere yet barely studied as living space. Sampling butts alongside leaf litter and soil, the team combined long-read gene sequencing, metagenomics, and transcript readings to compare community makeup, function, and evolution across the three homes.

Butt communities proved strikingly uniform across cities, ruled by firm deterministic forces, and rich in Proteobacteria, especially the Pseudomonadaceae family. Their strategy leaned fast and responsive, unlike the slower, resource-gathering style of litter microbes. Genes in butt Pseudomonas showed stronger positive selection, and lab exposure of a model strain switched key functional genes upward. The authors frame butts as a human-made niche actively reshaping microbial life and evolution.
pmc-13402823:
Lin, Wang, Wilson, and Zhang present, in 2026, TraceBind, a computational framework that cleans up transcription factor footprinting from ATAC-seq data. It corrects the cutting bias of the Tn5 enzyme separately for every sample. Footprints, the protected shadows proteins cast in open-chromatin data, drown in false positives because Tn5 prefers certain DNA sequences. The team shows that bias varies between samples, a hidden batch effect.

TraceBind fine-tunes a cleavage model on each sample's mitochondrial DNA reads, then detects footprints across scales with false discovery control. Against the tool TOBIAS, its false positive rate fell by more than 60-fold on average in benchmark comparisons. Sensitivity stayed high against naked DNA controls, matched ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN data, and factor-degradation experiments. The footprints improved transcription factor activity inference and cell age prediction from single-cell data, and many high-confidence footprints escaped DNA foundation models.
pmc-13403023:
Peter O'Reilly and co-authors check whether final-year radiography students judge chest X-ray quality as consistently as experienced radiographers. Repeat exposures cost radiation, so shared quality standards matter. Working from 70 de-identified chest films taken during the COVID-19 pandemic at a Sydney teaching hospital, both groups scored positioning, sharpness, and visibility across pathology types. A consensus read by two radiologists set the reference.

No significant differences separated students from veterans in any domain or disease category. Bland-Altman checks showed students scoring a touch lower with narrow agreement limits, a caution bias rather than real discord. Overall reliability landed at an ICC of 0.90, in the good-to-excellent band. The authors, noting the single-center setting, conclude training already instills the structured criteria well by graduation.
pmc-13403523:
Huairuo Shi and co-authors studied in 2026 what dim blue light at night does to the spleen in mice fed a fatty diet. Light at night is now a common strain on body rhythms and immune health. Male mice lived under dim blue light in their dark phase for 12 weeks.

Their spleens shrank, immune cell growth slowed, and stress hormone levels climbed. Alarm and cell-stress signals in the spleen rose as protective signals fell. Drugs that blocked the stress hormone or its sensor eased part of the change. The work links night light, diet, and immune strain in one model.
pmc-13404623:
Anne J J The heads the Dutch-TIMELINESS project, a 2026 protocol to speed gallbladder surgery after bile duct stone treatment across the Netherlands. National guidance since 2016 advises removing the gallbladder within 72 hours of the duct-clearing procedure called ERCP. In practice, waits often run longer and complications follow.

All 61 Dutch hospitals doing this work take part. First, cases from January to March 2023 set a benchmark for each site. Each hospital then writes its own plan to meet the guideline, guided by its benchmark figures. A final phase from December 2025 to March 2026 checks the new routines with live monitoring. The goal is adherence of 85 percent or higher nationwide.
pmc-13404923:
Haley I Tupper, Yulei Angelina Gao and Amy L Cummings map lung cancer screening in California in a 2026 landscape analysis. Low-dose CT screening lowers deaths, yet California posts some of the lowest uptake in the United States. Gaps fall hardest on racial and ethnic minorities and poorer communities.

Their review of published and grey literature follows scoping review guidance and covers policy, care systems, delivery sites and risk patterns. Lung screening, they find, lacks supports that older programmes for breast, bowel and cervical cancer enjoy, such as firm federal frameworks and quality systems. Safety-net services carrying the highest-risk patients feature throughout. The report aims to show officials where investment could close the equity gap.
pmc-13405623:
Isabelle G Henshall and colleagues remove a major surface protein from the malaria parasite to test its true role, in 2026 work. PfMSP2 coats Plasmodium falciparum merozoites, the forms that invade red blood cells, and vaccine makers have long targeted it. Its actual job in invasion was unproven.

Gene editing deleted the protein from two parasite lines with no loss of growth or invasion ability in the lab. Surprisingly, antibodies against other invasion proteins then worked better, hitting their targets more strongly. Adding purified PfMSP2 blocked antibody binding to PfAMA1 in a dose-related way. The authors suggest the abundant protein shields the parasite from immune attack rather than driving invasion.
pmc-13406623:
Maria Kirillova and a large team expose rats to repeated low oxygen and examine their colons, in a 2026 study. Animals differ in natural tolerance to oxygen shortage, judged by three hypoxia genes in blood cells. Whether that tolerance shapes gut barrier and microbe changes was the question.

Rats breathed thin air equivalent to 5,000 or 7,000 metres altitude for one hour daily over twenty-one days. Under normal air, oxygen-sensitive rats already carried more mucus-producing goblet cells and fewer Parabacteroides bacteria. Exposure then pushed the colon and microbiome in different directions depending on starting tolerance and dose. Tissue staining and genetic microbe checks supply the evidence.
pmc-13407823:
Garrett R. Jackson and co-authors review, in 2026, using a camera probe inside the shoulder to investigate pain after shoulder replacement surgery. Pain, stiffness, or suspected infection after joint replacement is a hard problem. Keyhole inspection offers a low-invasive way to look and sometimes to treat. It applies across total, reverse, and partial replacements.

Reported uses span loose socket components, worn plastic, rotator cuff and biceps problems, stiffness, impingement, and suspected joint infection. Outcomes suggest relief for selected patients, especially after socket removal, biceps procedures, and releases of scar tissue. Tissue samples taken through the scope beat needle aspiration and blood markers for diagnosing infection. The authors detail entry strategies that protect the implant, while noting the scope cannot replace revision when failure is clear-cut.
pmc-13408123:
Dimitra Kanopoulou and co-authors review, in 2026, modern therapy for balance in children with Down syndrome, whose muscle, sensory, and nerve differences undermine postural control and everyday mobility. Searching two sources for randomised trials from 2015 to 2025, the team gathered fourteen trials with 462 patients testing everything from trampoline jumping to horse riding.

Options spanned isokinetic training, Pilates, dual-task exercise, whole-body vibration, foot strengthening, swimming, taping, and vestibular stimulation. Balance outcomes improved across a broad range of them, especially when layered onto standard therapy. Study quality ran fair to high. The authors back technology-assisted, task-oriented practice while demanding larger, longer, higher-quality trials before firm prescriptions, since follow-up in the current literature is short.
pmc-13409323:
Edward Lau and colleagues link Australian census and prescription records in 2026. They ask how often the other medicines an older person with dementia takes collide with a newly started antipsychotic, and what that costs. Over nine thousand people aged sixty-five and over who began one of five common antipsychotics were followed for ninety days. Interaction checking used a standard commercial database and counted severity and mechanism.

Three quarters of patients were exposed to at least one interaction, and nearly all of those were classed major in severity, most often involving other nervous-system drugs. One or more interactions came with a forty-three percent higher risk of death within ninety days. Two or more pushed the increase to about eighty percent. The authors argue interaction screening deserves the same seriousness as the decision to prescribe the antipsychotic itself.
pmc-13409823:
Rita Rocío Márquez-Díaz and colleagues present in 2026 a new scale that measures how caregivers feel about baby-led weaning. In that feeding style, babies feed themselves soft family foods instead of taking purées from a spoon. No checked tool existed for these views, so the team built one and tested it with Spanish caregivers.

Building the scale used past studies, expert review, and trial runs with caregivers. A group of 256 caregivers then completed the final version, while 92 more repeated it later to check stability. The 16 items fell into three groups: openness to the method, confidence in feeding, and hands-on skills. Scores held up well across checks of consistency and repeat testing.
pmc-13411023:
Eunhye Kim, Jae Hun Choi, Dae Soo Jung, and Yun Chan Kang report in 2026 a three-dimensional host that tames lithium metal in batteries. Lithium metal stores huge energy, yet it grows needle-like spikes and swells during charging, which ruins cells. A porous host can spread the metal out evenly.

The blend conducts well and welcomes lithium, so deposits formed smoothly without spikes. A protective skin rich in a helpful lithium compound also formed. Test cells ran over 1,300 hours with steady voltage, and full cells paired with a common cathode kept capacity well across 600 cycles.
pmc-13411223:
Apolline Blazer and a large team set out in 2026 a study plan for judging a program that helps breast cancer survivors return to work. Treatment leaves many women facing barriers from fatigue to inflexible jobs. The FASTRACS program aims to ease and sustain that return, and realism asks what works, for whom, and under which conditions.

Findings will be woven with trial numbers across five domains, from personal situation to how tools were used. Funding arrived in 2022, with final analyses due by the end of 2026.
pmc-13411323:
Jaqueline Martins Ramos and colleagues watch in 2026 nurses at work in women's health visits in Brazil, hunting for prevention skills in action. Sixty-nine taped visits by 22 nurses in four towns were scored for moves that promote health and ward off disease.

Birth control was offered in about three in ten visits, while advice on infections passed through sex appeared in under three percent. Screening followed set rules in nearly half the visits, and lifestyle advice in about a quarter. No steps to prevent later harm appeared at all, and no printed handouts were used. Better training and stronger backup are the fixes proposed, since nurses cannot carry prevention on goodwill alone.
pmc-13412023:
Macarena González-Dossi and colleagues confirm in 2026 that a parasitoid wasp, Campsomeriella whitelyi, lives farther south in Chile than records previously showed. Scoliid wasps hunt soil-dwelling beetle larvae, which makes them useful allies against farm pests. Earlier Chilean sightings of this species rested on mistaken identifications, so the team rechecked specimens by detailed body features and modelled where the climate and land suit it.

Confirmed records now place the wasp in the semi-arid farming landscapes of north-central Chile, among irrigated crops and sandy soils. The authors argue that careful name-checking, paired with habitat modelling, sharpens biodiversity maps. Verified presence also supports counting this native wasp in sustainable pest management plans.
pmc-13412323:
Ariel Zylberberg and colleagues reanalyze food-choice experiments in 2026 to test whether attention shapes decisions while they form, or merely mirrors them afterwards. Popular models claim looking at an item multiplies its value during choosing, which makes two testable predictions about final fixations and conflicted choices. The team checked those predictions against several existing eye-tracking datasets from snack choice tasks.

Neither prediction held up in the data they re-examined. A rival account, in which gaze patterns largely reflect a choice already made, explained the last-fixation bias, the gaze cascade, and how overall value speeds responses. One link between looking time and choice still escaped that account, so the authors conclude both processes probably run together.
pmc-13414423:
Luca Galassi and co-authors review in 2026 how to stop plaque squeezing through carotid stent struts during stenting, a mechanism behind strokes around the procedure.
